title: AI Use Log
text:
This log records uses of AI that influenced my portfolio.


Tool used: Claude (Anthropic)
Claude was used throughout Section 1 primarily as a learning and coding support tool. I used it to clarify concepts from the lecture notes, check my exercise answers, translate mathematical formulations into LaTeX, and help implement methods in R where I had first worked through the underlying formulas or pseudocode myself. It was also used to explain unfamiliar R functions and model output, and to assist with formatting my Section 1 workthrough.


I asked Claude to create interactive HTML revision files from the Section 1 notes. These summarised the key concepts and included questions that I could work through before revealing the answers.

Section 1A: Chapters 1–6
Section 1B: Conditional Variance Models
Section 1C: Spectral Analysis
Section 1 workthrough










AI-assisted area
How Claude was used
What I checked or did myself




Conceptual explanations
Claude was used to clarify concepts that I did not initially understand, including missing data in discrete and continuous time series, different realisations of a stochastic process, the frequency-domain view of a series, conditional variance models and spectral analysis.
I checked explanations against the lecture notes and used follow-up questions where necessary until I could explain and apply the concepts myself.


Mathematical notation and model formulations
Claude helped format model definitions and derivations in LaTeX and made the notation in my workthrough more consistent.
I checked the equations against the formulations in the notes before including them.


R implementation and exercises
Claude helped explain R functions and translate methods or pseudocode into R while I worked through the Section 1 exercises and tutorials.
I ran all code myself and checked the results against the theory, lecture material and expected model behaviour.


Conditional variance models
Claude explained ADF and KPSS testing, how to use the relevant R functions, how to interpret GARCH output, and helped write code for extracting model-selection quantities such as AIC and BIC.
I ran the tests and models myself and interpreted the results in the context of the exercises and lecture material.


Spectral analysis
Claude walked through the provided Spectral Analysis R tutorial line by line and explained concepts such as the Nyquist frequency and how to interpret a periodogram.
I checked that I could interpret the output myself and used the lecture notes or other course material where an AI explanation was insufficient.


Interactive revision files
Claude converted the lecture material into the three interactive HTML revision resources linked above, including summaries and self-test questions.
I checked the content against the notes and attempted the questions before viewing the answers.








Tool used: Claude (Anthropic)
Claude was used in Section 2 in a similar way to Section 1: primarily to help me understand new modelling frameworks, translate mathematical procedures or pseudocode into R, debug implementations and create interactive revision resources. Because Section 2 involved more algorithmic methods, particularly state-space models and Hidden Markov Models, I also used Claude to step through algorithms and explain how the mathematical formulation related to the code.


I asked Claude to create interactive HTML revision files from the Section 2 material, using the same approach as for Section 1. These were used as supplementary revision resources rather than replacements for the lecture notes.

Section 2: Exponential Smoothing
Section 2: State-Space Models
Section 2: Regression
Section 2: Hidden Markov Models










AI-assisted area
How Claude was used
What I checked or did myself




Conceptual explanations
Claude was used to clarify the relationship between exponential smoothing and state-space models, the role of observed and latent states, and how the different Section 2 modelling frameworks were connected.
I checked the explanations against the lecture material and made sure I could interpret the models independently before applying them.


Exponential smoothing
Claude helped connect the exponential-smoothing recursions to their state-space representation and assisted with coding implementations based on pseudocode.
I checked the recursions against the model formulation, ran the implementations and compared their behaviour with package-based results where appropriate.


State-space models and filtering
Claude was used to step through state-space notation and filtering procedures and to explain how sequential updating works computationally.
I worked through the calculations and checked that I understood the interpretation of the latent state, prediction and updating steps rather than relying only on generated code.


Regression and time-series errors
Claude assisted with explanations and implementation details where regression was combined with time-series structure, including how predictors and serial dependence should be handled.
I checked model specifications and output against the lecture material and interpreted the fitted relationships myself.


Hidden Markov Models
Claude explained the main HMM components and algorithms, including the forward recursion and Viterbi algorithm, and helped translate pseudocode into reusable R functions. This later formed the basis of the first-principles toolkit used in Project 4.
I checked the functions against the HMM equations and validated the implementation against package-based results where possible.


HMM software and diagnostics
Claude helped explain how to use depmixS4, fit models with different numbers of regimes, work with multiple starting values, assess parameter precision and implement model diagnostics such as pseudo-residuals.
I ran and compared the models myself, investigated poor solutions and used the statistical output and diagnostics to make the final modelling decisions.


Code debugging and streamlining
Claude assisted with debugging and reorganising repeated Section 2 code into clearer functions and workflows, particularly for algorithms that were later reused in Project 4.
I checked that refactoring did not change the numerical results and retained responsibility for the final implementations.


Interactive revision files
Claude generated the four Section 2 HTML revision resources linked above from the course material, including summaries and questions for self-testing.
I checked the material against the notes and used the resources to test and clarify my understanding.

title: AI Use Log
text:
Portfolio-wide AI assistance
In addition to the project-specific uses documented below, Claude (Anthropic) was used throughout the portfolio for spell-checking, grammar and wording improvements, LaTeX and Quarto formatting, and periodic checks against the portfolio guidelines. Statistical interpretations and final modelling decisions remained my responsibility.

title: AI Use Log
text:
Project 1
Tool used: Claude (Anthropic)









AI-assisted task
How Claude was used
What I checked or did myself




Data-access instructions
Claude helped me locate and understand how to access the electricity-demand data required for the project.
I accessed the data myself, checked that the required period and variables were present and documented the data source used in the project.


Reading the data into R
Claude assisted with the R code required to import the data, parse dates and place the series into a form suitable for time-series analysis.
I ran the import code, checked the date range, observation frequency and resulting values against the source data.


Initial data-quality checks
Claude helped write code to check missing observations, duplicated dates/observations and other basic data-quality issues.
I inspected the identified issues and decided how they should be handled before modelling.


Plotting code
Claude assisted with all major plotting code, including time-series plots, decompositions, diagnostic plots and forecast/evaluation figures.
I decided what needed to be visualised, checked the plotted values and edited labels, annotations and presentation where required.


Structural-break testing
I asked Claude to explain how a structural-break test could be implemented for the electricity-demand series.
I used the test as supporting evidence rather than treating the estimated break dates as automatically correct, and interpreted the break in the context of the COVID-19 period and the modelling objective.


Stepping through structural-break pseudocode
Claude helped me work through the structural-break procedure step by step and translate the required workflow into R code.
I ran the procedure, inspected the candidate break dates and compared them with the observed series and relevant dates.


Strengthening the structural-break assessment
Claude suggested checking multiple values of the minimum segment length / trimming parameter rather than relying on one setting.
I ran the alternative specifications and used the sensitivity of the estimated break dates as part of my decision about the training period.


Holt–Winters from first principles
I supplied the Holt–Winters formulas/pseudocode and asked Claude to help translate the recursions into an R implementation from first principles.
I checked each recursion against the model definition, compared the behaviour with package-based exponential-smoothing output and interpreted the fitted components myself.


Rolling-window evaluation
Claude helped write reusable model-fitting and forecasting functions so that several models could be evaluated consistently over rolling/expanding forecast origins.
I determined the training, validation and test design, checked that each forecast used only information available at the forecast origin and interpreted the resulting errors.


imap() / purrr workflow
Claude explained how imap() could be used to streamline repeated fitting or forecasting across named model specifications and helped adapt my code to use it.
I checked that each model name was correctly matched to its forecast output and that the streamlined workflow reproduced the original calculations.


Diebold–Mariano test
Claude explained the purpose of the Diebold–Mariano test and assisted with the R implementation for comparing forecast accuracy.
I selected the forecasts/losses being compared and interpreted the test in conjunction with the observed forecast errors rather than using the p-value alone.


Empirical prediction intervals
Claude helped me check the construction of empirical prediction intervals based on forecast/residual errors and identify issues with how the intervals were being calculated.
I checked interval coverage and width against the observed holdout values and discussed the limitations of constructing intervals from the available residual information.


Annual-cycle adjustment
After comparing model behaviour, Claude suggested testing whether removing the additional annual-cycle adjustment simplified or improved the forecasting approach.
I compared the competing specifications using the validation/test framework and made the final modelling decision based on the evaluation results.


Fourier terms for the annual cycle
Claude helped write a function to generate the required sine and cosine Fourier terms for an annual cycle.
I checked the frequencies/periods used, inspected the generated terms and assessed whether adding them improved forecast performance.


Inline values
Claude helped write inline R expressions so numerical results in the text were populated directly from fitted objects and evaluation results.
I checked the rendered values against the underlying R objects.


Table formatting
Claude assisted with formatting all result and diagnostic tables for the rendered portfolio.
I checked that the values, labels, units and captions agreed with the analysis output.





AI errors identified and corrected









Issue identified
What was wrong
How it was corrected




First-principles Holt–Winters smoothing parameter
In the first-principles Holt–Winters implementation, the estimated smoothing parameter () reached the boundary at 1, while ets() estimated approximately 0.915.
I checked the first-principles estimate against the ets() fit and revised the discussion so that () is explicitly described as a boundary estimate rather than being treated as directly equivalent to the package estimate.

title: AI Use Log
text:
Project 2
Tool used: Claude (Anthropic)









AI-assisted task
How Claude was used
What I checked or did myself




Data-access instructions
Claude assisted with locating/accessing the City of Cape Town dam-level data and the NOAA/TAO sea-surface-temperature data used in the project.
I accessed the sources myself, checked the periods and variables available and documented the final sources used.


Reading the datasets into R
Claude helped with code to import the dam-level and SST datasets, parse dates and place the series on compatible time scales.
I ran the import code and checked the resulting dates and values against the source files.


Cleaning the data
Claude assisted with cleaning code for inconsistent dates, duplicated observations, missing values and reshaping the data for analysis.
I inspected the identified problems and made the final decisions about exclusions, transformations and aggregation.


Missing SST observations / filling gaps
Claude helped identify and implement ways of handling gaps in the buoy series so that aggregation and subsequent analysis did not silently fail.
I inspected the missingness pattern and considered the implications of filling/interpolating values before using the resulting series.


SST aggregation across buoys
I raised the concern that the TAO/TRITON buoys came from different locations/latitudes and that the set of reporting buoys changed over time. Claude suggested an aggregation/adjustment strategy to reduce artificial variation caused by changing buoy composition.
I checked the buoy coverage over time, assessed the resulting aggregate series and explicitly discussed changing buoy availability as a limitation.


Seasonal and ordinary differencing
Claude refined my code for determining and applying the required seasonal and first differences to the series.
I used the observed series, ACF/diagnostics and stationarity considerations to decide whether the resulting transformation was reasonable.


Prewhitening
Claude explained the purpose of prewhitening and assisted with code to prewhiten the series before calculating the cross-correlation function.
I checked the filtered series and interpreted how prewhitening changed the apparent lead–lag relationship between SST and dam levels.


Dynamic-regression workflow
Claude assisted with implementation details for including SST information in the dam-level forecasting model and aligning lagged predictors with the response.
I selected the candidate relationship, fitted and evaluated the models and concluded that inclusion of SST did not improve forecasts over the univariate model.


CRPS extraction for inline reporting
Claude helped extract CRPS values from the relevant evaluation objects and format them for inline R references in the text.
I checked the extracted values against the evaluation output and used them in the final model comparison.


Plotting code
Claude assisted with all plotting code, including dam/SST time-series figures, decomposition/diagnostic plots, cross-correlation displays and forecast plots.
I specified the comparisons I wanted to show, checked the plotted values and edited presentation and annotations where needed.


Table formatting
Claude assisted with formatting the project tables in Quarto/HTML.
I checked all reported estimates, errors and captions against the analysis objects.





AI errors identified and corrected









Issue identified
What was wrong
How it was corrected




Cross-correlation analysis
The original cross-correlation analysis used the raw seasonal series. The apparent relationship was largely driven by the shared seasonal structure rather than a reliable lead–lag relationship.
I replaced the raw CCF with a prewhitened cross-correlation analysis based on seasonally differenced series.

Tool used: Claude (Anthropic)









AI-assisted task
How Claude was used

Data-access instructions
Claude helped with instructions for obtaining the JSE index-price data required for the project.
I accessed the data, checked the time period and constructed/verified the return series used in the analysis.


Reading and preparing the data
Claude assisted with import code, date handling and preparation of the price/return series.
I checked the resulting returns, missing observations and summary statistics before modelling.


Streamlining repeated code
Claude helped refactor repeated GARCH fitting, forecasting and evaluation code into more concise functions/workflows.
I checked that the streamlined code reproduced the original fitted values, forecasts and evaluation metrics.


GARCH(1,1) from first principles
I supplied the GARCH(1,1) model equations/pseudocode and asked Claude to help translate the variance recursion and likelihood into R.
I checked the recursion and constraints against the model definition and compared the resulting estimates/volatility with package-based fits.


GJR-GARCH with Student-(t) innovations
Claude suggested including a GJR-GARCH-(t) specification so that the model could accommodate both asymmetric responses to shocks and heavy-tailed returns.
I fitted and diagnosed the model, compared it with the other candidate specifications and retained it based on the empirical results rather than the suggestion alone.


QLIKE loss
Claude explained QLIKE and assisted with implementing it as a loss function for volatility-forecast evaluation.
I checked the calculation and used it alongside the other forecast measures when comparing models.


Value-at-Risk backtests
Drawing on the connection with my Portfolio Theory course, I asked Claude to help implement VaR forecasts and the associated backtests for the fitted volatility models.
I selected the VaR levels, checked the violation counts and test output and interpreted the results in relation to the assumed innovation distributions and market risk.


Forecast-evaluation workflow
Claude helped streamline the repeated out-of-sample forecasts and evaluation of competing conditional-variance models.
I determined the evaluation sample and model comparisons and checked that forecasts were genuinely out of sample.


Plotting and tables
As part of the portfolio-wide assistance described above, Claude generated/assisted with the plotting and table-formatting code used for the volatility, diagnostic and forecast-comparison results.
I checked all plotted and tabulated quantities against the fitted objects and wrote the substantive interpretation myself.

title: AI Use Log
text:
Project 4
Tool used: Claude (Anthropic)









AI-assisted task
How Claude was used
What I checked or did myself




Data-access instructions
Claude assisted with instructions for accessing the earthquake data used for validating the HMM implementation and the JSE data used for the substantive analysis.
I accessed the datasets and checked that the variables, dates and sample periods matched the intended analyses.


Reading and preparing the data
Claude helped write the import and preparation code required to create the series used by the HMM functions.
I ran the code, checked the resulting observations and verified the training/test splits and return calculations.


First-principles HMM toolkit from pseudocode
I supplied the model formulation and pseudocode/required steps for the HMM algorithms. Claude helped translate these into R functions for the likelihood/forward algorithm, decoding and related calculations.
I worked through the functions, checked them against the HMM equations and validated the implementation using known/package-based results where possible.


Streamlining the functions into a toolkit
Once the individual HMM functions were working, Claude helped reorganise them into a reusable toolkit so that the same code could be applied to the earthquake example and JSE models with different numbers of states.
I checked that the refactoring did not change the numerical results and used the common toolkit throughout the analysis.


Viterbi algorithm
Claude explained the Viterbi algorithm step by step and how it differs from local decoding/filtering, and assisted with implementation details.
I checked the recursion against the model formulation and interpreted the resulting global state sequence myself.


Using depmixS4
Claude explained how to specify, fit and extract results from a Gaussian HMM using depmixS4 so that I could compare the package result with my first-principles implementation.
I ran the fits, compared the likelihood/parameters with my implementation and investigated why the default fit could converge to a poor solution.


Fitting multiple numbers of regimes
Claude helped streamline fitting one-, two-, three- and four-state models, including looping over model sizes and storing comparable fit objects.
I compared BIC, diagnostics and interpretability across the fitted regime numbers and made the final model-selection decision.


Multiple/random starting values
Claude assisted with code for refitting each HMM from several random starts after the sensitivity of the likelihood optimisation became apparent.
I compared the attained log-likelihoods and retained the best solution, while noting that multiple starts reduce but do not eliminate the possibility of a local optimum.


Precision / standard errors of estimates
Claude explained how the Hessian could be used to approximate the covariance matrix of the estimated parameters and how the delta method could be used for derived quantities such as expected regime durations.
I checked the resulting standard errors, reported their approximate nature and discussed the limitations of Hessian/delta-method uncertainty.


Pseudo-residuals
Claude helped implement normal pseudo-residuals for model checking and the associated Ljung–Box diagnostics for the residuals and their squares.
I checked the formula against the one-step-ahead predictive distribution and interpreted the diagnostics across the candidate HMMs.


Newey–West SE of a mean
Claude helped write a function for a Newey–West standard error of the mean difference in log scores so that predictive performance could be compared while allowing for serial dependence.
I checked the lag rule and calculation, applied it to the out-of-sample log-score differences and interpreted the resulting comparison with GJR-GARCH.


Shiny application
I specified what I wanted the JSE regime explorer to do, including the required controls, regime displays, crisis-period exploration and comparison with GJR-GARCH. Claude wrote the majority of the Shiny implementation code.
I ran and tested the application, checked that its plots and reported quantities agreed with the Project 4 analysis, identified problems and requested/reviewed revisions before deployment.


Plotting and tables
Claude assisted with plotting and table-formatting code for state probabilities, decoded regimes, diagnostics, forecast densities and model comparisons.
I checked that all visualised/tabulated results agreed with the fitted models and analysis objects and wrote the final interpretation.





AI errors identified and corrected









Issue identified
What was wrong
How it was corrected




Comparison with depmixS4
The original text stated that depmixS4 “agreed closely” with my first-principles toolkit. On closer inspection, the default depmixS4 fit had effectively collapsed to a one-state solution, so this comparison was misleading.
I refitted depmixS4 using both its default starting values and selected starting values, compared the resulting likelihoods and state parameters, and revised the discussion to explain the collapsed default solution explicitly.


HMM versus GARCH volatility comparison
I initially compared HMM volatility constructed from smoothed state probabilities with GARCH volatility. Smoothed probabilities use observations from the future, whereas the GARCH volatility forecast at time (t) only uses information available up to that point, making the comparison unfair.
I replaced the primary comparison with HMM volatility based on filtered probabilities so that both methods use only information available at the time. The smoothed-probability result is still reported separately as a retrospective description of the regimes.


Single set of HMM starting values
The HMMs were initially fitted from only one set of starting values. Because the HMM likelihood can contain local optima, convergence from one start did not provide enough evidence that the fitted solution was the best available one.
I added five random initialisations for each model specification and retained the fit with the highest attained log-likelihood. The final discussion now acknowledges the sensitivity of HMM optimisation to starting values.

title: Lagged & Loaded
text:
R Code and Scripts
The code for each project is embedded in its detailed analysis (see Computational Notebooks and Reports). The standalone scripts below are shared between pages or run outside the portfolio. Click a script name to show the code.

HMM toolkit
scripts/hmm-toolkit.R: my hidden Markov model functions (scaled forward and backward algorithms, local decoding, the Viterbi algorithm, the stationary distribution, the working-parameter transformation and matrix powers for forecasting). Used by Project 4 and the Hidden Markov Models part of Section 2.


hmm-toolkit.R
# =============================================================================
# HMM toolkit, written from first principles (Time Series Analysis portfolio)
#
# Used by projects/project-04-analysis.qmd and section-2/section-2.qmd.
# Every function works with the matrix of state-dependent densities
# dens[t, i] = p_i(x_t), so the same code handles Poisson, Gaussian and
# categorical observations.
# =============================================================================

# Log-likelihood only (fast version, used inside optim()):
hmm_loglik = function(dens, delta, Gamma) {
  T_len = nrow(dens)
  v = delta * dens[1, ]
  ll = log(sum(v))
  phi = v / sum(v)
  if (T_len > 1) {
    for (t in 2:T_len) {
      v = as.numeric(phi %*% Gamma) * dens[t, ]
      u = sum(v)
      ll = ll + log(u)
      phi = v / u
    }
  }
  ll
}

# Scaled forward algorithm: log-likelihood, log u_t, filtered probabilities and log alpha:
hmm_forward = function(dens, delta, Gamma) {
  T_len = nrow(dens)
  m = ncol(dens)
  phi_mat = matrix(NA, T_len, m)
  lu = numeric(T_len)
  for (t in 1:T_len) {
    v = if (t == 1) delta * dens[1, ] else as.numeric(phi %*% Gamma) * dens[t, ]
    u = sum(v)
    lu[t] = log(u)                # log p(x_t | x_{1:t-1})
    phi = v / u                   # P(C_t = i | x_{1:t})
    phi_mat[t, ] = phi
  }
  list(loglik = sum(lu), lu = lu, phi = phi_mat,
       lalpha = cumsum(lu) + log(phi_mat))   # log alpha_t(i)
}

# Scaled backward algorithm: log beta (Zucchini et al., 2016):
hmm_backward = function(dens, Gamma) {
  T_len = nrow(dens)
  m = ncol(dens)
  lbeta = matrix(0, T_len, m)     # log beta_T = 0
  phi = rep(1 / m, m)
  lscale = log(m)
  if (T_len > 1) {
    for (t in (T_len - 1):1) {
      v = as.numeric(Gamma %*% (dens[t + 1, ] * phi))
      lbeta[t, ] = log(v) + lscale
      phi = v / sum(v)
      lscale = lscale + log(sum(v))
    }
  }
  lbeta
}

# Local decoding: P(C_t = i | x_{1:T}) = alpha_t(i) beta_t(i) / L_T:
hmm_local = function(dens, delta, Gamma) {
  fwd = hmm_forward(dens, delta, Gamma)
  lbeta = hmm_backward(dens, Gamma)
  exp(fwd$lalpha + lbeta - fwd$loglik)
}

# Global decoding with the Viterbi algorithm (log scale):
hmm_viterbi = function(dens, delta, Gamma) {
  T_len = nrow(dens)
  m = ncol(dens)
  lG = log(Gamma)
  ld = log(dens)
  xi = matrix(NA, T_len, m)
  xi[1, ] = log(delta) + ld[1, ]
  if (T_len > 1) {
    for (t in 2:T_len) {
      for (j in 1:m) {
        xi[t, j] = max(xi[t - 1, ] + lG[, j]) + ld[t, j]
      }
    }
  }
  # Back-tracing:
  states = numeric(T_len)
  states[T_len] = which.max(xi[T_len, ])
  if (T_len > 1) {
    for (t in (T_len - 1):1) {
      states[t] = which.max(xi[t, ] + lG[, states[t + 1]])
    }
  }
  list(states = states, xi = xi)
}

# Stationary distribution: solve delta (I - Gamma + U) = 1:
stat_dist = function(Gamma) {
  m = nrow(Gamma)
  solve(t(diag(m) - Gamma + 1), rep(1, m))
}

# Working (unconstrained) parameters -> transition probability matrix:
gamma_w2n = function(w, m) {
  G = diag(m)
  G[!G] = exp(w)                  # off-diagonal elements, relative to the diagonal
  G / rowSums(G)
}

# h-step transition matrix Gamma^h:
mat_pow = function(M, h) {
  R = diag(nrow(M))
  for (i in seq_len(h)) R = R %*% M
  R
}

# =============================================================================
# JSE regime explorer: precompute the model fits used by app.R
#
# Run once from the root of the portfolio project (the folder with _quarto.yml):
#   source("scripts/shiny-app/precompute.R")
#
# It fits Gaussian HMMs with 1-4 states and GJR-GARCH(1,1)-t on the training
# set (Jul 1995 - Dec 2012), exactly as in the Project 4 analysis, runs every
# model through the whole series with the parameters fixed, and saves the
# results to scripts/shiny-app/app_data.rds. The app only reads that file, so
# it starts instantly and does not need rugarch or readxl when deployed.
# =============================================================================

library(readxl)
library(rugarch)

set.seed(2026)

data_path  = "_data/PT-DATA-ALBI-JIBAR-JSEIND-Daily-1994-2017.xlsx"
out_path   = "scripts/shiny-app/app_data.rds"
sheet_name = "JSE Various Indices"
train_end  = as.Date("2012-12-31")

if (!file.exists(data_path)) {
  stop("Could not find ", data_path, ". Run this script from the portfolio root folder.")
}

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# HMM toolkit (same functions as in project-04-analysis.qmd)
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

hmm_loglik = function(dens, delta, Gamma) {
  T_len = nrow(dens)
  v = delta * dens[1, ]
  ll = log(sum(v))
  phi = v / sum(v)
  if (T_len > 1) {
    for (t in 2:T_len) {
      v = as.numeric(phi %*% Gamma) * dens[t, ]
      u = sum(v)
      ll = ll + log(u)
      phi = v / u
    }
  }
  ll
}

hmm_forward = function(dens, delta, Gamma) {
  T_len = nrow(dens)
  m = ncol(dens)
  phi_mat = matrix(NA, T_len, m)
  lu = numeric(T_len)
  for (t in 1:T_len) {
    v = if (t == 1) delta * dens[1, ] else as.numeric(phi %*% Gamma) * dens[t, ]
    u = sum(v)
    lu[t] = log(u)
    phi = v / u
    phi_mat[t, ] = phi
  }
  list(loglik = sum(lu), lu = lu, phi = phi_mat,
       lalpha = cumsum(lu) + log(phi_mat))
}

hmm_backward = function(dens, Gamma) {
  T_len = nrow(dens)
  m = ncol(dens)
  lbeta = matrix(0, T_len, m)
  phi = rep(1 / m, m)
  lscale = log(m)
  if (T_len > 1) {
    for (t in (T_len - 1):1) {
      v = as.numeric(Gamma %*% (dens[t + 1, ] * phi))
      lbeta[t, ] = log(v) + lscale
      phi = v / sum(v)
      lscale = lscale + log(sum(v))
    }
  }
  lbeta
}

hmm_local = function(dens, delta, Gamma) {
  fwd = hmm_forward(dens, delta, Gamma)
  lbeta = hmm_backward(dens, Gamma)
  exp(fwd$lalpha + lbeta - fwd$loglik)
}

hmm_viterbi = function(dens, delta, Gamma) {
  T_len = nrow(dens)
  m = ncol(dens)
  lG = log(Gamma)
  ld = log(dens)
  xi = matrix(NA, T_len, m)
  xi[1, ] = log(delta) + ld[1, ]
  for (t in 2:T_len) {
    for (j in 1:m) xi[t, j] = max(xi[t - 1, ] + lG[, j]) + ld[t, j]
  }
  states = numeric(T_len)
  states[T_len] = which.max(xi[T_len, ])
  for (t in (T_len - 1):1) states[t] = which.max(xi[t, ] + lG[, states[t + 1]])
  states
}

stat_dist = function(Gamma) {
  m = nrow(Gamma)
  solve(t(diag(m) - Gamma + 1), rep(1, m))
}

gamma_w2n = function(w, m) {
  G = diag(m)
  G[!G] = exp(w)
  G / rowSums(G)
}

norm_hmm_nll = function(w, x, m) {
  mu = w[1:m]
  sigma = exp(w[(m + 1):(2 * m)])
  Gamma = if (m == 1) matrix(1) else gamma_w2n(w[(2 * m + 1):(2 * m + m * (m - 1))], m)
  delta = if (m == 1) 1 else stat_dist(Gamma)
  dens = sapply(1:m, function(j) dnorm(x, mu[j], sigma[j]))
  -hmm_loglik(matrix(dens, ncol = m), delta, Gamma)
}

norm_hmm_unpack = function(w, m) {
  mu = w[1:m]
  sigma = exp(w[(m + 1):(2 * m)])
  Gamma = if (m == 1) matrix(1) else gamma_w2n(w[(2 * m + 1):(2 * m + m * (m - 1))], m)
  ord = order(sigma)
  Gamma = Gamma[ord, ord, drop = FALSE]
  list(m = m, mu = mu[ord], sigma = sigma[ord], Gamma = Gamma,
       delta = if (m == 1) 1 else stat_dist(Gamma))
}

norm_dens = function(x, pars) {
  matrix(sapply(1:pars$m, function(j) dnorm(x, pars$mu[j], pars$sigma[j])), ncol = pars$m)
}

norm_pseudo = function(x, pars) {
  fwd = hmm_forward(norm_dens(x, pars), pars$delta, pars$Gamma)
  T_len = length(x)
  pred = rbind(pars$delta, fwd$phi[-T_len, , drop = FALSE] %*% pars$Gamma)
  cdf = matrix(sapply(1:pars$m, function(j) pnorm(x, pars$mu[j], pars$sigma[j])), ncol = pars$m)
  qnorm(pmin(pmax(rowSums(pred * cdf), 1e-10), 1 - 1e-10))
}

# Newey-West standard error of a mean (Bartlett kernel):
nw_se = function(d, L = 6) {
  n = length(d)
  u = d - mean(d)
  s = sum(u^2) / n
  for (l in 1:L) s = s + 2 * (1 - l / (L + 1)) * sum(u[-(1:l)] * u[1:(n - l)]) / n
  sqrt(s / n)
}

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Data (same cleaning as Projects 3 and 4)
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

find_col = function(hdr, code, field) {
  idx = which(unlist(hdr[1, ]) == code & unlist(hdr[2, ]) == field)
  if (length(idx) != 1) stop(paste("Could not uniquely find", code, field))
  idx
}

hdr = read_excel(data_path, sheet = sheet_name, col_names = FALSE, n_max = 4)
raw = read_excel(data_path, sheet = sheet_name, col_names = FALSE, skip = 4,
                 na = c("#N/A", "", "NA"), guess_max = 10000)

date_col = which(sapply(raw, function(x) inherits(x, c("POSIXct", "Date"))))[1]
alsi_col = find_col(hdr, "J203:XJSE:IND", "TRI")

alsi = data.frame(date = as.Date(raw[[date_col]]), tri = as.numeric(raw[[alsi_col]]))
alsi = alsi[!is.na(alsi$date) & !is.na(alsi$tri), ]
alsi = alsi[order(alsi$date), ]
alsi = alsi[!duplicated(alsi$date), ]
alsi$r = c(NA, 100 * diff(log(alsi$tri)))
alsi = alsi[!is.na(alsi$r), ]

r_all   = alsi$r
n_train = sum(alsi$date <= train_end)
r_train = r_all[1:n_train]
train_idx = 1:n_train
test_idx  = (n_train + 1):length(r_all)

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Gaussian HMMs with 1-4 states (same starting values as the analysis)
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

jse_starts = list(
  c(mean(r_train), log(sd(r_train))),
  c(0.1, -0.1, log(0.8), log(2), rep(-3, 2)),
  c(0.1, 0.05, -0.3, log(0.6), log(1.1), log(2.5), rep(-4, 6)),
  c(0.12, 0.08, 0, -0.3, log(0.5), log(0.85), log(1.4), log(2.8), rep(-4, 12))
)

models = lapply(1:4, function(m) {
  message("Fitting the ", m, "-state HMM ...")
  fit = optim(jse_starts[[m]], norm_hmm_nll, x = r_train, m = m, method = "BFGS",
              control = list(maxit = 2000))
  pars = norm_hmm_unpack(fit$par, m)

  # Run through the whole series with the training parameters fixed:
  dens_all = norm_dens(r_all, pars)
  fwd = hmm_forward(dens_all, pars$delta, pars$Gamma)

  k = m^2 + m
  logL = -fit$value
  c(pars, list(
    logL        = logL,
    k           = k,
    AIC         = -2 * logL + 2 * k,
    BIC         = -2 * logL + k * log(n_train),
    convergence = fit$convergence,
    filtered    = fwd$phi,                                     # P(C_t | x_1:t)
    smoothed    = hmm_local(dens_all, pars$delta, pars$Gamma), # P(C_t | x_1:T)
    viterbi     = hmm_viterbi(dens_all, pars$delta, pars$Gamma),
    ls          = fwd$lu,                                      # one-step-ahead log scores
    pz          = norm_pseudo(r_train, pars)                   # pseudo-residuals (training)
  ))
})

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# GJR-GARCH(1,1) with Student-t errors and an AR(1) mean (Project 3 model)
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

message("Fitting GJR-GARCH(1,1)-t ...")
spec_gjr = ugarchspec(variance.model     = list(model = "gjrGARCH", garchOrder = c(1, 1)),
                      mean.model         = list(armaOrder = c(1, 0), include.mean = TRUE),
                      distribution.model = "std")
gjr_fit = ugarchfit(spec = spec_gjr, data = r_train, solver = "hybrid")

spec_fixed = spec_gjr
setfixed(spec_fixed) = as.list(coef(gjr_fit))
gjr_filt = ugarchfilter(spec = spec_fixed, data = r_all)

gjr_mu    = as.numeric(fitted(gjr_filt))
gjr_sigma = as.numeric(sigma(gjr_filt))
gjr_ls    = log(ddist("std", y = r_all, mu = gjr_mu, sigma = gjr_sigma,
                      shape = coef(gjr_fit)["shape"]))

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Log-score comparison table
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

scores = do.call(rbind, lapply(1:4, function(m) {
  d = models[[m]]$ls[test_idx] - gjr_ls[test_idx]
  data.frame(model = paste0("Gaussian HMM, ", m, " state", if (m > 1) "s" else ""),
             m = m,
             train = mean(models[[m]]$ls[train_idx]),
             test  = mean(models[[m]]$ls[test_idx]),
             diff  = mean(d),
             p     = 2 * pnorm(-abs(mean(d) / nw_se(d))))
}))
scores = rbind(scores, data.frame(model = "GJR-GARCH(1,1)-t", m = NA,
                                  train = mean(gjr_ls[train_idx]),
                                  test  = mean(gjr_ls[test_idx]),
                                  diff  = NA, p = NA))

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Save
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

app_data = list(
  series   = data.frame(date = alsi$date, r = r_all),
  n_train  = n_train,
  models   = models,
  gjr      = list(sigma = gjr_sigma, mu = gjr_mu, ls = gjr_ls, coef = coef(gjr_fit)),
  scores   = scores,
  created  = Sys.time(),
  versions = c(R = R.version.string, rugarch = as.character(packageVersion("rugarch")))
)

saveRDS(app_data, out_path)
message("Saved ", out_path, " (", round(file.size(out_path) / 1e6, 1), " MB).")

# Quick check against the Project 4 analysis (expected about -7276, -6660, -6551, -6514):
print(round(sapply(models, `[[`, "logL"), 1))

# Small helper for clean HTML tables with an optional highlighted row:
html_table = function(df, digits = 3, highlight = NULL) {
  # Format each column: whole-number columns without decimals, missing values as a dash.
  cells = lapply(df, function(x) {
    if (!is.numeric(x)) return(as.character(x))
    ok = !is.na(x) & is.finite(x)
    d = if (all(x[ok] == round(x[ok]))) 0 else digits
    out = rep("–", length(x))
    out[ok] = formatC(x[ok], format = "f", digits = d, big.mark = ",")
    out
  })
  body = lapply(seq_len(nrow(df)), function(i) {
    tags$tr(class = if (!is.null(highlight) && i %in% highlight) "selected-row",
            lapply(cells, function(col) tags$td(HTML(col[i]))))
  })
  tags$table(class = "table table-sm table-hover align-middle mb-0",
             tags$thead(tags$tr(lapply(names(df), tags$th))),
             tags$tbody(body))
}

### What this app shows

A **hidden Markov model** (HMM) assumes the market is always in one of *m* unobserved
regimes. Each regime has its own mean return and volatility, and the market moves between
regimes according to a Markov chain with transition matrix Γ. Because regimes are
persistent, an HMM reproduces volatility clustering and heavy tails.

**Ways of assigning regimes**

- **Global decoding (Viterbi):** the single most likely *sequence* of regimes, given all the data.
- **Local decoding (smoothed):** for each day separately, the most likely regime given all the data,
  P(C<sub>t</sub> | x<sub>1</sub>, ..., x<sub>T</sub>). It uses future returns, so it is a description of the past, not a forecast.
- **Filtered (real time):** the regime probabilities using only returns up to that day,
  P(C<sub>t</sub> | x<sub>1</sub>, ..., x<sub>t</sub>). This is what an investor could have known on the day,
  and it is the fair comparison with GJR-GARCH.

**Comparison with GJR-GARCH.** The GJR-GARCH(1,1) model with Student-*t* errors and an
AR(1) mean is the model selected in Project 3. Both models are evaluated with the
one-step-ahead log score: the log of the forecast density at the return that actually happened.

### Data and methods

Daily FTSE/JSE All Share total return index (J203), 30 June 1995 to 3 February 2017.
Source: Gebbie, T. (2020). *Daily Sampled South African Market Index Data 1994–2017*.
University of Cape Town. <https://doi.org/10.25375/uct.11302325.v1>

All HMM algorithms (scaled forward and backward algorithms, Viterbi, pseudo-residuals) were
written from first principles and the likelihood was maximised with `optim()`. GJR-GARCH
was fitted with `rugarch`. Parameters are estimated on the training set only and kept fixed
for the test period. The fits are precomputed (see `precompute.R`), so the app does no
estimation itself.

### References

- Hamilton, J. D. (1989). A new approach to the economic analysis of nonstationary time series
  and the business cycle. *Econometrica*, 57(2), 357–384.
- Zucchini, W., MacDonald, I. L., & Langrock, R. (2016). *Hidden Markov models for time series:
  An introduction using R* (2nd ed.). CRC Press.
"))
    )
  )
)

server = function(input, output, session) {

  m     = reactive(as.integer(input$m))
  mod   = reactive(app_data$models[[m()]])
  cols  = reactive(regime_cols(m()))
  nms   = reactive(regime_names(m()))

  probs = reactive(if (input$decode == "filtered") mod()$filtered else mod()$smoothed)

  states = reactive({
    if (input$decode == "viterbi") mod()$viterbi
    else max.col(probs(), ties.method = "first")
  })

  x_range = reactive({
    z = zooms[[input$zoom]]
    if (is.null(z)) as.character(range(series$date)) else z
  })

  # HMM volatility (% per day) for the chosen way of assigning regimes:
  hmm_vol = reactive({
    md = mod()
    if (input$decode == "viterbi") return(md$sigma[states()])
    p = probs()
    mean_t = as.numeric(p %*% md$mu)
    sqrt(pmax(as.numeric(p %*% (md$sigma^2 + md$mu^2)) - mean_t^2, 0))
  })

  test_shade = list(type = "rect", xref = "x", yref = "paper",
                    x0 = test_start, x1 = max(series$date), y0 = 0, y1 = 1,
                    fillcolor = "rgba(46,35,56,0.06)", line = list(width = 0), layer = "below")

  # ---- Sidebar legend --------------------------------------------------------

  output$legend = renderUI({
    md = mod()
    div(class = "mb-2",
        tags$label(class = "form-label", "Regimes"),
        lapply(seq_len(m()), function(j) {
          div(class = "note", style = "color: inherit;",
              span(class = "swatch", style = paste0("background:", cols()[j], ";")),
              sprintf("%s: %.0f%% volatility", nms()[j], md$sigma[j] * ann))
        }))
  })

  # ---- Value boxes -----------------------------------------------------------

  output$value_boxes = renderUI({
    md = mod(); mm = m()
    top = nms()[mm]
    bics = sapply(app_data$models, `[[`, "BIC")
    d_bic = md$BIC - min(bics)
    test_ls = app_data$scores$test[mm]
    gjr_ls  = app_data$scores$test[5]

    layout_column_wrap(
      width = "200px", fill = FALSE, class = "mb-3",
      value_box(
        title = paste(if (mm == 1) "Volatility" else paste(top, "regime volatility")),
        value = sprintf("%.0f%%", md$sigma[mm] * ann),
        showcase = bs_icon("activity"), theme = soft_box,
        p(if (mm == 1) "annualised" else sprintf("annualised; calm regime %.0f%%", md$sigma[1] * ann))
      ),
      value_box(
        title = if (mm == 1) "Mean return" else paste("Time in", tolower(top), "regime"),
        value = if (mm == 1) sprintf("%.3f%%", md$mu[1]) else sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * md$delta[mm]),
        showcase = bs_icon("hourglass-split"), theme = soft_box,
        p(if (mm == 1) "per day" else sprintf("a spell lasts %.0f trading days on average",
                                             1 / (1 - md$Gamma[mm, mm])))
      ),
      value_box(
        title = "BIC (training set)",
        value = formatC(md$BIC, format = "f", digits = 0, big.mark = ","),
        showcase = bs_icon("bar-chart-steps"), theme = soft_box,
        p(if (d_bic < 1e-8) "best of the four models" else sprintf("%.1f above the best model", d_bic))
      ),
      value_box(
        title = "Test log score",
        value = sprintf("%.3f", test_ls),
        showcase = bs_icon("bullseye"), theme = soft_box,
        p(sprintf("GJR-GARCH: %.3f (higher is better)", gjr_ls))
      )
    )
  })

  # ---- Regime timeline -------------------------------------------------------

  output$timeline = renderPlotly({
    mm = m(); cl = cols(); nm = nms(); st = states(); pr = probs()
    lab = factor(nm[st], levels = nm)
    hover = sprintf("<b>%s</b><br>Return: %.2f%%<br>Regime: %s<br>P(%s): %.2f",
                    format(series$date, "%d %b %Y"), series$r, nm[st], nm[mm], pr[, mm])

    p1 = plot_ly(x = series$date, y = series$r, type = "scattergl", mode = "markers",
                 color = lab, colors = setNames(cl, nm),
                 marker = list(size = 4, opacity = 0.85),
                 text = hover, hoverinfo = "text")

    p2 = plot_ly()
    for (j in seq_len(mm)) {
      p2 = add_trace(p2, x = series$date, y = pr[, j], type = "scatter", mode = "lines",
                     stackgroup = "probs", line = list(width = 0.4, color = cl[j]),
                     fillcolor = cl[j], name = nm[j], showlegend = FALSE,
                     hovertemplate = paste0(nm[j], ": %{y:.2f}<extra></extra>"))
    }

    prob_title = if (input$decode == "filtered") "Filtered probability" else "Smoothed probability"

    subplot(p1, p2, nrows = 2, shareX = TRUE, heights = c(0.62, 0.38),
            titleY = TRUE, margin = 0.04) |>
      style_plot(
        xaxis  = list(range = x_range(), title = ""),
        yaxis  = list(title = "Daily return (%)", zeroline = FALSE, gridcolor = "#EEE8F0"),
        yaxis2 = list(title = prob_title, range = c(0, 1), gridcolor = "#EEE8F0"),
        legend = list(orientation = "h", x = 0, y = 1.07),
        shapes = list(test_shade),
        annotations = list(list(x = test_start, y = 1, xref = "x", yref = "paper",
                                text = "Test period", showarrow = FALSE,
                                xanchor = "left", yanchor = "bottom",
                                font = list(size = 11, color = "#6c6375")))
      )
  })

  output$timeline_note = renderText({
    switch(input$decode,
      viterbi  = "Points are coloured by the most likely sequence of regimes (Viterbi). The bottom panel shows the smoothed regime probabilities.",
      smoothed = "Points are coloured by the most likely regime on each day, using all the data. These probabilities use future returns too.",
      filtered = "Points are coloured by the most likely regime using only returns up to that day, which is what was knowable in real time.")
  })

  # ---- Regimes tab -----------------------------------------------------------

  output$regime_tbl = renderUI({
    md = mod(); mm = m()
    stay = diag(md$Gamma)
    html_table(data.frame(
      Regime                 = sprintf("<span class='swatch' style='background:%s'></span>%s", cols(), nms()),
      `Mean (% per day)`     = md$mu,
      `SD (% per day)`       = md$sigma,
      `Volatility (%)`       = md$sigma * ann,
      `Share of time (%)`    = 100 * md$delta,
      `Expected spell (days)` = ifelse(stay >= 1, NA, 1 / (1 - stay)),
      check.names = FALSE
    ), digits = 2)
  })

  output$tpm = renderPlotly({
    md = mod(); nm = nms(); mm = m()
    grid = expand.grid(from = 1:mm, to = 1:mm)
    z = md$Gamma[cbind(grid$from, grid$to)]
    labels = lapply(seq_along(z), function(k) {
      list(x = nm[grid$to[k]], y = nm[grid$from[k]], xref = "x", yref = "y",
           text = formatC(z[k], format = "f", digits = 3), showarrow = FALSE,
           font = list(color = if (z[k] > 0.5) "#FFFFFF" else ink, size = 13))
    })
    plot_ly(x = nm, y = nm, z = md$Gamma, type = "heatmap",
            colorscale = list(list(0, "#FFFFFF"), list(0.15, "#E9D3EC"), list(1, purple)),
            zmin = 0, zmax = 1, showscale = FALSE, xgap = 2, ygap = 2,
            hovertemplate = "From %{y} to %{x}: %{z:.4f}<extra></extra>") |>
      style_plot(xaxis = list(title = "To", side = "top", type = "category"),
                 yaxis = list(title = "From", autorange = "reversed", type = "category"),
                 annotations = labels)
  })

  output$ladder = renderPlotly({
    md = mod(); nm = nms(); cl = cols()
    plot_ly(x = md$sigma * ann, y = md$mu * 252, type = "scatter", mode = "markers+text",
            text = nm, textposition = "top center",
            marker = list(size = 14 + 60 * md$delta, color = cl,
                          line = list(color = "#FFFFFF", width = 1.5)),
            hovertemplate = paste0("%{text}<br>Volatility: %{x:.1f}%<br>",
                                   "Mean return: %{y:.1f}% per year<extra></extra>")) |>
      style_plot(xaxis = list(title = "Annualised volatility (%)", rangemode = "tozero",
                              gridcolor = "#EEE8F0"),
                 yaxis = list(title = "Annualised mean return (%)", gridcolor = "#EEE8F0",
                              zerolinecolor = "#CFC6D4"),
                 showlegend = FALSE)
  })

  # ---- Model fit tab ---------------------------------------------------------

  output$ic_tbl = renderUI({
    ms = app_data$models
    bics = sapply(ms, `[[`, "BIC")
    html_table(data.frame(
      Regimes          = 1:4,
      Parameters       = sapply(ms, `[[`, "k"),
      `Log-likelihood` = sapply(ms, `[[`, "logL"),
      AIC              = sapply(ms, `[[`, "AIC"),
      BIC              = bics,
      `ΔBIC`      = bics - min(bics),
      check.names = FALSE
    ), digits = 1, highlight = m())
  })

  output$qq = renderPlotly({
    z = sort(mod()$pz)
    q = qnorm(ppoints(length(z)))
    lim = range(c(q, z))
    plot_ly() |>
      add_trace(x = lim, y = lim, type = "scatter", mode = "lines",
                line = list(color = "#B9AFC0", dash = "dash"), hoverinfo = "skip") |>
      add_trace(x = q, y = z, type = "scattergl", mode = "markers",
                marker = list(size = 4, color = purple, opacity = 0.6),
                hovertemplate = "Theoretical: %{x:.2f}<br>Sample: %{y:.2f}<extra></extra>") |>
      style_plot(xaxis = list(title = "Standard normal quantiles", gridcolor = "#EEE8F0"),
                 yaxis = list(title = "Pseudo-residual quantiles", gridcolor = "#EEE8F0"),
                 showlegend = FALSE)
  })

  output$acf = renderPlotly({
    z = mod()$pz
    a = acf(z^2, lag.max = 30, plot = FALSE)$acf[-1]
    bound = 1.96 / sqrt(length(z))
    plot_ly(x = 1:30, y = a, type = "bar", marker = list(color = pink),
            hovertemplate = "Lag %{x}: %{y:.3f}<extra></extra>") |>
      style_plot(xaxis = list(title = "Lag (trading days)"),
                 yaxis = list(title = "Autocorrelation", gridcolor = "#EEE8F0"),
                 shapes = list(
                   list(type = "line", xref = "paper", x0 = 0, x1 = 1, y0 = bound, y1 = bound,
                        line = list(color = "#6c6375", dash = "dot", width = 1)),
                   list(type = "line", xref = "paper", x0 = 0, x1 = 1, y0 = -bound, y1 = -bound,
                        line = list(color = "#6c6375", dash = "dot", width = 1))),
                 showlegend = FALSE)
  })

  output$diag_note = renderText({
    z = mod()$pz
    kurt = mean((z - mean(z))^4) / mean((z - mean(z))^2)^2 - 3
    lb = Box.test(z^2, lag = 10, type = "Ljung-Box")$p.value
    sprintf("Excess kurtosis %.2f; Ljung-Box test on the squares (lag 10): p = %.3f. If the model is right, pseudo-residuals are independent N(0, 1), so the points should follow the line and the bars should stay inside the dotted bounds.",
            kurt, lb)
  })

  # ---- HMM vs GJR-GARCH tab --------------------------------------------------

  output$vol = renderPlotly({
    hv = hmm_vol() * ann
    gv = app_data$gjr$sigma * ann
    plot_ly(x = series$date) |>
      add_lines(y = gv, name = "GJR-GARCH(1,1)-t", line = list(color = purple, width = 1),
                hovertemplate = "GJR-GARCH: %{y:.1f}%<extra></extra>") |>
      add_lines(y = hv, name = paste0("HMM, ", m(), if (m() > 1) " regimes" else " regime"),
                line = list(color = pink, width = 1.4),
                hovertemplate = "HMM: %{y:.1f}%<extra></extra>") |>
      style_plot(xaxis = list(range = x_range(), title = ""),
                 yaxis = list(title = "Annualised volatility (%)", gridcolor = "#EEE8F0",
                              rangemode = "tozero"),
                 legend = list(orientation = "h", x = 0, y = 1.1),
                 hovermode = "x unified",
                 shapes = list(test_shade))
  })

  output$vol_note = renderText({
    r = cor(hmm_vol(), app_data$gjr$sigma)
    paste0(sprintf("Correlation between the two volatility series: %.2f. ", r),
           switch(input$decode,
             viterbi  = "The HMM curve is the volatility of the Viterbi regime on each day, so it jumps between a few fixed levels.",
             smoothed = "The HMM curve uses smoothed probabilities, which look ahead, so it is smoother than anything available in real time.",
             filtered = "Both curves now use only past returns, so this is the like-for-like comparison."))
  })

  output$cumscore = renderPlotly({
    idx = (n_train + 1):n_all
    p = plot_ly()
    for (j in 1:4) {
      d = cumsum(app_data$models[[j]]$ls[idx] - app_data$gjr$ls[idx])
      sel = j == m()
      p = add_lines(p, x = series$date[idx], y = d,
                    name = paste0(j, if (j > 1) " regimes" else " regime"),
                    line = list(color = if (sel) pink else "#C9BFD0", width = if (sel) 2.4 else 1.2),
                    hovertemplate = paste0(j, "-regime HMM: %{y:.1f}<extra></extra>"))
    }
    p |>
      style_plot(xaxis = list(title = ""),
                 yaxis = list(title = "Cumulative difference", gridcolor = "#EEE8F0",
                              zerolinecolor = "#6c6375"),
                 legend = list(orientation = "h", x = 0, y = 1.12))
  })

  output$score_tbl = renderUI({
    s = app_data$scores
    html_table(data.frame(
      Model                 = s$model,
      Train                 = s$train,
      Test                  = s$test,
      `Difference to GJR`   = s$diff,
      `p-value`             = s$p,
      check.names = FALSE
    ), digits = 3, highlight = m())
  })
}

title: Learning Journal
text:
This journal documents my learning progress throughout the course, one entry per lecture: what I did, what I learned, and the questions I still had. My use of AI tools is recorded separately in the AI Use Log.


Date: 27 July 2026
Topic covered: Foundations
What I Did:
Plotted time series plots for discrete and continuous time series data: Section 1
What I Learned:
A time series is an ordered sequence of observations collected over time. The ordering matters since observations are often dependent on previous observations (sequential correlation).






Assumption



Equally spaced measurements.








Assumption



Autocorrelation across time.


A time series is a single measurement taken at multiple points through time to give a series of measurements through time.
Noise (stochastic) in data introduces different realisations. An observed time series is only one realisation of an underlying stochastic process. This is important as we are not just trying to model the observations but the process that generated them.
Questions:
Q: How does noise introduce different realisations?
A: In normal regression the pattern is fixed and the noise sits on top of it:
\[
y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + e_i,
\] where each error term is independent.
In an AR process the noise actually builds the pattern. This means that every apparent trend is made of past shocks that haven’t died away yet. A different set of shocks will give a different shape because the shape of the path comes from noise. It isn’t that time series errors are correlated but that each observation is a weighted sum of every past shock making observations correlated.


Code
set.seed(1)
par(mfrow = c(2, 3))
for (i in 1:6) plot(arima.sim(list(ar = 0.9), n = 100), main = paste("Realisation", i), ylab = "y")





What to Do Next:
The Forecasting Problem
Links: AI Log



Date: 3 August 2026
Topic covered: The Forecasting Problem
What I Did:
Looked at stationary AR processes: Section 1
What I Learned:
A forecast horizon is how far into the future you try to predict values. When looking at time series data we are looking for stable, informative patterns (not just a lot of data).






Forecasting vs Goal setting vs Planning



A forecast is a prediction about what will happen in the future based on evidence that we have (with some uncertainty). Goal setting is what we want to happen in the future and planning is how we reach our goal.


The uncertainty associated with forecasting gives rise to forecast intervals (not just point estimates).
A random walk is a process where memory is permanent. Every future shock accumulates endlessly resulting in forecast variance growing linearly. A stationary AR is a process where memory decays geometrically. Shocks die out, forcing the forecast back to the process mean.
Questions:
Q: If a process changes over time, at what point can we discard previous observations when forecasting?
A: This is decided by the model and is called the model’s memory. A mean benchmark will use every observation and just forecast the mean, the naive benchmark will use the most recent observation, exponential smoothing uses all observations but weights them differently (older observations are given less weight). You would also discard observations if a structural break occurs.






Note



When determining the number of observations to estimate the model (training set) more is usually better, unless the process has changed.


What to Do Next:
Exploring a Series
Links: AI Log



Date: 17 August 2026
Topics covered: Exploring a Series, Benchmarks and Forecast Accuracy
What I Did:
Worked through Time Series Analysis in R using the AirPassengers dataset: Section 1
What I Learned:
Time domain looks at previous observations whereas the frequency domain looks at cycles at different frequencies. Often you will need to look at both of these domains.






Trend vs Seasonality vs Cycles



A trend is the long-run direction of movement in a time series. Seasonality models a pattern that repeats itself at a fixed AND known interval. A cycle is a long oscillation where the length is NOT fixed.


When dealing with time series data you may encounter changing variability. Here you need to transform the data to stabilise variance and difference to remove trend and seasonality. When structural breaks are present in the data you can either use an indicator variable at the break or you can fit separate models on either side of the break.
There are 4 benchmark forecasting models: Mean, Naive, Seasonal naive and Drift.






Residuals are not forecast errors



Residuals are for diagnostics; forecast errors are for evaluation!


You cannot run normal cross-validation on time series data since the ordering of observations matters. Future observations must never be used when estimating a forecasting model.
Questions:
Q: How do you identify a significant structural break?
A: This can be done using formal tests, dependent on whether the date of the break is known prior to looking at the data. If the date is known in advance (e.g. a policy change), you can use Chow’s test. Chow’s test fits the model before and after the date of the break and uses an F-test to check if there is a statistically significant difference in model parameters. If the date is unknown you can run a Chow test at every possible date and take the largest F, compared against adjusted critical values. This is a sup-F test and accounts for having searched over every date, making it harder to declare a break.
What to Do Next:
Operators, Stationarity and White Noise
Links: AI Log



Date: 19 August 2026
Topic covered: Three Validation Strategies, Linear Models for the Conditional Mean
What I Did:
Continued working through Time Series Analysis in R using the AirPassengers dataset: Section 1
What I Learned:
Since you can’t perform regular cross-validation on time series data you use a different approach. Walk-forward validation advances the forecast origin one step at a time and re-estimates the model at each step. Expanding window validation keeps every historical observation while moving the forecast origin forward. Sliding window validation keeps the training window length fixed while moving the forecast origin forward.
Expanding window is good for stable processes whereas sliding window is good for rapidly changing processes.
We want our data to be stationary and for the residuals to be white noise. To restore stationarity you can transform the data to stabilise the variance and take linear/seasonal differences to remove trend and seasonality. Log-transformations reduce a multiplicative model to an additive model.
Weak white noise requires uncorrelated observations with zero mean and constant variance but strict white noise requires iid observations.
Questions:
Q: What is the difference between walk-forward and expanding window?
A: In the notes they are the same procedure: the training set always starts at \(y_1\) and grows by one observation each time the forecast origin moves forward. “Walk-forward” describes how the origin moves and “expanding window” describes what is kept. The slides list them as separate strategies, but note that they use the same growth rule. The difference is that walk-forward re-estimates the model at every step, so it has a higher computational cost. The real contrast is with the sliding window, which drops the oldest observation at each step.

Conditional Variance Models

Date: 24 August 2026
Topic covered: Linear Models for the Conditional Mean
What I Did:
Fit both ARIMA and SARIMA to the AirPassengers dataset: Section 1
What I Learned:
The moving average, MA(\(q\)), model is driven by lagged shocks. The dependence is based on errors not actual observations. The model has short memory. An MA(\(q\)) is always stationary and is restricted to be invertible.
The autoregressive, AR(\(p\)), model regresses a series on its own path.
ARMA combines both MA and AR models and is fitted by maximum likelihood, not OLS, since the past shocks are never observed.






Note



ACF and PACF graphs are used to determine which ARMA model to fit. An AR(\(p\)) has a PACF that cuts off after lag \(p\). An MA(\(q\)) has an ACF that cuts off after lag \(q\).


The ARIMA(\(p,d,q\)) model allows for differencing and the SARIMA model includes seasonality.
Questions:
Q: How can you determine if there is additional seasonality in a dataset after differencing or if it is just noise? For example in Section 1, there were still spikes at some lags in the PACF after log-transforming and differencing the AirPassengers dataset.
A: You can check if the residuals look like white noise by using a Ljung-Box test. A non-significant test means that there is no evidence of remaining autocorrelation (even if there are still a few lags that spike in the ACF/PACF). At the 5% level about 1 in 20 lags will spike by chance.

Date: 16 September 2026
Topic covered: Conditional Variance Models (ARCH and GARCH)
What I Did:
Worked through the provided Lab: Section 1
What I Learned:
All previous models have simply modelled the conditional mean and assumed constant variance. This fails for financial return data as it understates risk during periods where risk is highest and overstates risk when it is lowest. We now have both a mean (predictable component of the series) and a variance (conditional variance) equation.






Note



A series can be uncorrelated and still highly predictable in magnitude.


The ARCH model specifies conditional variance as a function of past squared innovations. The simplest case being \(\sigma^2_t = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1 \varepsilon_{t-1}^2\).






Volatility clustering



Large changes tend to follow large changes and small changes tend to follow small changes. Returns are often uncorrelated, hence why the ACF of returns indicates very little, however squared returns can be strongly autocorrelated.


The GARCH model adds the previous conditional variance to the ARCH equation. This makes it equivalent to an ARCH model with infinite memory. A GARCH(1,1) model is usually sufficient in practice.
\[
\sigma_t^2 = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1 \varepsilon_{t-1}^2 + \beta_1 \sigma_{t-1}^2,
\] where \(\alpha_1\) measures how strongly volatility reacts to a new shock, \(\beta_1\) measures how long that reaction lasts, \(\alpha_1 + \beta_1\) is the persistence.
Questions:
Q: Why must \(\alpha_1 + \beta_1 < 1\)?
A: When \(\alpha_1 + \beta_1 < 1\) this ensures that the long-run variance is \(\bar{\sigma}^2 = \frac{\alpha_0}{1- \alpha_1 - \beta_1}\) and that the process has a benchmark variance for the volatility to return to. When \(\alpha_1 + \beta_1 = 1\) (IGARCH) the shocks to volatility are permanent. This means that all the weight is on the past and none is on the long-run level. This is the variance equivalent of a random walk.
What to Do Next:
Spectral Analysis

Date: 14 September 2026
Topic covered: Exponential Smoothing
What I Did:
Worked through Exponential Smoothing Exercises: Section 2
What I Learned:
Exponential smoothing forecasts are weighted averages of past observations. Weights decrease exponentially the further back in time you go. The smoothing parameter \(\alpha\) adjusts the weight put on past observations. A large \(\alpha\) puts a lot of weight on the most recent observation, similar to the Naive forecast. A small \(\alpha\) averages over a long history, similar to the Mean forecast. This is similar to GARCH but applied to observations instead of squared shocks.






SES vs Holt vs Holt-Winters



Simple exponential smoothing (SES) only updates a level resulting in flat forecasts. Holt’s method adds a trend equation, that describes the slope, so forecasts follow a straight line. Holt-Winters adds a seasonal equation. Each component gets its own smoothing parameter (\(\alpha\), \(\beta\), \(\gamma\)).


The smoothing parameters and initial states (\(\ell_0\), \(b_0\)) are estimated by minimising the sum of squared one-step-ahead errors. Fitted values are one-step-ahead forecasts, so residuals are always one-step-ahead errors.
To turn the exponential smoothing algorithm into a state-space model we can write it in error-correction form: \(y_t = \ell_{t-1} + e_t\), \(\ell_t = \ell_{t-1} + \alpha e_t\). This allows us to estimate \(\sigma\) and build prediction intervals.
This is what ets() does.

Standard prediction intervals only capture the random error and ignore the uncertainty in parameter estimates and choice of model.

Q: How do we get variances of SES forecasts (\(\sigma^2[1+\alpha^2(h-1)]\)) if the point forecasts are flat?
A: The point forecast stays at \(\ell_T\), but every future error also moves the level by \(\alpha e_t\). These shifts add up, so uncertainty grows linearly with \(h\) even though the mean does not change.

Topic covered: State-Space Models
What I Did:

What I Learned:
A state-space model has both an observation equation and a state equation.
The observation equation \(y_t = F\theta_t + v_t\) links what we observe to an unobserved state whereas the state equation \(\theta_t = G\theta_{t-1} + w_t\) describes how the state changes over time.






Note



Regression, ARIMA and exponential smoothing models can all be written in state-space form. State-space models don’t need stationarity since trend and seasonality are modelled directly and allowed to change over time.


The Kalman filter is a recursive algorithm that first predicts and then updates. First the state, \(a_t, R_t\), and the next observation, \(f_t, Q_t\), are predicted. Then the state estimate, \(m_t, C_t\), is updated. The updated estimate is a weighted average of the prediction and the new observation where the Kalman gain decides how much weight is assigned to the observation.






Bayesian Framework



The Kalman filter works in a Bayesian way where, \(\text{posterior} \propto \text{prior} \times \text{likelihood}\). The posterior becomes the prior of the next step.


Questions:
Q: How do I decide which variances in \(W\) should be allowed to be non-zero?
A: A non-zero variance lets that state change over time and a zero variance keeps it fixed. The structure of the model decides which states can have noise. In the CO\(_2\) model in Section 2 only the level, slope and current seasonal effect get noise, because the other seasonal states are just the previous effects shifted along. The size of the variances can then be estimated by maximum likelihood. If an estimated variance is essentially zero, that state can be fixed, and models can be compared with the likelihood or AIC, e.g. static (\(W = 0\)) vs time-varying coefficients in the US consumption example.

Date: 5 October 2026
Topic covered: Kalman Filter
What I Did:
Continued working through the dlm practical and the State Space and Kalman Filter tutorial: Section 2
What I Learned:
The Kalman filter is used to filter and forecast in dynamic linear Gaussian systems. This filter is recursive so we can process new observations as they arrive. The Kalman smoother starts at the end of a series and works backwards. This is better for looking backwards (not prediction).






Filtering vs Smoothing vs Forecasting



If we estimate the state at time \(t\) using data up to time \(s\):

\(s < t\) = forecasting
\(s = t\) = filtering
\(s > t\) = smoothing



Forecasting and filtering are done using the Kalman filter. Smoothing is done using the Kalman smoother.
The likelihood is the product of one-step-ahead predictive densities, \(y_t \mid y_{1:t-1} \sim N(f_t, Q_t)\). The unknown variances, \(V\) and \(W\), can be estimated by maximum likelihood.
Prediction intervals use \(Q_t = FR_tF' + V\). They are prediction intervals (not confidence intervals) because they are for a future observation and include the observation noise, \(V\), as well as the uncertainty about the state.
If there are missing observations present in the data, there is nothing to update with and the Kalman gain will be zero. Consecutive missing observations increase uncertainty.






Method




The prior predicts the next state from the previous estimate of the state, with some uncertainty (state equation).
The likelihood asks how likely the new observation is given all possible states (observation equation).
The new posterior, for the current state, is given by combining the likelihood and the prior.



Questions:
Q: Why does the Kalman filter only work for linear Gaussian state-space models?
A: The Kalman filter does a linear transformation of a Gaussian which gives another Gaussian.
\[
\text{Gaussian prior} \times \text{Gaussian likelihood} \propto \text{Gaussian posterior}
\] The Kalman filter only keeps track of the mean and variance. When we have a non-linear or non-Gaussian distribution we either end up with a skewed distribution or a posterior with no closed form.

Topic covered: Hidden Markov Models 1
What I Did:
Worked through Questions 1, 3, 4 and 7 of the HMM tutorial and wrote the forward algorithm from first principles: Section 2
What I Learned:
A hidden Markov model (HMM) has an unobserved state process, \(C_t\), that follows a Markov chain and an observed process, \(X_t\), whose distribution depends only on the current state. Each state has its own state-dependent distribution (e.g. Poisson or Gaussian).






Assumption



The next state only depends on the current state (Markov property).


The Markov chain is described by the transition probability matrix \(\Gamma\), where \(\gamma_{ij} = P(C_{t+1} = j \mid C_t = i)\), and the initial distribution \(\boldsymbol{\delta}\). A large diagonal in \(\Gamma\) means that the states are persistent.






Independent mixture vs HMM



An independent mixture draws a new state at every time point, independently of the last one. An HMM lets the state depend on the previous state, which creates autocorrelation in the observations.


The likelihood, \(L_T = \boldsymbol{\delta}\mathbf{P}(x_1)\Gamma\mathbf{P}(x_2)\cdots\Gamma\mathbf{P}(x_T)\mathbf{1}'\), is calculated with the forward algorithm and maximised numerically. The forward probabilities are scaled at every step to avoid underflow.
Questions:
Q: Why does an HMM produce autocorrelated observations if the observations are conditionally independent given the states?
A: The observations are only independent once we know the states. A large observation makes a high-mean state more likely and, since the states are persistent, the next observation is likely to come from that same state.

What I Did:

What I Learned:
Once an HMM has been fitted we usually want to know which state the process was in. This is called decoding.






Local vs global decoding



Local decoding finds the most likely state at each time point separately, using the forward and backward probabilities. Global decoding finds the most likely sequence of states using the Viterbi algorithm. The two can disagree.


The number of states is chosen with AIC or BIC. The likelihood of an HMM often has several local maxima, so the model should be fitted from several different starting values.

Q: Why can’t short visits to a state be recovered by decoding?
A: A single visit to a state needs two unlikely transitions, there and back, and if the state-dependent distributions overlap, the observation is often also likely under the surrounding state. In the Viterbi exercise in Section 2, the single visit to state C at time 2 was decoded as A.

Topic covered: Foundations
What I Did:
Plotted time series plots for discrete and continuous time series data: Section 1
What I Learned:
A time series is an ordered sequence of observations collected over time. The ordering matters since observations are often dependent on previous observations (sequential correlation).






Assumption



Equally spaced measurements.








Assumption



Autocorrelation across time.


A time series is a single measurement taken at multiple points through time to give a series of measurements through time.
Noise (stochastic) in data introduces different realisations. An observed time series is only one realisation of an underlying stochastic process. This is important as we are not just trying to model the observations but the process that generated them.
Questions:
Q: How does noise introduce different realisations?
A: In normal regression the pattern is fixed and the noise sits on top of it:
\[
y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + e_i,
\] where each error term is independent.
In an AR process the noise actually builds the pattern. This means that every apparent trend is made of past shocks that haven’t died away yet. A different set of shocks will give a different shape because the shape of the path comes from noise. It isn’t that time series errors are correlated but that each observation is a weighted sum of every past shock making observations correlated.

set.seed(1)
par(mfrow = c(2, 3))
for (i in 1:6) plot(arima.sim(list(ar = 0.9), n = 100), main = paste("Realisation", i), ylab = "y")

Date: 3 August 2026
Topic covered: The Forecasting Problem
What I Did:
Looked at stationary AR processes: Section 1
What I Learned:
A forecast horizon is how far into the future you try to predict values. When looking at time series data we are looking for stable, informative patterns (not just a lot of data).






Forecasting vs Goal setting vs Planning



A forecast is a prediction about what will happen in the future based on evidence that we have (with some uncertainty). Goal setting is what we want to happen in the future and planning is how we reach our goal.


The uncertainty associated with forecasting gives rise to forecast intervals (not just point estimates).
A random walk is a process where memory is permanent. Every future shock accumulates endlessly resulting in forecast variance growing linearly. A stationary AR is a process where memory decays geometrically. Shocks die out, forcing the forecast back to the process mean.
Questions:
Q: If a process changes over time, at what point can we discard previous observations when forecasting?
A: This is decided by the model and is called the model’s memory. A mean benchmark will use every observation and just forecast the mean, the naive benchmark will use the most recent observation, exponential smoothing uses all observations but weights them differently (older observations are given less weight). You would also discard observations if a structural break occurs.






Note



When determining the number of observations to estimate the model (training set) more is usually better, unless the process has changed.

Date: 17 August 2026
Topics covered: Exploring a Series, Benchmarks and Forecast Accuracy
What I Did:
Worked through Time Series Analysis in R using the AirPassengers dataset: Section 1
What I Learned:
Time domain looks at previous observations whereas the frequency domain looks at cycles at different frequencies. Often you will need to look at both of these domains.






Trend vs Seasonality vs Cycles



A trend is the long-run direction of movement in a time series. Seasonality models a pattern that repeats itself at a fixed AND known interval. A cycle is a long oscillation where the length is NOT fixed.


When dealing with time series data you may encounter changing variability. Here you need to transform the data to stabilise variance and difference to remove trend and seasonality. When structural breaks are present in the data you can either use an indicator variable at the break or you can fit separate models on either side of the break.
There are 4 benchmark forecasting models: Mean, Naive, Seasonal naive and Drift.






Residuals are not forecast errors



Residuals are for diagnostics; forecast errors are for evaluation!


You cannot run normal cross-validation on time series data since the ordering of observations matters. Future observations must never be used when estimating a forecasting model.
Questions:
Q: How do you identify a significant structural break?
A: This can be done using formal tests, dependent on whether the date of the break is known prior to looking at the data. If the date is known in advance (e.g. a policy change), you can use Chow’s test. Chow’s test fits the model before and after the date of the break and uses an F-test to check if there is a statistically significant difference in model parameters. If the date is unknown you can run a Chow test at every possible date and take the largest F, compared against adjusted critical values. This is a sup-F test and accounts for having searched over every date, making it harder to declare a break.
