# Lagged response: 
y_lag = c(NA, y[-length(y)])







Figure 38: ACF and PACF of the residuals from the ARMAX model.




The residual autocorrelation is much smaller but still present (Figure 38). The coefficient of \(x\) (-4.506) is closer to \(-4\), but it only measures the immediate effect of \(x\), since \(y_{t-1}\) carries part of the past effect of \(x\). If \(x\) increased by one unit permanently, the long-run effect would be \(\hat{\beta}_1/(1-\hat{\phi}) = -10.21\), which is far from the true \(-4\). Thus, the ARMAX model is misspecified. The data were generated with AR(1) errors, which also require the term \(-\phi\beta_1 x_{t-1}\).


Click to toggle source code
# Autoregressive distributed lag model (x_{t-1} included):
x_lag = c(NA, x[-length(x)])
adl   = lm(y ~ y_lag + x + x_lag)
coef(adl)


(Intercept)       y_lag           x       x_lag 
 -0.1922132   0.9576004  -3.9691383   3.8473506 


Click to toggle source code
c(coef_x_lag = unname(coef(adl)["x_lag"]),
  minus_phi_times_beta = unname(-coef(adl)["y_lag"] * coef(adl)["x"]))


          coef_x_lag minus_phi_times_beta 
            3.847351             3.800848 


The inclusion of \(x_{t-1}\) results in the autoregressive distributed lag model. Its coefficients approximately satisfy the “common factor” restriction \(\gamma = -\phi\beta_1\), where \(\gamma\) is the coefficient of \(x_{t-1}\). This is what the regression with AR(1) errors implies. Thus, the regression model with AR(1) errors is an ARMAX model that includes \(x_{t-1}\) with its coefficient restricted to \(-\phi \beta_1\).


Regression with AR(1) errors


Click to toggle source code
a2 = arima(y, order = c(1, 0, 0), xreg = x)
a2



Call:
arima(x = y, order = c(1, 0, 0), xreg = x)

Coefficients:
         ar1  intercept        x
      0.9762     4.7905  -3.9967
s.e.  0.0188     3.2704   0.0830

sigma^2 estimated as 1.021:  log likelihood = -144.46,  aic = 296.92


When we model the errors as an AR(1) process we obtain a slope of -3.997 with a standard error of 0.083. This is very close to the true value of \(-4\), and the standard error is much smaller when compared to OLS (0.495). The intercept is poorly estimated (4.79 instead of 1). Since \(\hat{\phi}\) is close to 1 the errors behave almost as a random walk. Therefore, the intercept and the level of the error process are difficult to separate. In this simulation the errors did not start at their mean of 0 but at \(\eta_1 = 10\). arima() estimates the model by maximum likelihood using the state-space form and the Kalman filter.


Transforming the variables
Equation 1 in the notes motivates a transformation that removes the serial correlation. Defining \(y_t^* = y_t - \phi y_{t-1}\) and \(x_t^* = x_t - \phi x_{t-1}\) gives
\[
y_t^* = \beta_0(1-\phi) + \beta_1 x_t^* + e_t,
\]
where \(e_t\) is white noise, so the OLS assumptions hold for the transformed model. Since \(\phi\) is unknown, it is replaced by \(\hat{\phi}\), the lag 1 autocorrelation of the OLS residuals, which makes this a feasible two-step estimator.


Click to toggle source code
phi_hat = acf(resid(a1), plot = FALSE)$acf[2]
phi_hat


[1] 0.9037115


Click to toggle source code
y_star = y-phi_hat*y_lag
x_star = x-phi_hat*x_lag

a_star = lm(y_star ~ x_star)
summary(a_star)$coefficients


             Estimate Std. Error   t value     Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept)  0.202568 0.11196307   1.80924 7.351125e-02
x_star      -3.992501 0.08782497 -45.45975 3.308591e-67


The estimated slope (-3.993) is close to the true value of \(-4\), even though \(\hat{\phi} = 0.9\) underestimates \(\phi = 0.95\). However, the response is now \(y_t^*\) as opposed to \(y_t\), so \(\beta_1\) describes how \(y\) responds to \(x\) after removing the carried-over error. When \(\phi\) is close to 1 this is approximately the change in \(y\) for a change in \(x\). The intercept estimates \(\beta_0(1-\phi)\), not \(\beta_0\). Since the response differs, the AIC of this model cannot be compared with those of the other models.


Generalised least squares


Click to toggle source code
m_gls = gls(y ~ x, correlation = corAR1(), method = "ML")
summary(m_gls)$tTable


                Value Std.Error    t-value      p-value
(Intercept)  4.789836 3.2008467   1.496428 1.377559e-01
x           -3.996669 0.0838432 -47.668376 1.315676e-69


Click to toggle source code
coef(m_gls$modelStruct$corStruct, unconstrained = FALSE)  # estimated phi


      Phi 
0.9762058 


gls() estimates the regression coefficients and the AR(1) parameter jointly by maximum likelihood. For a given \(\phi\), the coefficients are the GLS estimator from the notes,
\[
\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} = (Z'V^{-1}Z)^{-1}Z'V^{-1}\mathbf{y}, \qquad V_{ij} \propto \phi^{|i-j|},
\]
where \(Z\) is the design matrix and \(V\) is the correlation structure implied by AR(1) errors. Iterating between estimating \(\phi\) from the residuals and refitting with the updated \(V\) (feasible GLS) gives very similar estimates. The estimates match those from arima() because both fit the same model by maximum likelihood.


Minimising the independent SSE from first principles
For a regression with AR(1) errors, the independent errors are \(e_t = (y_t - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_t) - \phi(y_{t-1} - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_{t-1})\), so the parameters can be estimated by minimising \(\sum_{t=2}^{n} e_t^2\).


Click to toggle source code
# Sum of squared errors:
sse_ar1_err = function(par, y, x) {
  b0  = par[1]
  b1  = par[2]
  phi = par[3]
  eta = y-b0-b1*x                         # regression errors
  e   = eta[-1]-phi*eta[-length(eta)]         # independent errors
  sum(e^2)
}

fit_sse = optim(par = c(coef(a1), 0.5), fn = sse_ar1_err, y = y, x = x,
                method = "BFGS", control = list(maxit = 1000))

# Fitting arima() for comparison:
a2_css = arima(y, order = c(1, 0, 0), xreg = x, method = "CSS")

kable(data.frame(
  Method = c("My SSE + optim()", "arima(), CSS", "arima(), ML", "gls(), ML", "True value"),
  Intercept = c(fit_sse$par[1], coef(a2_css)["intercept"], coef(a2)["intercept"],
                coef(m_gls)[1], 1),
  Slope = c(fit_sse$par[2], coef(a2_css)[3], coef(a2)[3], coef(m_gls)[2], -4),
  phi = c(fit_sse$par[3], coef(a2_css)["ar1"], coef(a2)["ar1"],
          coef(m_gls$modelStruct$corStruct, unconstrained = FALSE), 0.95)
), digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)

Minimising the sum of squared independent errors with optim() reproduces arima(method = "CSS") exactly, since both use the same conditional sum of squares criterion. All four methods agree closely on the slope and \(\phi\), but differ on the intercept. CSS conditions on the first observation, so the starting value \(\eta_1 = 10\) has no influence, and the intercept (1.134) is close to the true value of 1. Maximum likelihood (arima() and gls()) treats \(\eta_1\) as a draw from the stationary distribution with mean 0, so the intercept is pushed up to 4.790 to account for the high starting value.


Model comparison


Click to toggle source code
kable(data.frame(
  Model = c("a1: OLS", "arx1: ARMAX", "a2: AR(1) errors"),
  df = c(3, 4, 4),
  AIC = c(AIC(a1), AIC(arx1), AIC(a2))
), digits = 1, row.names = FALSE)

The regression with AR(1) errors has the lowest AIC (296.9, compared with 466.5 for the ARMAX model and 577.7 for OLS). This is expected, since it matches the data-generating process. The differences in AIC are large so the rankings hold even though the comparison is only approximate. The ARMAX model is fitted to 99 observations, whereas OLS and the exact maximum likelihood fit from arima() use all 100. In addition, arima() evaluates the likelihood through the state-space representation, which is not identical to the Gaussian likelihood lm() computes for independent errors.


Forecasting with a regression with AR(1) errors
Forecasting \(y_{T+h}\) requires values of \(x_{T+h}\), which are not observed. Here \(x\) is assumed to remain at its sample mean for the next 10 periods. The \(h\)-step forecast is then
\[
\hat{y}_{T+h} = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 x_{T+h} + \hat{\phi}^h \hat{\eta}_T,
\]
so the error component decays geometrically from its last estimated value \(\hat{\eta}_T\) towards zero, and the forecasts converge to the regression line \(\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 \bar{x}\).

The prediction intervals widen quickly with the horizon (Figure 39). This is due to \(\hat{\phi}\) being close to 1, so the error process has long memory. The forecast variance \(\sigma^2(1 + \phi^2 + \dots + \phi^{2(h-1)})\) keeps growing. These intervals are conditional on the future values of \(x\) (assumed known). If \(x\) was forecast as well, they would underestimate the uncertainty.

title: Overview
text:
Dynamic linear models with dlm
A dynamic linear model (DLM) is a linear, Gaussian state-space model. “Dynamic” means that the state \(\theta_t\) (level, slope, seasonal effects, regression coefficients) is allowed to change over time.

Random walk plus noise
The local level model has \(F = G = 1\): the level follows a random walk and we observe it with noise.


Click to toggle source code
# Simulate from a random walk plus noise model:
rwpn = function(V = 0.8, W = 0.2, m0 = 0, C0 = 100, n = 100) {
  y = numeric(n)
  mu = numeric(n)
  for (i in 1:n) {
    if (i == 1) {
      mu[i] = rnorm(1, m0, sqrt(C0))        # initial state from the prior
    } else {
      mu[i] = rnorm(1, mu[i - 1], sqrt(W))  # state equation
    }
    y[i] = rnorm(1, mu[i], sqrt(V))         # observation equation
  }
  return(list(y = y, mu = mu))
}

set.seed(10)
sim_rw = rwpn()
y_rw = sim_rw$y








rnorm() takes a standard deviation



In the original prac code rnorm(1, m0, C0) uses \(C_0 = 100\) as a standard deviation, while the model treats \(V\), \(W\) and \(C_0\) as variances. This is why the original simulated series started around \(-11\). I used sqrt() so that the simulation matches the model that is fitted below.



Defining the model


Click to toggle source code
# Define the model through its matrices:
mod_rwpn = dlm(FF = 1, V = 0.8, GG = 1, W = 0.2, m0 = 0, C0 = 100)
mod_rwpn

dlmModPoly(order = 1, dV = 0.8, dW = 0.2, C0 = 100)

order = 1 gives a random walk for the state (local level model) and order = 2 gives a random walk plus drift for the level (local linear trend). Individual matrices can be changed with the replacement functions:


Click to toggle source code
mod_copy = mod_rwpn
C0(mod_copy) = 80
C0(mod_copy)


     [,1]
[1,]   80




Kalman filter and smoother


Click to toggle source code
filt_rw = dlmFilter(y_rw, mod_rwpn)
names(filt_rw)


[1] "y"   "mod" "m"   "U.C" "D.C" "a"   "U.R" "D.R" "f"  


Click to toggle source code
# Note: m has one more element than y (first element is m0)
length(filt_rw$m)


[1] 101


Click to toggle source code
# Filtered variances C_t (from SVD stored by dlm):
C_rw = unlist(dlmSvd2var(filt_rw$U.C, filt_rw$D.C))

# Kalman smoother:
smooth_rw = dlmSmooth(filt_rw)
S_rw = unlist(dlmSvd2var(smooth_rw$U.S, smooth_rw$D.S))


dlmFilter() returns the filtered states m (\(\theta_t \mid y_{1:t} \sim N(m_t, C_t)\)), the one-step-ahead state predictions a (\(\theta_t \mid y_{1:t-1} \sim N(a_t, R_t)\)), the one-step-ahead forecasts of the observations f, and the variances in SVD form (U.C, D.C, U.R, D.R). dlmSvd2var() turns these back into variance matrices.





Figure 40: Simulated random walk plus noise data (grey points), true level (black), filtered level with 95% interval (pink) and smoothed level (blue).




The filtered level (pink) only uses observations up to time \(t\), so it reacts to changes with a delay. The smoothed level (blue) also uses later observations, so it is smoother and closer to the true level (black) (Figure 40). The smoothed variances are smaller than the filtered ones (average 0.198 vs 0.319), except at the end of the series where they are the same: at \(t = T\) there is no future information to add.


Maximum likelihood
If \(V\) and \(W\) are unknown, the Kalman filter gives the likelihood through the one-step-ahead prediction errors, and dlmMLE() passes it to optim(). The variances are estimated on the log scale so they stay positive.


Click to toggle source code
# Function to build model from log parameters:
build_rw = function(par) {
  dlmModPoly(order = 1, dV = exp(par[1]), dW = exp(par[2]))
}

# Maximise the likelihood:
fit_rw = dlmMLE(y_rw, parm = c(0, 0), build = build_rw, hessian = TRUE)
fit_rw$convergence  # 0 = converged


[1] 0


Click to toggle source code
# Estimates with 95% CIs (log scale, then back-transformed):
se_log = sqrt(diag(solve(fit_rw$hessian)))
kable(data.frame(
  Parameter = c("V", "W"),
  True = c(0.8, 0.2),
  Estimate = exp(fit_rw$par),
  Lower = exp(fit_rw$par - 1.96 * se_log),
  Upper = exp(fit_rw$par + 1.96 * se_log)
), digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)

The confidence intervals are wide, especially for \(W\). With 100 observations it is hard to separate “the level moved” from “the observation was noisy”, because both create variation in \(y_t\). The signal-to-noise ratio \(W/V\) is what matters for the filter.


Forecasting
For a random walk plus noise model, the forecast is flat at the last filtered level (just like SES), and the uncertainty grows linearly with the horizon.


Click to toggle source code
mod_rw_fit = build_rw(fit_rw$par)
filt_rw_fit = dlmFilter(y_rw, mod_rw_fit)
fc_rw = dlmForecast(filt_rw_fit, nAhead = 10)

str(fc_rw, max.level = 1)

 $ R:List of 10

 $ Q:List of 10


dlmForecast() returns forecasts of the state (a, with variances R) and of the observations (f, with variances Q). Note that \(Q_t = R_t + V\).





Figure 41: Ten-step forecasts for the random walk plus noise model: 95% interval for the level (dark pink, uses R) and 95% prediction interval for new observations (light pink, uses Q).










State interval vs prediction interval



The original prac plotted \(a_t \pm 1.96\sqrt{R_t}\). That is an interval for the future level, not for future observations. A prediction interval for \(y_{T+h}\) must use \(Q_t = R_t + V\), which also includes the observation noise. In Figure 41 the prediction interval is much wider.

Because the smoother uses future observations, it starts dropping before 1898, while the filtered level only reacts afterwards.

Figure 44: Filtered level with 95% intervals for the full Nile series (blue) and with 1910–1915 removed (pink).




When an observation is missing there is nothing to update with: the Kalman gain is zero, so \(m_t = a_t\) and \(C_t = R_t = C_{t-1} + W\). The filtered level stays flat through the gap and the interval widens by \(W\) every year (Figure 44). As soon as observations return, the interval shrinks back.


Seasonality: basic structural model for CO\(_2\)
The basic structural model adds 11 seasonal states (12 monthly effects that sum to zero) to the local linear trend:
\[
\begin{aligned}
y_t &= \mu_t + s_t + v_t, & v_t \sim N(0, V) \\
\mu_t &= \mu_{t-1} + \beta_{t-1} + w_t, & w_t \sim N(0, \sigma^2_w) \\
\beta_t &= \beta_{t-1} + \gamma_t, & \gamma_t \sim N(0, \sigma^2_\gamma) \\
s_t &= -\sum_{j=1}^{S-1} s_{t-j} + \delta_t, & \delta_t \sim N(0, \sigma^2_\delta)
\end{aligned}
\]





Figure 45: Monthly atmospheric CO2 concentration at Mauna Loa, 1959–1997.




Figure 45 shows a steady upward trend and a regular yearly cycle with a constant amplitude (additive seasonality).

lik_s1 = function(p) {
  mod = dlmModPoly() + dlmModSeas(12)
  Wm = W(mod)
  diag(Wm)[1:3] = exp(p[1:3])  # level, slope and seasonal variances
  W(mod) = Wm
  V(mod) = exp(p[4])           # observation variance
  return(mod)
}

The prior is very vague (\(m_0 = 0\), \(C_0 = 10^7 I\) for all 13 states). After the first observation the filter knows that level + season ≈ 315, but it cannot tell how much of that is level and how much is the January effect. Until it has seen roughly a year of data, the seasonal effects are not identified, so the filtered level and seasonal states jump around wildly (right panel of Figure 46). After about a year the filter has learned the seasonal pattern and the level settles down.
The one-step-ahead forecasts filt_s1$f are the fitted values. After the first year they lie almost on top of the observations.

Seasonality with trigonometric terms
Instead of 11 seasonal states, the seasonal pattern can be built from sine and cosine waves (harmonics). The \(j\)th harmonic has frequency \(\omega_j = 2\pi j / s\) and needs two states. With \(q\) harmonics there are \(2q\) seasonal states, so \(q = 1\) gives a pure sine-shaped season with only 2 states. This links directly to the harmonics in Spectral Analysis in Section 1.

    Wm = W(mod)
    diag(Wm) = c(exp(p[1]), exp(p[2]), rep(exp(p[3]), k - 2))
    W(mod) = Wm
    V(mod) = exp(p[4])
    return(mod)
  }
}

title: Overview
section: The Kalman filter from first principles
text:
The Kalman filter from first principles
The function below implements the three steps for a univariate observation and a state of any dimension. \(F_t\) and \(G_t\) can be given either as fixed matrices or as functions of \(t\) (for time-varying models), and missing values (NA) are handled by skipping the update. The output is stored the same way as in dlmFilter(): row 1 of m (and element 1 of C) is the prior at time 0.


Click to toggle source code
# Function to code the Kalman filter from first principles: 
kalman_filter = function(y, FF, GG, V, W, m0, C0) {
  n = length(y)
  p = length(m0)

  # Define F_t and G_t:
  get_F = if (is.function(FF)) FF else function(t) FF
  get_G = if (is.function(GG)) GG else function(t) GG

  a = matrix(NA, n, p)        # prior means
  R = vector("list", n)
  m = matrix(NA, n + 1, p)    # posterior means
  C = vector("list", n + 1)
  f = Q = e = rep(NA, n)      # forecasts

  m[1, ] = m0                
  C[[1]] = as.matrix(C0)
  loglik = 0

  for (t in 1:n) {
    Ft = matrix(get_F(t), nrow = 1)
    Gt = as.matrix(get_G(t))

    # 1. Predict the state:
    a[t, ] = Gt %*% m[t, ]
    R[[t]] = Gt %*% C[[t]] %*% t(Gt) + W

    # 2. Predict the observation:
    f[t] = drop(Ft %*% a[t, ])
    Q[t] = drop(Ft %*% R[[t]] %*% t(Ft)) + V

    # 3. Update with y_t:
    if (is.na(y[t])) {
      # No observation = no update
      m[t + 1, ] = a[t, ]
      C[[t + 1]] = R[[t]]
    } else {
      e[t] = y[t] - f[t]                    # one-step-ahead prediction error
      K = R[[t]] %*% t(Ft) / Q[t]           # Kalman gain 
      m[t + 1, ] = a[t, ] + drop(K) * e[t]
      C[[t + 1]] = R[[t]] - K %*% Ft %*% R[[t]]
      loglik = loglik + dnorm(y[t], f[t], sqrt(Q[t]), log = TRUE)
    }
  }

  list(m = m, C = C, a = a, R = R, f = f, Q = Q, e = e, loglik = loglik)
}




Click to toggle source code
# Function to code the Kalman smoother from first principles: 
kalman_smoother = function(kf, GG) {
  n = nrow(kf$a)
  p = ncol(kf$a)
  get_G = if (is.function(GG)) GG else function(t) GG

  s = matrix(NA, n + 1, p)    # smoothed means
  S = vector("list", n + 1)

  # At last time point smoothed:
  s[n + 1, ] = kf$m[n + 1, ]
  S[[n + 1]] = kf$C[[n + 1]]

  # Backwards recursion:
  for (t in n:1) {
    Gt = as.matrix(get_G(t))
    J = kf$C[[t]] %*% t(Gt) %*% solve(kf$R[[t]])   # smoother gain
    s[t, ] = kf$m[t, ] + J %*% (s[t + 1, ] - kf$a[t, ])
    S[[t]] = kf$C[[t]] + J %*% (S[[t + 1]] - kf$R[[t]]) %*% t(J)
  }

  list(s = s, S = S)
}








Indexing



\(G_t\) is used in the prediction step for \(\theta_t\) (moving from \(t-1\) to \(t\)), and \(F_t\) is used to predict \(y_t\) from \(\theta_t\). Using \(G_{t-1}\) or \(F_{t-1}\) by mistake is easy and gives wrong results that still look reasonable. The extra row for time 0 in m is another place where off-by-one errors happen.



Checking my filter against dlm: the Nile data
I maximise my log-likelihood over \(\log V\) and \(\log W\) with optim(), using the same vague prior as dlmModPoly() (\(m_0 = 0\), \(C_0 = 10^7\)).

}

title: Overview
section: Topic exploration: exponential smoothing is a Kalman filter
text:
Topic exploration: exponential smoothing is a Kalman filter
Question: how is simple exponential smoothing related to the Kalman filter for the local level model?
For the local level model (\(F = G = 1\)), the update step is
\[
m_t = m_{t-1} + K_t(y_t - m_{t-1}),
\]
which is exactly the error-correction form of SES, \(\ell_t = \ell_{t-1} + \alpha(y_t - \ell_{t-1})\), with a time-varying \(\alpha = K_t\). The recursions for \(R_t\), \(C_t\) and \(K_t\) do not involve \(y_t\), so \(K_t\) is a fixed sequence that can be computed before seeing any data, and for the local level model it converges to a steady state. Setting \(C_t = C_{t-1} = C\) in \(R_t = C_{t-1} + W\), \(K_t = R_t/(R_t + V)\) and \(C_t = (1 - K_t)R_t\) and solving gives
\[
K_\infty = \frac{-q + \sqrt{q^2 + 4q}}{2}, \qquad q = \frac{W}{V} \ (\text{the signal-to-noise ratio}).
\]
\(K_\infty\) increases from 0 to 1 as \(q\) increases. So, after a few observations, the Kalman filter for the local level model is SES with \(\alpha = K_\infty\). The local level model also implies an ARIMA(0,1,1) for \(y_t\) (with \(\theta = K_\infty - 1 \in (-1, 0)\)), and the ARIMA(0,1,1) forecast is SES with \(\alpha = 1 + \theta\). Table 16 compares the steady-state gain with the gain from my filter, the ARIMA(0,1,1) estimate and the ses() estimate for the Nile data:


Click to toggle source code
q_nile = W_own / V_own
K_inf = (-q_nile + sqrt(q_nile^2 + 4 * q_nile)) / 2

# Kalman gain at each time point from own filter (F = 1, so K_t = R_t / Q_t):
K_t = unlist(kf_nile$R) / kf_nile$Q

# SES and ARIMA(0,1,1) fitted to the same data:
ses_nile = ses(Nile)
arima_nile = Arima(Nile, order = c(0, 1, 1))

kable(data.frame(
  Quantity = c("Steady-state Kalman gain $K_\\infty$ (from $\\hat{V}$ and $\\hat{W}$)",
               "Kalman gain $K_{100}$ from my filter",
               "$1 + \\hat{\\theta}$ from ARIMA(0,1,1)",
               "$\\hat{\\alpha}$ from `ses()`"),
  Value = c(K_inf, K_t[100], 1 + coef(arima_nile)["ma1"], ses_nile$model$par["alpha"])
), digits = 4, row.names = FALSE, escape = FALSE)

Figure 50: Kalman gain \(K_t\) of the local level model for the Nile data (pink), converging to its steady state \(K_\infty\) (purple dashed). The grey dotted line is the smoothing parameter estimated by ses().




The Kalman gain starts close to 1 (the vague prior means the first observation gets almost all the weight) and settles at \(K_\infty \approx 0.267\) within about ten years (Figure 50). \(1 + \hat{\theta} = 0.267\) from the ARIMA(0,1,1) is almost identical, because the local level model is an ARIMA(0,1,1) with \(\theta\) restricted to \((-1, 0)\), and both are fitted by maximum likelihood. The SES estimate is close but smaller (\(\hat{\alpha} = 0.246\)). The difference comes from how the parameters are estimated: ses() fits the single-source-of-error model ETS(A,N,N) and estimates \(\ell_0\) as a parameter, while the local level model has two independent errors and a vague prior on the initial level. With the same \(\alpha\) the three approaches would give identical forecasts once the filter has reached its steady state. With the estimated values the forecasts differ only slightly.
This gives the smoothing parameter \(\alpha\) a clear meaning: it is determined by the signal-to-noise ratio \(q = W/V\). A noisy series with a slowly moving level (small \(q\), like the Nile) gives a small \(\alpha\), so the forecast averages over many years. A series whose level moves a lot compared to the noise (like the oil data in Question 2) gives \(\alpha\) close to 1, so the forecast is essentially the last observation.

Tutorial: State-space models and the Kalman filter

Question 1: Simulation and a Kalman filter from first principles
\[
\begin{aligned}
y_t &= F_t\theta_t + v_t, \qquad v_t \sim N(0, V = 2) \\
\theta_t &= G_t\theta_{t-1} + w_t, \qquad w_t \sim N(0, W = 1) \\
\theta_0 &\sim N(0, 1)
\end{aligned}
\]
with \(G_t = \frac{1}{2}\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2}[2t+1]\right) = \frac{(-1)^t}{2}\) (since \(\sin(\pi t + \pi/2) = \cos(\pi t) = (-1)^t\)), and \(F_t \sim N(1, 0.2^2)\) rounded to one decimal, playing the role of an explanatory variable.
Because \(G_t\) alternates in sign, half of the previous state carries over with a flipped sign every step. This creates the cyclical (zig-zag) behaviour in \(\theta_t\).


Click to toggle source code
set.seed(42)

n_kf = 100
h_kf = 5
N_kf = n_kf + h_kf
V_true = 2
W_true = 1

# Time-varying system matrices (F_t also needed for forecast period):
FF_t = round(rnorm(N_kf, 1, 0.2), 1)
GG_t = (-1)^(1:N_kf) / 2

# Simulate the states and observations:
theta_kf = numeric(N_kf)
y_kf = numeric(N_kf)
theta_prev = rnorm(1, 0, 1)                                     # theta_0
for (t in 1:N_kf) {
  theta_kf[t] = GG_t[t] * theta_prev + rnorm(1, 0, sqrt(W_true)) # state equation
  y_kf[t] = FF_t[t] * theta_kf[t] + rnorm(1, 0, sqrt(V_true))    # observation equation
  theta_prev = theta_kf[t]
}

# Observed series (last 5 values held out to check forecasts):
y_obs = c(y_kf[1:n_kf], rep(NA, h_kf))



Parameter estimation
I use my kalman_filter() from above, with \(F_t\) and \(G_t\) passed as functions of \(t\). The likelihood is maximised over \(\log V\) and \(\log W\). The 5 NAs at the end do not contribute to the likelihood.


Click to toggle source code
# Function to calculate negative log-likelihood from log variances:
negll = function(parm, y, FF, GG) {
  -kalman_filter(y, FF = function(t) FF[t], GG = function(t) GG[t],
                 V = exp(parm[1]), W = exp(parm[2]), m0 = 0, C0 = 1)$loglik
}

fit_kf = optim(par = c(0, 0), fn = negll, y = y_obs, FF = FF_t, GG = GG_t,
               method = "BFGS", hessian = TRUE)

se_kf = sqrt(diag(solve(fit_kf$hessian)))
kable(data.frame(
  Parameter = c("V", "W"),
  True = c(V_true, W_true),
  Estimate = exp(fit_kf$par),
  Lower = exp(fit_kf$par - 1.96 * se_kf),
  Upper = exp(fit_kf$par + 1.96 * se_kf)
), digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)

W_hat = exp(fit_kf$par[2])
kf_out = kalman_filter(y_obs, FF = function(t) FF_t[t], GG = function(t) GG_t[t],
                       V = V_hat, W = W_hat, m0 = 0, C0 = 1)

# Filtered states and variances (without time-0 row):
m_kf = kf_out$m[-1, 1]
C_kf = unlist(kf_out$C[-1])


Both true values lie inside their 95% intervals (\(\hat{V} = 2.1\) and \(\hat{W} = 0.46\)), but the intervals are wide, especially for \(W\), whose upper limit is more than ten times its lower limit. The two variances are not easy to separate. Since \(|G_t| = 1/2\), the state forgets its past quickly, so \(\theta_t\) is close to white noise and \(y_t\) looks like noise with variance \(F_t^2\,\text{Var}(\theta_t) + V\). The changing \(F_t\) helps a little, because it scales the state part but not the observation noise, but the confidence intervals are still wide.
Check against dlm. dlm allows time-varying matrices through JFF, JGG and X: the entries of JFF/JGG say which column of X holds the value at each time.

mod_tv = dlm(FF = matrix(1), V = matrix(V_hat), GG = matrix(1), W = matrix(W_hat),
             m0 = 0, C0 = matrix(1),
             JFF = matrix(1), JGG = matrix(2), X = cbind(FF_t, GG_t))
filt_tv = dlmFilter(y_obs, mod_tv)

# Largest difference between own and dlm filtered states:
max(abs(as.numeric(dropFirst(filt_tv$m)) - m_kf))

Forecasts for \(h = 1, \ldots, 5\)
Adding NAs to the end of \(y\) makes the filter skip the update step, so \(m_t = a_t\), \(C_t = R_t\), and \(f_t, Q_t\) are the forecasts and their variances.

The forecasts shrink towards zero almost immediately: after one step only half of the last state survives (with a sign flip), after two steps a quarter, and so on. The prediction intervals quickly reach their long-run width, \(\pm 1.96\sqrt{F_t^2 \text{Var}(\theta) + V}\) with \(\text{Var}(\theta) = W/(1 - 1/4)\).

Residuals

lb_kf = Box.test(std_res, lag = 10, type = "Ljung-Box", fitdf = 2)
lb_kf



    Box-Ljung test

data:  std_res
X-squared = 10.646, df = 8, p-value = 0.2226


The standardised prediction errors \(e_t/\sqrt{Q_t}\) should be independent \(N(0,1)\) if the model is correct, which it is here (we simulated from it). The ACF (Figure 52) and the Ljung–Box test (\(p = 0.223\)) are consistent with this.
Discussion. The filtered state follows the zig-zag pattern of the true state, but with wide intervals: with \(V = 2\) and a state variance of only about \(1.33\), a single observation carries limited information about \(\theta_t\) (Figure 51). The filter gives the most weight to the observation when \(F_t\) is large, because then the state part of \(y_t\) is larger relative to the noise.



Question 2: A noisy AR(2) process
\[
x_t = -0.9x_{t-2} + w_t, \qquad y_t = x_t + v_t.
\]

a) State-space form
Let \(\theta_t = (x_t, x_{t-1})'\). Then
\[
\theta_t = \begin{pmatrix} x_t \\ x_{t-1} \end{pmatrix}
= \underbrace{\begin{pmatrix} 0 & -0.9 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}}_{G}
\begin{pmatrix} x_{t-1} \\ x_{t-2} \end{pmatrix} +
\begin{pmatrix} w_t \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad
W = \begin{pmatrix} \sigma^2_w & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix},
\]
\[
y_t = \underbrace{\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}}_{F}\theta_t + v_t, \qquad V = \sigma^2_v,
\qquad \theta_0 = (x_0, x_{-1})'.
\]


b) Initial variances for stationarity
\(x_t\) only depends on \(x_{t-2}\), so the even and odd time points form two independent AR(1) processes (in steps of two) with coefficient \(-0.9\). For \(x_t\) (and hence \(y_t\)) to be stationary from the start, \(x_0\) and \(x_{-1}\) must come from the stationary distribution:
\[
\sigma^2_0 = \sigma^2_1 = \frac{\sigma^2_w}{1 - 0.9^2} = \frac{\sigma^2_w}{0.19},
\]
and \(x_0\) and \(x_{-1}\) are uncorrelated, since \(\text{Cov}(x_t, x_{t-1}) = 0\) for this process. With \(\sigma_w = 1\) this gives \(\sigma^2_0 = \sigma^2_1 = 5.263\). Then \(\text{Var}(y_t) = \sigma^2_w/0.19 + \sigma^2_v\) for every \(t\).


c) and d) Simulation with \(\sigma_v = 1\) and \(\sigma_v = 10\)


Click to toggle source code
# Simulate x and y:
sim_q2 = function(n, sigma_w, sigma_v) {
  s2_0 = sigma_w^2 / (1 - 0.9^2)              # stationary variance
  x_all = numeric(n + 2)
  x_all[1:2] = rnorm(2, 0, sqrt(s2_0))        # x_{-1}, x_0
  for (t in 3:(n + 2)) {
    x_all[t] = -0.9 * x_all[t - 2] + rnorm(1, 0, sigma_w)
  }
  x = x_all[-(1:2)]
  y = x + rnorm(n, 0, sigma_v)                # observation noise
  return(list(x = ts(x), y = ts(y)))
}

# Same seed so both cases share the same x:
set.seed(8)
q2_v1 = sim_q2(100, sigma_w = 1, sigma_v = 1)
set.seed(8)
q2_v10 = sim_q2(100, sigma_w = 1, sigma_v = 10)







Figure 53: The AR(2) state process \(x_t\) (pink) and the noisy observations \(y_t\) (grey) for \(\sigma_v = 1\) (left) and \(\sigma_v = 10\) (right).









Figure 54: Sample ACF and PACF of \(x_t\) and \(y_t\). Rows: \(x_t\), \(y_t\) with \(\sigma_v = 1\), and \(y_t\) with \(\sigma_v = 10\).






Click to toggle source code
# Theoretical ACF of x:
round(ARMAacf(ar = c(0, -0.9), lag.max = 8), 3)


     0      1      2      3      4      5      6      7      8 
 1.000  0.000 -0.900  0.000  0.810  0.000 -0.729  0.000  0.656

# Factor by which observation noise shrinks autocorrelations of y:
var_x = 1 / 0.19
c(sigma_v_1 = var_x / (var_x + 1), sigma_v_10 = var_x / (var_x + 100))


 sigma_v_1 sigma_v_10 
 0.8403361  0.0500000 



\(x_t\): the theoretical ACF is zero at odd lags and \((-0.9)^{k}\) at lag \(2k\), so it alternates in sign at even lags and decays slowly. The PACF has a single large spike of about \(-0.9\) at lag 2, as expected for an AR(2) with \(\phi_1 = 0\). The time plot (Figure 53) shows a regular cycle with a period of about 4 time steps.
\(y_t\) with \(\sigma_v = 1\): the autocorrelations of \(y\) are those of \(x\) multiplied by \(\text{Var}(x)/(\text{Var}(x) + \sigma^2_v) = 0.84\), so the pattern is still clearly visible. The PACF no longer cuts off exactly after lag 2: adding white noise to an AR(2) gives an ARMA(2, 2), so smaller partial autocorrelations appear at later lags.
\(y_t\) with \(\sigma_v = 10\): the shrinkage factor is only 0.05. The signal is buried in the noise: the ACF and PACF of \(y\) look like white noise even though \(x\) is strongly autocorrelated (Figure 54).

This is exactly the situation where a state-space model helps: we model \(x\) directly and treat \(v\) as measurement error. As an extra check I ran my Kalman filter and smoother with the true parameters to recover \(x\) from \(y\):


Click to toggle source code
G_q2 = matrix(c(0, 1, -0.9, 0), 2, 2)   # [0 -0.9; 1 0]

# Function to compute smoothed estimate of x_t (first state) with own filter and smoother:
smooth_x = function(y, sigma_v) {
  kf = kalman_filter(as.numeric(y), FF = c(1, 0), GG = G_q2, V = sigma_v^2,
                     W = diag(c(1, 0)), m0 = c(0, 0), C0 = diag(1 / 0.19, 2))
  kalman_smoother(kf, GG = G_q2)$s[-1, 1]
}
x_hat_v1 = smooth_x(q2_v1$y, sigma_v = 1)
x_hat_v10 = smooth_x(q2_v10$y, sigma_v = 10)

# Correlation between true x and its smoothed estimate:
c(sigma_v_1 = cor(q2_v1$x, x_hat_v1), sigma_v_10 = cor(q2_v10$x, x_hat_v10))


 sigma_v_1 sigma_v_10 
 0.9790651  0.8772303 


With \(\sigma_v = 1\) the smoothed estimate of \(x\) is very close to the truth (correlation 0.98). With \(\sigma_v = 10\) the correlation drops to 0.88, which is still surprisingly high given that the ACF and PACF of \(y\) looked like white noise. The smoother can recover so much because it is given the true model. It knows that \(x\) follows a strong cycle with period 4, so it can average over many noisy observations that carry information about the same cycle. In practice the parameters would have to be estimated, and with this much noise that would be challenging



Question 3: Second differences of the linear growth model
The linear growth model is
\[
Y_t = \mu_t + v_t, \qquad \mu_t = \mu_{t-1} + \beta_{t-1} + w_t, \qquad \beta_t = \beta_{t-1} + \gamma_t,
\]
with \(v_t\), \(w_t\), \(\gamma_t\) independent white noise with variances \(\sigma^2_v, \sigma^2_w, \sigma^2_\gamma\).
First difference of the level: \(\Delta\mu_t = \mu_t - \mu_{t-1} = \beta_{t-1} + w_t\).
Second difference of the level: \(\Delta^2\mu_t = (\beta_{t-1} - \beta_{t-2}) + (w_t - w_{t-1}) = \gamma_{t-1} + w_t - w_{t-1}\).
Second difference of the noise: \(\Delta^2 v_t = v_t - 2v_{t-1} + v_{t-2}\).
So
\[
Z_t = \Delta^2 Y_t = \gamma_{t-1} + w_t - w_{t-1} + v_t - 2v_{t-1} + v_{t-2}.
\]
\(Z_t\) is a finite linear combination of white noise terms at lags 0, 1 and 2, so its mean (0) and autocovariances do not depend on \(t\) (it is stationary). Using the independence of all the noise terms, the autocovariances are
\[
\begin{aligned}
\gamma_Z(0) &= \sigma^2_\gamma + 2\sigma^2_w + (1 + 4 + 1)\sigma^2_v = \sigma^2_\gamma + 2\sigma^2_w + 6\sigma^2_v \\
\gamma_Z(1) &= \text{Cov}(Z_t, Z_{t-1}) = -\sigma^2_w + (-2)(1)\sigma^2_v + (1)(-2)\sigma^2_v = -\sigma^2_w - 4\sigma^2_v \\
\gamma_Z(2) &= \text{Cov}(Z_t, Z_{t-2}) = (1)(1)\sigma^2_v = \sigma^2_v \\
\gamma_Z(k) &= 0, \quad k \geq 3
\end{aligned}
\]
An autocovariance function that is non-zero up to lag 2 and zero afterwards is exactly the ACF of an MA(2) process. (Any stationary process whose autocovariances cut off after lag \(q\) can be written as an MA(\(q\)).) So the linear growth model is an ARIMA(0,2,2) model.
Simulation check:


Click to toggle source code
set.seed(9)

Question 4: Regression coefficients with a Kalman filter
The tutorial uses usconsumption from the (older) fpp package. The same quarterly growth rates for US personal consumption and disposable income are in uschange in fpp2 (with more recent data, 1970–2016), so I used those.


Click to toggle source code
# Read in data:
data(uschange)
# View(uschange)

y_us = uschange[, "Consumption"]
z_us = uschange[, "Income"]









(a) Time plot







(b) Scatter plot




Figure 55: Quarterly percentage changes in US consumption and income (left) and consumption against income with the least squares line (right).


Figure 55 shows that consumption and income growth move together, but income growth is much more volatile, and the scatter plot shows a positive but noisy relationship.


Click to toggle source code
# Ordinary least squares:
lm_us = lm(y_us ~ z_us)
summary(lm_us)$coefficients


             Estimate Std. Error  t value     Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept) 0.5451038 0.05568668 9.788765 1.700914e-18
z_us        0.2806012 0.04744194 5.914624 1.577409e-08



The Kalman filter for regression
As a state-space model, \(\theta_t = (a_t, b_t)'\), \(G = I\), \(W = 0\) (the coefficients do not change), \(F_t = (1, z_t)\) and \(V = \sigma^2\). This is my kalman_filter() with \(F_t\) given as a function of \(t\):


Click to toggle source code
n_us = length(y_us)
z_vec = as.numeric(z_us)

kf_reg = function(sigma2) {
  kalman_filter(as.numeric(y_us), FF = function(t) c(1, z_vec[t]), GG = diag(2),
                V = sigma2, W = matrix(0, 2, 2), m0 = c(0, 0), C0 = diag(1e7, 2))
}

kf_us_1 = kf_reg(sigma2 = 1)
kf_us_100 = kf_reg(sigma2 = 100)

# Filtered coefficients and diagonal of C_t (without time-0 row):
coef_path = kf_us_1$m[-1, ]
C_diag = t(sapply(kf_us_1$C[-1], diag))

kable(data.frame(
  Coefficient = c("a (intercept)", "b (slope)"),
  OLS = coef(lm_us),
  KF_sigma2_1 = kf_us_1$m[n_us + 1, ],
  KF_sigma2_100 = kf_us_100$m[n_us + 1, ]
), digits = 5, row.names = FALSE, escape = FALSE,
col.names = c("Coefficient", "OLS", "Kalman filter ($\\sigma^2 = 1$)", "Kalman filter ($\\sigma^2 = 100$)"))











Coefficient

The final filtered estimates \(m_T\) are identical to the OLS estimates (up to the effect of the very vague prior), whatever value of \(\sigma^2\) is used.






Why \(\sigma^2\) does not matter



With \(W = 0\) and a prior variance proportional to \(\sigma^2\) (\(C_0 = \sigma^2 C_0^*\)), every variance in the filter (\(R_t\), \(C_t\) and \(Q_t\)) is proportional to \(\sigma^2\). The Kalman gain \(K_t = R_tF_t'/Q_t\) is a ratio of these, so \(\sigma^2\) cancels and the filtered means \(m_t\) do not depend on it. Only the variances \(C_t\) do. Here \(C_0 = 10^7 I\) is fixed rather than scaled by \(\sigma^2\), but it is so vague that its effect on \(m_t\) is negligible for both \(\sigma^2 = 1\) and \(\sigma^2 = 100\).




Estimating \(\sigma^2\)
Run the filter with \(\sigma^2 = 1\). The standardised prediction errors \(e_t/\sqrt{Q_t}\) then have variance \(\sigma^2\). The first two have (almost) zero weight because the prior is vague and two coefficients have to be learned first, so
\[
\hat{\sigma}^2 = \frac{1}{T-2}\sum_{t=3}^{T} \frac{e_t^2}{Q_t}.
\]


Click to toggle source code
sigma2_kf = sum(kf_us_1$e[-(1:2)]^2 / kf_us_1$Q[-(1:2)]) / (n_us - 2)
c(kalman_filter = sigma2_kf, lm = summary(lm_us)$sigma^2)


kalman_filter            lm 
    0.3631358     0.3631358 


These are the same: the sum of squared standardised one-step-ahead errors (the recursive residuals) equals the OLS residual sum of squares.


Recursive coefficient estimates





Figure 56: Recursive (filtered) estimates of the intercept and slope, with approximate 95% intervals, from quarter 10 onwards. Dashed lines: full-sample OLS estimates.




\(m_t\) is (up to the vague prior) the OLS estimate using only the data up to quarter \(t\) (Figure 56). If the relationship were constant, these estimates should settle down and then only fluctuate within their intervals. Systematic drift (for example a slope that keeps decreasing) suggests that the coefficients change over time.
Here the estimates do not settle down smoothly. After the noisy start, the slope stays around 0.4 to 0.5 until the early 1980s and then drifts down to the full-sample value of about 0.28, with sudden jumps around 1980, 2001 and 2013. Even after 100 or more quarters a single quarter can move the recursive slope noticeably, which suggests that a few quarters with unusually large income changes are influential, or that the relationship has changed over time.
Recursive estimates are a weak test, though, because every new estimate still uses all the earlier data. A more direct approach is to let the coefficients follow random walks (\(W > 0\)) and compare the likelihoods.

build_tvp = function(p) dlmModReg(z_us, dV = exp(p[1]), dW = exp(p[2:3]))

fit_tvp = dlmMLE(y_us, parm = c(log(var(y_us)), -5, -5), build = build_tvp)

  x_q1[t, ] = MASS::mvrnorm(1, mu = mu_q1[z_q1[t], ], Sigma = sigma_q1[, , z_q1[t]])

Figure 58: Twenty observations simulated from the three-state bivariate Gaussian HMM, coloured by the true state. The grey arrows show the time path and the crosses mark the state means.




Figure 58 shows the three state distributions: state 1 is centred at \((-10, 0)\) with positive correlation, state 2 at \((10, 0)\) with negative correlation and state 3 at \((0, 10)\) with a much larger variance in \(x_1\) than in \(x_2\). Because the diagonal of \(\Gamma\) is 0.8, the process stays in a state for five steps on average (\(1/(1-0.8)\)), so consecutive points tend to come from the same cluster, and the path jumps between clusters only occasionally.
Given only the observations, we would need:

the transition probabilities: \(3 \times 2 = 6\),
the state means: \(3 \times 2 = 6\),
the covariance matrices: \(3 \times 3 = 9\),
the initial distribution \(\boldsymbol{\delta}\): 2 more.

That is 21 parameters (23 with \(\boldsymbol{\delta}\)), estimated from 20 bivariate observations (40 numbers). With so few observations the estimates would be very unreliable, and some states might not be visited often enough to estimate their covariance matrices at all.

The Viterbi algorithm fills in \(\xi_{ti}\), the log-probability of the most likely path that ends in state \(i\) at time \(t\) (together with the observations up to \(t\)):
\[
\xi_{1i} = \log\delta_i + \log p_i(x_1), \qquad \xi_{tj} = \max_i\left(\xi_{t-1,i} + \log\gamma_{ij}\right) + \log p_j(x_t).
\]
The most likely final state is the one with the largest \(\xi_{Ti}\), and the path is traced back with \(S_t = \text{argmax}_i(\xi_{ti} + \log\gamma_{i,S_{t+1}})\). Working on the log scale turns the products into sums and avoids underflow.
The most likely state sequence is AAAAAAABBB, which agrees with the true sequence at 9 of the 10 time points. The first seven observations are all “x”, which state A emits with probability 0.6 (compared with 0.1 and 0.3 for B and C). A is the least persistent state (\(\gamma_{AA} = 0.5\)), but the emission probabilities outweigh this, so the algorithm stays in A. At time 8 the path switches to B. “z” is equally likely in B and C (0.4), and B and C are equally persistent (\(\gamma_{BB} = \gamma_{CC} = 0.6\)), but A moves to B more often than to C (0.3 vs 0.2) and the final “y” is more likely in B (0.5 vs 0.3).
The only mistake is at time 2, where the true state is C. A single “x” from C between “x”s from A is impossible to detect: it would need two unlikely transitions (A to C and C to A), and “x” is more likely in A anyway. This illustrates the main limitation of decoding: when the state distributions overlap, short visits to a state cannot be recovered. The local decoding probabilities in the table give the same sequence here, but they also show the uncertainty: \(P(A \mid \mathbf{x})\) is only about 0.75 for the first observations, and at time 8 the probabilities for B and C are close.

Question 3: Probability of three observations from a Poisson HMM
The two-state Poisson HMM has \(\Gamma = \begin{pmatrix} 0.1 & 0.9 \\ 0.4 & 0.6 \end{pmatrix}\) and \(\boldsymbol{\lambda} = (1, 3)\). Since the HMM is stationary, \(\boldsymbol{\delta}\) is the stationary distribution, which solves \(\boldsymbol{\delta}\Gamma = \boldsymbol{\delta}\): \(\boldsymbol{\delta} = (4/13, 9/13)\).
a) Summing over all \(2^3 = 8\) state sequences:
\[
P(X_1 = 0, X_2 = 2, X_3 = 1) = \sum_{c_1, c_2, c_3} \delta_{c_1}\gamma_{c_1c_2}\gamma_{c_2c_3} \, p_{c_1}(0)\,p_{c_2}(2)\,p_{c_3}(1).
\]

x_q3 = c(0, 2, 1)

  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(`P(states)` = delta_q3[C1] * Gamma_q3[cbind(C1, C2)] * Gamma_q3[cbind(C2, C3)],
         `P(x | states)` = dpois(x_q3[1], lambda_q3[C1]) * dpois(x_q3[2], lambda_q3[C2]) *
                           dpois(x_q3[3], lambda_q3[C3]),

With \(m\) states and \(T\) observations, listing the sequences takes \(m^T\) terms (each a product of about \(2T\) factors), while the matrix product (the forward algorithm) takes about \(Tm^2\) operations. title: Overview
section: Question 4: The independent mixture as a special case
text:
Question 4: The independent mixture as a special case
If the Markov chain degenerates to a sequence of independent random variables, then \(P(C_t = j \mid C_{t-1} = i) = P(C_t = j) = \delta_j\) for every \(i\). So every row of \(\Gamma\) equals \(\boldsymbol{\delta}\), i.e. \(\Gamma = \mathbf{1}'\boldsymbol{\delta}\), and \(\boldsymbol{\delta}\) is also the initial distribution. Then for any \(x\),
\[
\mathbf{P}(x_{t-1})\Gamma = \mathbf{P}(x_{t-1})\mathbf{1}'\boldsymbol{\delta},
\]
and therefore every factor can be split off:
\[
\begin{aligned}
L_T &= \boldsymbol{\delta}\mathbf{P}(x_1)\Gamma\mathbf{P}(x_2)\Gamma\cdots\Gamma\mathbf{P}(x_T)\mathbf{1}' \\
&= \boldsymbol{\delta}\mathbf{P}(x_1)\mathbf{1}'\,\boldsymbol{\delta}\mathbf{P}(x_2)\mathbf{1}'\,\boldsymbol{\delta}\cdots\mathbf{1}'\,\boldsymbol{\delta}\mathbf{P}(x_T)\mathbf{1}' \\
&= \prod_{t=1}^{T}\boldsymbol{\delta}\mathbf{P}(x_t)\mathbf{1}' = \prod_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\delta_i\,p_i(x_t;\theta_i),
\end{aligned}
\]
because each \(\boldsymbol{\delta}\mathbf{P}(x_t)\mathbf{1}' = \sum_i \delta_i p_i(x_t)\) is a scalar. This is the likelihood of an independent mixture model with mixing weights \(\delta_1, \dots, \delta_m\), as required.

The string has a very regular structure. It always cycles through
\[
\underbrace{A\cdots A}_{\text{run of A's}}\ \underbrace{B\cdots B}_{\text{run of B's}}\ A\ C,
\]
followed by the next run of A’s (the last segment, a single “A”, is the start of a new cycle). C is always preceded and followed by an A, and a run of B’s is always followed by exactly one A and then a C. So an “A” behaves differently depending on where it is: after a C, an A can be followed by more A’s or by a B, but after a B, an A is always followed by a C. One state for A is therefore not enough, and I propose a four-state HMM (Table 18):


Table 18: Proposed HMM for the first string.







State
Emits
Transitions




1: “A-run”
A (probability 1)
stay in 1 with probability \(p_A\), move to 2 with \(1-p_A\)


2: “B-run”
B (probability 1)
stay in 2 with probability \(p_B\), move to 3 with \(1-p_B\)


3: “single A”
A (probability 1)
move to 4 with probability 1


4: “C”
C (probability 1)
move to 1 with probability 1




\[
\Gamma = \begin{pmatrix} p_A & 1-p_A & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & p_B & 1-p_B & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad
B = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \ \ (\text{columns: A, B, C}), \qquad
\boldsymbol{\delta} = (1, 0, 0, 0).
\]
The string starts with a run of A’s, so the initial state is 1. The time spent in a state with stay probability \(p\) is geometric with mean \(1/(1-p)\), so \(p\) can be estimated from the run lengths: \(\hat{p} = (\text{total symbols} - \text{number of runs})/\text{total symbols}\). This gives \(\hat{p}_A = 0.72\) and \(\hat{p}_B = 0.5\) (mean runs of 3.6 A’s and 2 B’s). In this model the emissions are deterministic, so the “hidden” part is only that two states emit A. It is still an HMM, because A from state 1 and A from state 3 cannot be told apart without the context.

The cross-table of the first and second symbols shows that B and C are each followed by A and E about equally often, so it is reasonable to treat the emissions as independent given the state, which is what an HMM assumes. With only 20 triplets the emission probabilities are rough estimates.

title: Overview
text:
Question 6: The occasionally dishonest casino
This is the classic example from Durbin et al. (1998). A fair die (state 1) and a loaded die that rolls a six half of the time (state 2) are switched according to \(\Gamma = \begin{pmatrix} 0.95 & 0.05 \\ 0.10 & 0.90 \end{pmatrix}\).


Click to toggle source code
Gamma_cas = matrix(c(0.95, 0.05, 0.10, 0.90), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
emit_cas = rbind(fair   = rep(1/6, 6),
                 loaded = c(rep(1/10, 5), 5/10))
delta_cas = stat_dist(Gamma_cas)

# Simulate 300 rolls:
n_cas = 300
die = numeric(n_cas)
roll = numeric(n_cas)
for (t in 1:n_cas) {
  die[t] = if (t == 1) sample(1:2, 1, prob = delta_cas) else sample(1:2, 1, prob = Gamma_cas[die[t - 1], ])
  roll[t] = sample(1:6, 1, prob = emit_cas[die[t], ])
}

# Decode with the true parameters:
dens_cas = t(emit_cas[, roll])
vit_cas = hmm_viterbi(dens_cas, delta_cas, Gamma_cas)$states
local_cas = hmm_local(dens_cas, delta_cas, Gamma_cas)

c(stationary_P_loaded = delta_cas[2],
  share_loaded = mean(die == 2),
  six_rate_fair = mean(roll[die == 1] == 6),
  six_rate_loaded = mean(roll[die == 2] == 6),
  viterbi_accuracy = mean(vit_cas == die),
  local_accuracy = mean(apply(local_cas, 1, which.max) == die))


stationary_P_loaded        share_loaded       six_rate_fair     six_rate_loaded 
          0.3333333           0.3633333           0.1675393           0.5045872 
   viterbi_accuracy      local_accuracy 
          0.8200000           0.8333333 




Click to toggle source code
cas_df = tibble(t = 1:n_cas, roll = roll, loaded = die == 2,
                p_loaded = local_cas[, 2], viterbi = vit_cas - 1)

shade = cas_df |>
  filter(loaded) |>
  transmute(xmin = t - 0.5, xmax = t + 0.5)

p_rolls = ggplot(data = cas_df, mapping = aes(x = t, y = roll)) +
  geom_rect(data = shade, aes(xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf),
            inherit.aes = FALSE, fill = "grey85") +
  geom_point(col = col_main, size = 1) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = 1:6) +
  labs(title = "Rolls (grey = loaded die).", x = NULL, y = "Roll")+
  theme_minimal()

p_decode = ggplot(data = cas_df, mapping = aes(x = t)) +
  geom_rect(data = shade, aes(xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf),
            inherit.aes = FALSE, fill = "grey85") +
  geom_line(aes(y = p_loaded), col = col_main) +
  geom_step(aes(y = viterbi), col = col_accent) +
  labs(title = "Decoded state.", x = "Roll", y = "P(loaded | rolls)")+
  theme_minimal()

p_rolls / p_decode





Figure 59: Three hundred simulated rolls from the occasionally dishonest casino. Top: the rolls, with the periods when the loaded die was used shaded. Bottom: the posterior probability that the loaded die is used (local decoding), with the Viterbi path in pink.




The chain spends about a third of the time with the loaded die (\(\delta_2 = 1/3\)), and in the simulation sixes are much more frequent when the loaded die is used. The Viterbi path recovers the die correctly for 82% of the rolls (Figure 59). Decoding works because the loaded die is used for runs of about 10 rolls (\(1/(1-0.9)\)), so a cluster of sixes is good evidence of a switch. Short visits to the loaded die are usually missed, and the switches are detected a few rolls late, because a single six is also quite likely from the fair die.

title: Overview
text:
Question 7: A two-state Bernoulli HMM
With \(P(X_t = x \mid C_t = 1) = 0.5\) for \(x = 0, 1\) and \(P(X_t = 1 \mid C_t = 2) = 1\),
\[
\mathbf{P}(0) = \begin{pmatrix} 0.5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{P}(1) = \begin{pmatrix} 0.5 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}.
\]


Click to toggle source code
Gamma_q7 = matrix(c(0.5, 0.5, 0.25, 0.75), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
delta_q7 = c(1, 2) / 3
p1_q7 = c(0.5, 1)                         # P(X = 1 | C = i)

P_q7 = function(x) diag(if (x == 1) p1_q7 else 1 - p1_q7)

# Likelihood with the matrix product:
bern_hmm_lik = function(x, delta, Gamma) {
  L = delta %*% P_q7(x[1])
  for (t in seq_along(x)[-1]) L = L %*% Gamma %*% P_q7(x[t])
  as.numeric(L %*% rep(1, length(delta)))
}

c(check_stationary = stat_dist(Gamma_q7),
  P_X_equals_0 = as.numeric(delta_q7 %*% P_q7(0) %*% rep(1, 2)),
  P_X_equals_1 = as.numeric(delta_q7 %*% P_q7(1) %*% rep(1, 2)),
  L_111 = bern_hmm_lik(c(1, 1, 1), delta_q7, Gamma_q7),
  `29/48` = 29 / 48,
  L_111_forward = exp(hmm_loglik(t(sapply(c(1, 1, 1), function(x) diag(P_q7(x)))), delta_q7, Gamma_q7)))


check_stationary1 check_stationary2      P_X_equals_0      P_X_equals_1 
        0.3333333         0.6666667         0.1666667         0.8333333 
            L_111             29/48     L_111_forward 
        0.6041667         0.6041667         0.6041667 


The stationary distribution is \(\boldsymbol{\delta} = \frac{1}{3}(1, 2)\), so marginally \(P(X_t = 0) = \frac{1}{3}(0.5) = 1/6\) and \(P(X_t = 1) = 5/6\). The likelihood of three 1’s is \(\boldsymbol{\delta}\mathbf{P}(1)\Gamma\mathbf{P}(1)\Gamma\mathbf{P}(1)\mathbf{1}' = 29/48 \approx 0.604\), which both my matrix-product function and my forward algorithm reproduce. This is larger than \((5/6)^3 \approx 0.579\), the value if the observations were independent, because a 1 makes state 2 more likely, and state 2 is persistent and always emits 1.

Lecture 1
Date: 27 July 2026
Topic covered: Foundations
What I Did:
Plotted time series plots for discrete and continuous time series data: Section 1
What I Learned:
A time series is an ordered sequence of observations collected over time. The ordering matters since observations are often dependent on previous observations (sequential correlation).






Assumption



Equally spaced measurements.








Assumption



Autocorrelation across time.


A time series is a single measurement taken at multiple points through time to give a series of measurements through time.
Noise (stochastic) in data introduces different realisations. An observed time series is only one realisation of an underlying stochastic process. This is important as we are not just trying to model the observations but the process that generated them.
Questions:
Q: How does noise introduce different realisations?
A: In normal regression the pattern is fixed and the noise sits on top of it:
\[
y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + e_i,
\] where each error term is independent.
In an AR process the noise actually builds the pattern. This means that every apparent trend is made of past shocks that haven’t died away yet. A different set of shocks will give a different shape because the shape of the path comes from noise. It isn’t that time series errors are correlated but that each observation is a weighted sum of every past shock making observations correlated.


Click to toggle source code
set.seed(1)
par(mfrow = c(2, 3))
for (i in 1:6) plot(arima.sim(list(ar = 0.9), n = 100), main = paste("Realisation", i), ylab = "y")

Lecture 2
Date: 3 August 2026
Topic covered: The Forecasting Problem
What I Did:
Looked at stationary AR processes: Section 1
What I Learned:
A forecast horizon is how far into the future you try to predict values. When looking at time series data we are looking for stable, informative patterns (not just a lot of data).






Forecasting vs Goal setting vs Planning



A forecast is a prediction about what will happen in the future based on evidence that we have (with some uncertainty). Goal setting is what we want to happen in the future and planning is how we reach our goal.


The uncertainty associated with forecasting gives rise to forecast intervals (not just point estimates).
A random walk is a process where memory is permanent. Every future shock accumulates endlessly resulting in forecast variance growing linearly. A stationary AR is a process where memory decays geometrically. Shocks die out, forcing the forecast back to the process mean.
Questions:
Q: If a process changes over time, at what point can we discard previous observations when forecasting?
A: This is decided by the model and is called the model’s memory. A mean benchmark will use every observation and just forecast the mean, the naive benchmark will use the most recent observation, exponential smoothing uses all observations but weights them differently (older observations are given less weight). You would also discard observations if a structural break occurs.






Note



When determining the number of observations to estimate the model (training set) more is usually better, unless the process has changed.

title: Overview
text:
Lecture 3
Date: 17 August 2026
Topics covered: Exploring a Series, Benchmarks and Forecast Accuracy
What I Did:
Worked through Time Series Analysis in R using the AirPassengers dataset: Section 1
What I Learned:
Time domain looks at previous observations whereas the frequency domain looks at cycles at different frequencies. Often you will need to look at both of these domains.






Trend vs Seasonality vs Cycles



A trend is the long-run direction of movement in a time series. Seasonality models a pattern that repeats itself at a fixed AND known interval. A cycle is a long oscillation where the length is NOT fixed.


When dealing with time series data you may encounter changing variability. Here you need to transform the data to stabilise variance and difference to remove trend and seasonality. When structural breaks are present in the data you can either use an indicator variable at the break or you can fit separate models on either side of the break.
There are 4 benchmark forecasting models: Mean, Naive, Seasonal naive and Drift.






Residuals are not forecast errors



Residuals are for diagnostics; forecast errors are for evaluation!


You cannot run normal cross-validation on time series data since the ordering of observations matters. Future observations must never be used when estimating a forecasting model.
Questions:
Q: How do you identify a significant structural break?
A: This can be done using formal tests, dependent on whether the date of the break is known prior to looking at the data. If the date is known in advance (e.g. a policy change), you can use Chow’s test. Chow’s test fits the model before and after the date of the break and uses an F-test to check if there is a statistically significant difference in model parameters. If the date is unknown you can run a Chow test at every possible date and take the largest F, compared against adjusted critical values. This is a sup-F test and accounts for having searched over every date, making it harder to declare a break.

text:
Lecture 4
Date: 19 August 2026
Topic covered: Three Validation Strategies, Linear Models for the Conditional Mean
What I Did:
Continued working through Time Series Analysis in R using the AirPassengers dataset: Section 1
What I Learned:
Since you can’t perform regular cross-validation on time series data you use a different approach. Walk-forward validation advances the forecast origin one step at a time and re-estimates the model at each step. Expanding window validation keeps every historical observation while moving the forecast origin forward. Sliding window validation keeps the training window length fixed while moving the forecast origin forward.
Expanding window is good for stable processes whereas sliding window is good for rapidly changing processes.
We want our data to be stationary and for the residuals to be white noise. To restore stationarity you can transform the data to stabilise the variance and take linear/seasonal differences to remove trend and seasonality. Log-transformations reduce a multiplicative model to an additive model.
Weak white noise requires uncorrelated observations with zero mean and constant variance but strict white noise requires iid observations.
Questions:
Q: What is the difference between walk-forward and expanding window?
A: In the notes they are the same procedure: the training set always starts at \(y_1\) and grows by one observation each time the forecast origin moves forward. “Walk-forward” describes how the origin moves and “expanding window” describes what is kept. The slides list them as separate strategies, but note that they use the same growth rule. The difference is that walk-forward re-estimates the model at every step, so it has a higher computational cost. The real contrast is with the sliding window, which drops the oldest observation at each step.

Lecture 5
Date: 24 August 2026
Topic covered: Linear Models for the Conditional Mean
What I Did:
Fit both ARIMA and SARIMA to the AirPassengers dataset: Section 1
What I Learned:
The moving average, MA(\(q\)), model is driven by lagged shocks. The dependence is based on errors not actual observations. The model has short memory. An MA(\(q\)) is always stationary and is restricted to be invertible.
The autoregressive, AR(\(p\)), model regresses a series on its own path.
ARMA combines both MA and AR models and is fitted by maximum likelihood, not OLS, since the past shocks are never observed.






Note



ACF and PACF graphs are used to determine which ARMA model to fit. An AR(\(p\)) has a PACF that cuts off after lag \(p\). An MA(\(q\)) has an ACF that cuts off after lag \(q\).


The ARIMA(\(p,d,q\)) model allows for differencing and the SARIMA model includes seasonality.
Questions:
Q: How can you determine if there is additional seasonality in a dataset after differencing or if it is just noise? For example in Section 1, there were still spikes at some lags in the PACF after log-transforming and differencing the AirPassengers dataset.
A: You can check if the residuals look like white noise by using a Ljung-Box test. A non-significant test means that there is no evidence of remaining autocorrelation (even if there are still a few lags that spike in the ACF/PACF). At the 5% level about 1 in 20 lags will spike by chance.

text:
Additional Lecture with Sulaiman
Date: 16 September 2026
Topic covered: Conditional Variance Models (ARCH and GARCH)
What I Did:
Worked through the provided Lab: Section 1
What I Learned:
All previous models have simply modelled the conditional mean and assumed constant variance. This fails for financial return data as it understates risk during periods where risk is highest and overstates risk when it is lowest. We now have both a mean (predictable component of the series) and a variance (conditional variance) equation.






Note



A series can be uncorrelated and still highly predictable in magnitude.


The ARCH model specifies conditional variance as a function of past squared innovations. The simplest case being \(\sigma^2_t = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1 \varepsilon_{t-1}^2\).






Volatility clustering



Large changes tend to follow large changes and small changes tend to follow small changes. Returns are often uncorrelated, hence why the ACF of returns indicates very little, however squared returns can be strongly autocorrelated.


The GARCH model adds the previous conditional variance to the ARCH equation. This makes it equivalent to an ARCH model with infinite memory. A GARCH(1,1) model is usually sufficient in practice.
\[
\sigma_t^2 = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1 \varepsilon_{t-1}^2 + \beta_1 \sigma_{t-1}^2,
\] where \(\alpha_1\) measures how strongly volatility reacts to a new shock, \(\beta_1\) measures how long that reaction lasts, \(\alpha_1 + \beta_1\) is the persistence.
Questions:
Q: Why must \(\alpha_1 + \beta_1 < 1\)?
A: When \(\alpha_1 + \beta_1 < 1\) this ensures that the long-run variance is \(\bar{\sigma}^2 = \frac{\alpha_0}{1- \alpha_1 - \beta_1}\) and that the process has a benchmark variance for the volatility to return to. When \(\alpha_1 + \beta_1 = 1\) (IGARCH) the shocks to volatility are permanent. This means that all the weight is on the past and none is on the long-run level. This is the variance equivalent of a random walk.

Lecture 7
Date: 14 September 2026
Topic covered: Exponential Smoothing
What I Did:
Worked through Exponential Smoothing Exercises: Section 2
What I Learned:
Exponential smoothing forecasts are weighted averages of past observations. Weights decrease exponentially the further back in time you go. The smoothing parameter \(\alpha\) adjusts the weight put on past observations. A large \(\alpha\) puts a lot of weight on the most recent observation, similar to the Naive forecast. A small \(\alpha\) averages over a long history, similar to the Mean forecast. This is similar to GARCH but applied to observations instead of squared shocks.






SES vs Holt vs Holt-Winters



Simple exponential smoothing (SES) only updates a level resulting in flat forecasts. Holt’s method adds a trend equation, that describes the slope, so forecasts follow a straight line. Holt-Winters adds a seasonal equation. Each component gets its own smoothing parameter (\(\alpha\), \(\beta\), \(\gamma\)).


The smoothing parameters and initial states (\(\ell_0\), \(b_0\)) are estimated by minimising the sum of squared one-step-ahead errors. Fitted values are one-step-ahead forecasts, so residuals are always one-step-ahead errors.
To turn the exponential smoothing algorithm into a state-space model we can write it in error-correction form: \(y_t = \ell_{t-1} + e_t\), \(\ell_t = \ell_{t-1} + \alpha e_t\). This allows us to estimate \(\sigma\) and build prediction intervals.
This is what ets() does.






Prediction intervals are usually too narrow



Standard prediction intervals only capture the random error and ignore the uncertainty in parameter estimates and choice of model.


Questions:
Q: How do we get variances of SES forecasts (\(\sigma^2[1+\alpha^2(h-1)]\)) if the point forecasts are flat?
A: The point forecast stays at \(\ell_T\), but every future error also moves the level by \(\alpha e_t\). These shifts add up, so uncertainty grows linearly with \(h\) even though the mean does not change.

Lecture 8
Date: 21 September 2026
Topic covered: Time Series Regression Models
What I Did:
Worked through Chapter 2: Time Series Regression Models and the provided slides, rerunning the R code that had been included. Used a Kalman filter to estimate regression coefficients in the US consumption example: Section 2
What I Learned:
Time Series Regression includes explanatory variables in time series models. This allows one to include trend and seasonality covariates in the model instead of just differencing the series to make it stationary.






ARMAX vs regression with ARMA errors



ARMAX includes lagged values of the response as predictors, \(y_t = \beta x_t + \phi y_{t-1} + \dots\). This means that \(\beta\) can no longer be interpreted as the effect of \(x\) on the mean of \(y\). Regression with ARMA errors keeps the normal regression equation and lets the errors follow an ARMA process, \(y_t = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_t + \eta_t\), where \(\eta_t\) follows an ARMA process. This means that \(\beta_1\) can still be interpreted in the usual way.


Harmonic regression assumes that the seasonal pattern stays the same over time.






Autocorrelated errors



When errors are autocorrelated, OLS still gives unbiased estimates but they are no longer efficient. The usual standard errors are also wrong, so tests and intervals are too optimistic.


Questions:
Q: When should I add a lagged response instead of modelling the errors as ARMA?
A: It depends on whether the dependence is part of the process or a nuisance. If \(y\) depends on its own past (e.g. a stock that accumulates), a lagged response makes sense, but then \(\beta_1\) is only the immediate effect of \(x\) and the long-run effect is \(\beta_1/(1-\phi)\). If the goal is the effect of \(x\) on the mean of \(y\), the errors should be modelled as ARMA. In Example 4.1 in Section 2, the data were generated with AR(1) errors, so the model with a lagged response was misspecified unless \(x_{t-1}\) was also included. Regression with AR(1) errors is the same as this model with the coefficient of \(x_{t-1}\) restricted to \(-\phi\beta_1\).

Lecture 9
Date: 28 September 2026
Topic covered: State-Space Models
What I Did:
Worked through the dlm practical and the State Space and Kalman Filter tutorial: Section 2
What I Learned:
A state-space model has both an observation equation and a state equation.
The observation equation \(y_t = F\theta_t + v_t\) links what we observe to an unobserved state whereas the state equation \(\theta_t = G\theta_{t-1} + w_t\) describes how the state changes over time.






Note



Regression, ARIMA and exponential smoothing models can all be written in state-space form. State-space models don’t need stationarity since trend and seasonality are modelled directly and allowed to change over time.


The Kalman filter is a recursive algorithm that first predicts and then updates. First the state, \(a_t, R_t\), and the next observation, \(f_t, Q_t\), are predicted. Then the state estimate, \(m_t, C_t\), is updated. The updated estimate is a weighted average of the prediction and the new observation where the Kalman gain decides how much weight is assigned to the observation.






Bayesian Framework



The Kalman filter works in a Bayesian way where, \(\text{posterior} \propto \text{prior} \times \text{likelihood}\). The posterior becomes the prior of the next step.


Questions:
Q: How do I decide which variances in \(W\) should be allowed to be non-zero?
A: A non-zero variance lets that state change over time and a zero variance keeps it fixed. The structure of the model decides which states can have noise. In the CO\(_2\) model in Section 2 only the level, slope and current seasonal effect get noise, because the other seasonal states are just the previous effects shifted along. The size of the variances can then be estimated by maximum likelihood. If an estimated variance is essentially zero, that state can be fixed, and models can be compared with the likelihood or AIC, e.g. static (\(W = 0\)) vs time-varying coefficients in the US consumption example.

title: Overview
text:
Lecture 10
Date: 5 October 2026
Topic covered: Kalman Filter
What I Did:
Continued working through the dlm practical and the State Space and Kalman Filter tutorial: Section 2
What I Learned:
The Kalman filter is used to filter and forecast in dynamic linear Gaussian systems. This filter is recursive so we can process new observations as they arrive. The Kalman smoother starts at the end of a series and works backwards. This is better for looking backwards (not prediction).






Filtering vs Smoothing vs Forecasting



If we estimate the state at time \(t\) using data up to time \(s\):

\(s < t\) = forecasting
\(s = t\) = filtering
\(s > t\) = smoothing



Forecasting and filtering are done using the Kalman filter. Smoothing is done using the Kalman smoother.
The likelihood is the product of one-step-ahead predictive densities, \(y_t \mid y_{1:t-1} \sim N(f_t, Q_t)\). The unknown variances, \(V\) and \(W\), can be estimated by maximum likelihood.
Prediction intervals use \(Q_t = FR_tF' + V\). They are prediction intervals (not confidence intervals) because they are for a future observation and include the observation noise, \(V\), as well as the uncertainty about the state.
If there are missing observations present in the data, there is nothing to update with and the Kalman gain will be zero. Consecutive missing observations increase uncertainty.






Method




The prior predicts the next state from the previous estimate of the state, with some uncertainty (state equation).
The likelihood asks how likely the new observation is given all possible states (observation equation).
The new posterior, for the current state, is given by combining the likelihood and the prior.



Questions:
Q: Why does the Kalman filter only work for linear Gaussian state-space models?
A: The Kalman filter does a linear transformation of a Gaussian which gives another Gaussian.
\[
\text{Gaussian prior} \times \text{Gaussian likelihood} \propto \text{Gaussian posterior}
\] The Kalman filter only keeps track of the mean and variance. When we have a non-linear or non-Gaussian distribution we either end up with a skewed distribution or a posterior with no closed form.

text:
Lecture 11
Date: 12 October 2026
Topic covered: Hidden Markov Models 1
What I Did:
Worked through Questions 1, 3, 4 and 7 of the HMM tutorial and wrote the forward algorithm from first principles: Section 2
What I Learned:
A hidden Markov model (HMM) has an unobserved state process, \(C_t\), that follows a Markov chain and an observed process, \(X_t\), whose distribution depends only on the current state. Each state has its own state-dependent distribution (e.g. Poisson or Gaussian).






Assumption



The next state only depends on the current state (Markov property).


The Markov chain is described by the transition probability matrix \(\Gamma\), where \(\gamma_{ij} = P(C_{t+1} = j \mid C_t = i)\), and the initial distribution \(\boldsymbol{\delta}\). A large diagonal in \(\Gamma\) means that the states are persistent.






Independent mixture vs HMM



An independent mixture draws a new state at every time point, independently of the last one. An HMM lets the state depend on the previous state, which creates autocorrelation in the observations.


The likelihood, \(L_T = \boldsymbol{\delta}\mathbf{P}(x_1)\Gamma\mathbf{P}(x_2)\cdots\Gamma\mathbf{P}(x_T)\mathbf{1}'\), is calculated with the forward algorithm and maximised numerically. The forward probabilities are scaled at every step to avoid underflow.
Questions:
Q: Why does an HMM produce autocorrelated observations if the observations are conditionally independent given the states?
A: The observations are only independent once we know the states. A large observation makes a high-mean state more likely and, since the states are persistent, the next observation is likely to come from that same state.

title: Overview
text:
Lecture 12
Date: 19 October 2026
Topic covered: Hidden Markov Models 2
What I Did:
Worked through Questions 2, 5 and 6 of the HMM tutorial, wrote the backward algorithm, local decoding and the Viterbi algorithm from first principles, and fitted Poisson HMMs to the earthquake counts: Section 2, Project 4
What I Learned:
Once an HMM has been fitted we usually want to know which state the process was in. This is called decoding.






Local vs global decoding



Local decoding finds the most likely state at each time point separately, using the forward and backward probabilities. Global decoding finds the most likely sequence of states using the Viterbi algorithm. The two can disagree.


The number of states is chosen with AIC or BIC. The likelihood of an HMM often has several local maxima, so the model should be fitted from several different starting values.
Questions:
Q: Why can’t short visits to a state be recovered by decoding?
A: A single visit to a state needs two unlikely transitions, there and back, and if the state-dependent distributions overlap, the observation is often also likely under the surrounding state. In the Viterbi exercise in Section 2, the single visit to state C at time 2 was decoded as A.

All the code, data and Quarto source files for this portfolio are on GitHub: https://github.com/IsabellaLethbridge/Time_Series.
To reproduce any page, clone the repository, open Time_Series.Rproj in RStudio and render the page (or run quarto render for the whole site). The data files are in _data/ and projects/_data/.
