title: Forecasting South African daily electricity demand with exponential smoothing
text:
Forecasting South African daily electricity demand with exponential smoothing
Section and topic: Section 2 - Exponential smoothing (Holt-Winters and ETS state-space models).
Type of project: Implementation and model comparison on real-world data. Additive Holt-Winters (ETS(A,N,A)) coded from first principles, including its prediction intervals.
Aim: To forecast daily South African electricity demand 1 to 14 days ahead with exponential smoothing. To determine which exponential smoothing model forecasts best compared to the naive and seasonal naive benchmarks, whether its prediction intervals are reliable, and whether removing the annual cycle improves the forecasts.
Data used:

Hourly RSA contracted demand (MW), 1 April 2019 to 13 September 2023. Source: Eskom (2024), Eskom Data Portal, https://www.eskom.co.za/dataportal/. The data are aggregated system totals with no personal information.

The hourly data were averaged to daily mean demand. The models use 1 March 2021 to 13 September 2023, which leaves out the 2020 lockdown period. The training set ends on 19 July 2023 (871 days). Its last 8 weeks are a validation window for modelling choices. The last 8 weeks of the data (20 July 2023 to 13 September 2023) are the test set. Download instructions are in the detailed analysis.
Methods used: A Bai-Perron structural break test (with a sensitivity check on the minimum segment length) to choose the start date. Time plots, day-of-week boxplots, the ACF and an MSTL decomposition into weekly and annual components. SES, additive Holt-Winters with and without a damped trend and multiplicative Holt-Winters were fitted as ETS state-space models with forecast::ets() and compared by AICc. ETS(A,N,A) was also implemented from first principles: the error-correction filter, estimation by minimising the SSE with optim(), and the analytic forecast variance. Residual diagnostics included the Ljung-Box test and an analysis of the largest residuals against public holidays. The forecasts were evaluated against the naive and seasonal naive benchmarks with a rolling forecast origin (horizons 1 to 14 days, RMSE, MAE, MAPE and the Diebold-Mariano test). The coverage of the model-based prediction intervals was compared with empirical intervals built from in-sample multi-step errors. As an extension, a deterministic annual cycle (Fourier terms) was removed before smoothing, and this choice was made on the validation window rather than the test set.
Key findings:

The end of the lockdown disruption falls between 14 September 2020 and 22 March 2021 depending on the minimum segment length, so the modelling period starts on 1 March 2021, the move to alert level 1.
Daily demand has a strong and stable weekly pattern (Sunday demand is about 1,300 MW below the level and Tuesday to Thursday about 500 to 600 MW above it), a winter peak and no long-term trend. ETS(A,N,A) had the lowest AICc, which agrees with automatic selection (ETS(A,N,A)).
The estimates are \(\hat{\alpha} \approx\) 0.92 and \(\hat{\gamma} \approx 0\): the weekly pattern is fixed while the level moves almost like a random walk. My filter reproduces the ets() residuals exactly (maximum difference 3.6^{-12} MW). Estimated independently, my optimiser reached the boundary (\(\hat{\alpha} \approx\) 1) with a marginally lower SSE, which shows how flat the likelihood is in \(\alpha\).
Out of sample, ETS(A,N,A) had an RMSE of 674 MW (MAPE 2.1%), compared with 786 MW for the seasonal naive and 1,185 MW for the naive benchmark. My own code gave 675 MW. One day ahead it roughly halved the seasonal naive error (326 vs 658 MW, Diebold-Mariano p-value <0.001), but at 7 and 14 days ahead the two were equally accurate (p-values 0.8 and 0.86).
10 of the 10 largest residuals fall on a public holiday or the day after one. The residuals are autocorrelated and heavy-tailed (excess kurtosis 3.7).
The model-based prediction intervals were too wide (the 80% intervals covered 94% of the test values), because \(\hat{\alpha} \approx 1\) implies that uncertainty grows like a random walk and holidays inflate \(\hat{\sigma}\). Empirical intervals gave 83% coverage at the 80% level.
Removing the annual cycle gave opposite results in the two periods: worse on the validation window (RMSE 713 to 788 MW) and better on the test set (674 to 595 MW). The 2023 winter peak was much lower than in earlier years (mean June demand 27,200 MW in 2022 and 26,500 MW in 2023), so a fixed annual cycle is not reliable. It was left out of the final model.
The final forecast carries the high demand at the end of the series (27,588 MW, against 26,447 MW on the same day a week earlier) into every forecast for the next two weeks. This is the main practical weakness of a level with \(\hat{\alpha}\) close to 1.

What I would do differently next time:

Make modelling choices on a validation window from the start. I first judged the annual adjustment on the test set, where it looked like a clear improvement. On the validation window it made the forecasts worse.
Model public holidays explicitly, for example with holiday indicators in a regression with ETS errors, since they cause the largest errors and inflate the prediction intervals.
Use a method designed for multiple seasonal patterns (TBATS or double seasonal Holt-Winters), with temperature and load shedding as predictors, instead of a fixed annual adjustment.
Evaluate over several rolling windows covering a full year, including the Christmas period, and model unconstrained demand (adding back the load that was shed) rather than the demand that was actually supplied.

Introduction
The El Niño phase of the El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO) is characterised by anomalous warming of sea surface temperatures in the eastern and central Pacific Ocean. This phenomenon typically starts between March and June and peaks around the following December/January (Mason, 2001). An El Niño event typically causes warm and dry conditions over Southern Africa, with effects emerging within the year following the El Niño onset in the Pacific (Thomson et al., 2003). Over the 2015–2016 season, Southern Africa experienced a severe drought with the 2015/2016 El Niño being identified as a contributing factor. Dam levels dropped and severe water restrictions were implemented.
The South African Weather Service (SAWS) is warning of a super El Niño event in 2026–2027, as current sea surface temperatures rise beyond the threshold used to define a very strong El Niño (Mail & Guardian, 2026). This project focuses on Theewaterskloof Dam, the single largest reservoir in the Western Cape Water Supply System.
The aim of this project is to use seasonal ARIMA models to forecast Theewaterskloof Dam levels and eastern Pacific sea surface temperature (SST) along 95°W individually, and to test whether SST, used as a lagged predictor in a dynamic regression, improves dam-level forecasts. This tests the hypothesis that eastern Pacific SST is a leading indicator of drought risk in the Western Cape. Methods follow Hyndman and Athanasopoulos (2021) and the course notes (Department of Statistical Sciences, 2026), using the fable and feasts packages (O’Hara-Wild et al., 2024a, 2024b).

Model fitting
This section fits seasonal ARIMA models to both the dam level and SST series and compares them against the Mean, Naive, Seasonal naive and Drift benchmarks, as well as an exponential smoothing (ETS) model. A dynamic regression model is then fitted to the dam level series, with lagged SST as a predictor, to determine whether eastern Pacific SST improves the prediction of Theewaterskloof dam levels.
Each series is split into a training set and a test set, with the last two years held out for testing. The model is chosen using the training set only, based on AICc and rolling-origin cross-validation. The test set is only used once the model has been selected, to compare its forecasts against the benchmarks. The order of differencing is determined using unit root tests.

unitroot_fxn = function(dat) {
  D = dat |> features(current_mean, unitroot_nsdiffs)
  d = dat |>
    mutate(diff_mean = difference(current_mean, lag = 12)) |>
    filter(!is.na(diff_mean)) |>
    features(diff_mean, unitroot_ndiffs)
  tibble(D = D$nsdiffs, d = d$ndiffs)
}

Figure 12: ACF and PACF plots of the seasonally differenced dam capacity (top) and sea surface temperature (bottom) series.




Figure 12 shows the ACF and PACF of both series after seasonal differencing, which are used to choose the candidate models.
For both series, the ACF decays gradually from lag 1 rather than cutting off suddenly. This indicates autoregressive rather than moving average behaviour, so a pure MA(1) model is not considered. Both PACF plots have significant spikes at lags 1 and 2, which suggests an AR(1) or AR(2) structure. This is consistent with the AR(2) pattern identified in the EDA. The SST PACF also has smaller significant spikes at lags 3 and 4. An ARMA(1,1) model is included as a simpler alternative to AR(2).
For SST, the ACF has a large negative spike at lag 12. This is typical of a seasonal MA(1) term, which often appears after seasonal differencing (Hyndman & Athanasopoulos, 2021, Section 9.9). For dam capacity, there is no sharp spike at lag 12 in the ACF, but the PACF has significant spikes around lags 12 to 14 and at lag 25. This suggests that some seasonal dependence remains after differencing, but it is not clear from the plots alone whether a seasonal AR or seasonal MA term would fit better.
Based on these plots, seven candidate models are considered. All are fitted to the seasonally differenced series (\(D = 1\), \(d = 0\)):

AR(1) and AR(2) with no seasonal term,
AR(1) and AR(2) with a seasonal AR(1) term,
AR(1) and AR(2) with a seasonal MA(1) term, and
ARMA(1,1) with no seasonal term.

The same seven models are fitted to both series so that the results can be compared directly.

# Function to calculate out-of-sample error metrics:
accuracy_fxn = function(fc, data) {
  fc |>
    accuracy(data, measures = list(point_accuracy_measures, distribution_accuracy_measures)) |>
    select(.model, RMSE, MAE, MAPE, CRPS)
}

# Function for model selection on training set (AICc and rolling-origin CV,
# 12-step-ahead forecasts, origin moved forward 1 year at a time):
select_fxn = function(train, cv_end) {
  fit = train |> model(!!!cand_specs)

  ic = glance(fit) |>
    select(.model, sigma2, log_lik, AICc)

  cv_acc = train |>
    filter(year_month <= yearmonth(cv_end)) |>   # leave 12 months for last fold to forecast
    stretch_tsibble(.init = 120, .step = 12) |>
    model(!!!cand_specs) |>
    forecast(h = 12) |>
    accuracy_fxn(train) |>
    select(.model, cv_RMSE = RMSE, cv_CRPS = CRPS)

  tbl = left_join(ic, cv_acc, by = ".model") |> arrange(cv_CRPS)

  list(fit       = fit,
       tbl       = tbl,
       best      = tbl$.model[1],                    # lowest CV CRPS
       best_aicc = ic$.model[which.min(ic$AICc)])
}

select_tbl_fxn = function(sel) {
  sel$tbl |>
    mutate(Model = nm(.model)) |>
    select(Model, sigma2, log_lik, AICc, cv_RMSE, cv_CRPS) |>
    knitr::kable(digits = 3,
                 col.names = c("Model", "$\\sigma^2$", "Log-likelihood", "AICc", "CV RMSE", "CV CRPS"))
}

# Function for test-set evaluation of selected model vs benchmarks and ETS:
test_fxn = function(train, test, full, best) {
  train |>
    model(!!!c(bench_specs, cand_specs[best])) |>
    forecast(new_data = test) |>
    accuracy_fxn(full) |>
    arrange(CRPS)
}

test_tbl_fxn = function(acc) {
  acc |>
    mutate(Model = nm(.model)) |>
    select(Model, RMSE, MAE, MAPE, CRPS) |>
    knitr::kable(digits = 3, col.names = c("Model", "RMSE", "MAE", "MAPE (%)", "CRPS"))
}

# Function for Ljung-Box test on innovation residuals (dof = no. ARMA terms):
lb_fxn = function(fit, lag = 24) {
  dof = tidy(fit) |>
    as_tibble() |>
    group_by(.model) |>
    summarise(dof = sum(str_detect(term, "^s?(ar|ma)[0-9]+$")), .groups = "drop")

  augment(fit) |>
    as_tibble() |>
    left_join(dof, by = ".model") |>
    group_by(.model) |>
    summarise(
      lb_stat = unname(Box.test(na.omit(.innov), lag = lag, type = "Ljung-Box", fitdf = first(dof))$statistic),
      lb_p    = Box.test(na.omit(.innov), lag = lag, type = "Ljung-Box", fitdf = first(dof))$p.value,
      .groups = "drop"
    )
}

# Function for residual diagnostic plots:
resid_plot_fxn = function(fit, colour) {
  aug = augment(fit) |> as_tibble() |> select(year_month, .innov) |> as_tsibble(index = year_month)

  p_time = ggplot(aug, aes(x = year_month, y = .innov)) +
    geom_line(colour = colour) +
    labs(title = "Innovation residuals.", x = "Time (month)", y = "Residual")

  p_acf = aug |>
    ACF(.innov, lag_max = 36) |>
    autoplot() +
    labs(title = "ACF of residuals.")

  p_hist = ggplot(aug, aes(x = .innov)) +
    geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = colour, colour = "white") +
    labs(title = "Distribution of residuals.", x = "Residual", y = "Count")

  p_time / (p_acf + p_hist)
}

For the dam level series, the training set runs from January 2000 to December 2023 and the test set from January 2024 to January 2026. For SST, the training set runs from January 2000 to December 2019 and the test set from January 2020 to October 2021.
Models are selected using rolling-origin cross-validation on the training set, where each model repeatedly forecasts 12 months ahead from an expanding window of data. The model with the lowest average CRPS is selected, and AICc is reported alongside as an in-sample check. The continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) measures the accuracy of the whole forecast distribution rather than only the point forecast. It rewards forecasts that are both centred close to the observed value and appropriately narrow, and reduces to the absolute error for a point forecast, so it can be interpreted on the same scale as MAE (Hyndman & Athanasopoulos, 2021, Section 5.9).

Predicting drought using sea surface temperature
The models above forecast dam levels and SST individually. In this section, SST from previous months is used as a predictor of dam levels in a dynamic regression (SARIMAX) model. This tests whether eastern Pacific SST can be used to predict drought in the Western Cape, which is the main aim of this project.


Show code
# Restrict to window where SST has no structural gaps:
dam_sst = monthly_damlvl_ts |>
  filter(year_month <= yearmonth("2021 Oct")) |>
  left_join(
    monthly_ts_pre2021 |> as_tibble() |> select(year_month, sst_mean = current_mean),
    by = "year_month"
  ) |>
  as_tsibble(index = year_month)

dam_sst |>
  CCF(current_mean, sst_mean, lag_max = 24) |>
  autoplot() +
  labs(title = "Raw cross-correlation between dam capacity and SST.")





Figure 13: Raw cross-correlation between monthly dam capacity and sea surface temperature (January 2000 to October 2021). Positive lags: SST leads dam capacity.




The cross-correlation in Figure 13 is dominated by the seasonal pattern shared by both series, so it cannot be used to identify the lag at which SST affects dam levels. To remove this effect, both series are prewhitened before the cross-correlation is calculated (Cryer & Chan, 2008, Chapter 11). Both series are first seasonally differenced, to match the \(D = 1\) used in the dynamic regression. An autoregressive model is then fitted to the differenced SST series, and the same filter is applied to both series. This removes the autocorrelation within SST, so that any remaining cross-correlation reflects the relationship between the two series rather than their own seasonal patterns and persistence. This is done using the prewhiten() function from the TSA package (Chan & Ripley, 2022).


Show code
# Seasonally difference both series:
pw_dat = dam_sst |>
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(dam_d = difference(current_mean, 12),
         sst_d = difference(sst_mean, 12)) |>
  filter(!is.na(dam_d), !is.na(sst_d))

# Fit AR model to SST (order by AIC), filter both series and compute CCF:
pw = TSA::prewhiten(x = pw_dat$sst_d, y = pw_dat$dam_d, lag.max = 24, plot = FALSE)

# Note: prewhiten() correlates SST at t+k with dam at t, so SST leads at negative lags
# Flip lags so positive lags mean SST leads:
ccf_tbl  = tibble(lag = -as.numeric(pw$ccf$lag), ccf = as.numeric(pw$ccf$acf))
ccf_ci   = qnorm(0.975) / sqrt(pw$ccf$n.used)
ar_order = pw$model$order

# Strongest correlation with SST leading by 1-12 months:
lead_tbl = ccf_tbl |> filter(lag >= 1, lag <= 12)
best_lag = lead_tbl$lag[which.max(abs(lead_tbl$ccf))]
best_ccf = lead_tbl$ccf[which.max(abs(lead_tbl$ccf))]
n_sig    = sum(abs(lead_tbl$ccf) > ccf_ci)

ggplot(ccf_tbl, aes(x = lag, y = ccf)) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = lag, yend = 0)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(-ccf_ci, ccf_ci), linetype = "dashed", colour = "blue") +
  labs(title = "Prewhitened cross-correlation between dam capacity and SST.",
       x = "Lag (months)", y = "CCF")





Figure 14: Cross-correlation between prewhitened, seasonally differenced dam capacity and SST. Dashed lines: approximate 95% bounds. Positive lags: SST leads dam capacity.




Figure 14 shows the cross-correlation after both series have been prewhitened using an AR(23) model. A high order is needed because seasonal differencing leaves a seasonal pattern at lag 12 that an autoregressive model can only approximate using many lags. Compared with Figure 13, the 12-month oscillation is no longer visible, which shows that it was caused by the shared seasonality. Of the twelve lags where SST leads dam capacity by 1 to 12 months, 0 fall outside the approximate 95% bounds (±0.130). Since each lag has a 5% chance of falling outside the bounds by chance alone, about 0.6 of the twelve lags would be expected to do so even if there were no relationship. Some correlations outside the 1 to 12 month range do exceed the bounds, including negative correlations when SST leads by more than a year. However, positive correlations of a similar size also appear when dam levels lead SST, which cannot reflect a physical relationship. Since the dam series is highly persistent, neighbouring cross-correlations are themselves correlated, producing runs of similar values that cross the bounds more often than expected by chance. These longer-lag correlations are therefore not treated as evidence of a relationship. The strongest correlation is at lag 10 (CCF = -0.091), which is negative, as expected if warmer SST leads to lower dam levels. This lag is used in the regression models below. However, the prewhitened cross-correlation already gives little evidence of a real relationship between SST and dam levels.

The time series linear model in Table 6 estimates the coefficient of SST lagged by 10 months as \(\hat\beta\) = -2.779 (\(p\) = 0.012). This suggests that dam levels are significantly related to SST from earlier months. The negative coefficient suggests that warmer SST is associated with lower dam levels, which is consistent with the hypothesis. This model also assumes that the errors are independent, and Figure 15 shows that they are not.


Show code
reg_fit |> select(tslm) |> resid_plot_fxn(colour = col_main)





Figure 15: Residual diagnostics for the time series linear model baseline (dam capacity regressed on lagged SST).




Figure 15 shows strongly correlated residuals in the time series linear model, with the ACF decaying gradually from approximately 1 at lag 1. This is confirmed by the Ljung-Box test in Table 8. Thus, the residuals are not white noise, which violates the assumption of independent errors that time series linear models make. As a result, the standard errors of the coefficients are too small and the \(p\)-value for SST cannot be trusted. This is known as spurious regression, where two series appear to be related because they both follow similar patterns over time rather than because one affects the other (Hyndman & Athanasopoulos, 2021). This motivates modelling the errors with the ARIMA model selected for dam levels.

fc_plot_fxn = function(fc, history, colour, title, y_lab) {

    geom_ribbon(data = fc_int, aes(x = year_month, ymin = `80%_lower`, ymax = `80%_upper`),

}

# Function to calculate width of 95% interval at given horizon:
pi_width = function(fc, h) {
  fc |> hilo(level = 95) |> unpack_hilo(`95%`) |> as_tibble() |>
    slice(h) |> mutate(w = `95%_upper` - `95%_lower`) |> pull(w)
}

Discussion

Model recommendations
The recommended model for Theewaterskloof dam capacity is the ARIMA(1,0,0)(0,1,1)[12] model. The candidate models were motivated by the ACF and PACF of the seasonally differenced series (Figure 12). This model had the lowest cross-validated CRPS on the training set (Table 2), although AICc favoured the ARIMA(2,0,0)(0,1,1)[12] model. On the test set, it outperformed all four benchmarks and the ETS(A,N,A) model on every error measure (Table 3). For SST, the recommended model is the ARIMA(2,0,0)(0,1,1)[12] model, which had both the lowest cross-validated CRPS and the lowest AICc (Table 4). On the short SST test set, its CRPS was very close to that of the Seasonal naive model, while its RMSE, MAE and MAPE were lower (Table 5).
Lagged SST was not a useful predictor of dam capacity. The raw cross-correlation was dominated by the five to six month offset between the two seasonal cycles. After prewhitening, none of the twelve lags at which SST leads dam capacity were significant (Figure 14). The time series linear model found a significant negative relationship, as hypothesised, but its residuals were strongly autocorrelated. Once the errors were modelled, the SST coefficient was no longer significant (\(p\) = 0.663, Table 7) and the dynamic regression did not improve on the univariate model’s forecasts (Table 9).


Limitations

The long gaps in the SST series (November 2021 to March 2023 and October 2024 to March 2025) meant that the SST and regression models could only use data up to October 2021. This reduced the training data and meant that no model could forecast into the 2026/2027 El Niño period, which is the period of most interest.
Seven buoys along a single longitude (95°W) only give a limited picture of El Niño conditions. The adjustment for missing buoys prevents the average from jumping when a buoy is missing, but it cannot provide information about the wider Pacific Ocean.
The dynamic regression assumes a fixed relationship between SST and dam levels at a single lag. Figure 6 suggests that this relationship differs between the 2015 to 2016 decline and the 2018 to 2019 recovery, which a fixed coefficient cannot capture.
The residuals of the dam level models are still autocorrelated (Table 8), so their prediction intervals are likely to be too narrow. In the dynamic regression, the seasonal MA coefficient was estimated at −1, the boundary of what the model allows. This suggests the seasonal pattern in dam levels is almost the same every year, and a model with fixed monthly effects may be more appropriate.
The ranking of the models changes between the 2019 to 2021 and 2024 to 2026 test periods. Cross-validation reduces this sensitivity but does not remove it, since the training data only contains two major droughts.
The regression forecasts in Table 9 use the observed SST values over the test period, which would not be known in advance in practice. This gives the regression models an advantage over the univariate models.
Dam capacity is bounded between 0% and 100%, but the prediction intervals assume normally distributed errors and extend above 100% (Figure 17).



Improvements

Rainfall over the Theewaterskloof catchment could be used as a predictor, since rainfall directly affects dam inflows. Water-use data could also be included, since water restrictions contributed to the 2018 to 2019 recovery.
A standard El Niño index, such as the Oceanic Niño Index, could replace the single buoy line. It covers a wider region, has no gaps, and would allow forecasting into 2027.
A regime-switching model could allow the relationship between SST and dam levels to change between El Niño, La Niña and neutral phases.
Transforming the dam levels (for example, with a logit transformation) before modelling would keep forecasts and prediction intervals between 0% and 100%.



Practical implications
For water planning in Cape Town, these results suggest that monthly eastern Pacific SST along 95°W does not give useful advance warning of low Theewaterskloof dam levels beyond what the dam’s own history and seasonal pattern already provide. The ARIMA(1,0,0)(0,1,1)[12] model gives reasonable short-term forecasts, but its prediction intervals become very wide beyond about a year, and it cannot anticipate the start of a drought such as the one in 2015 to 2018.

title: Predicting drought in the Western Cape
text:
Predicting drought in the Western Cape
Section and topic: Section 1 - Linear models for the conditional mean (seasonal ARIMA and dynamic regression).
Type of project: Implementation and model comparison on real-world data. Includes a prewhitened cross-correlation analysis and a composition adjustment for incomplete buoy data.
Aim: To determine whether Theewaterskloof Dam capacity and eastern Pacific sea surface temperature (SST) can be forecast with seasonal ARIMA models, and whether lagged SST, as a leading indicator of El Niño, improves dam capacity forecasts.
Data used:

Daily Theewaterskloof Dam levels (% of capacity), January 2000 to January 2026. Source: City of Cape Town Open Data Portal, Dam levels from 2000, https://odp-cctegis.opendata.arcgis.com/.
Daily SST (°C) from the seven TAO/TRITON buoys along 95°W, January 2000 to April 2026 (models fitted to January 2000 to October 2021 because of long gaps in the record). Source: NOAA Pacific Marine Environmental Laboratory, https://www.pmel.noaa.gov/tao/drupal/disdel/.

Both series were aggregated to monthly means. Neither dataset contains personal information. Download instructions are in the detailed analysis and the code and data appendix.
Methods used: STL decomposition, ACF/PACF and unit root tests to choose the differencing and candidate orders. Seven seasonal ARIMA candidates selected by rolling-origin cross-validation (with AICc as a check) on the training data only, then evaluated once on a held-out test set against Mean, Naive, Seasonal naive, Drift and ETS(A,N,A). A prewhitened cross-correlation to choose the SST lag, a time series linear model, and a dynamic regression (SARIMAX). Accuracy measured with RMSE, MAE, MAPE and CRPS; residuals checked with Ljung-Box tests.
Key findings:

The selected dam capacity model is ARIMA(1,0,0)(0,1,1)[12] (test CRPS = 4.828, ranked 1 of 6 models, against 9.164 for Seasonal naive). Most of the predictability comes from the dam’s own persistence and seasonality.
The selected SST model is ARIMA(2,0,0)(0,1,1)[12] (test CRPS = 0.585, ranked 2 of 6). It performed very similarly to the Seasonal naive model on the short SST test set, with a slightly higher CRPS but lower RMSE, MAE and MAPE.
The two-year dam capacity forecast keeps the seasonal cycle (monthly means between 43.1% and 77.6%), but the 95% prediction interval widens to about 66 percentage points by the end of the horizon and exceeds 100% capacity. The dam model’s residuals are not fully white noise (Ljung-Box \(p\) = 0.001), so these intervals are probably too narrow.
The raw cross-correlation between dam levels and SST is dominated by their five-to-six-month seasonal offset, not by El Niño. After prewhitening, the strongest lead is at 10 months (CCF = -0.091), with 0 of 12 lead lags outside the 95% bounds.
A time series linear model finds a significant negative relationship between lagged SST and dam levels (\(\hat\beta\) = -2.779, \(p\) = 0.012), as hypothesised, but its residuals are strongly autocorrelated. With ARIMA errors, the SST coefficient is -0.341 (\(p\) = 0.663), and the dynamic regression’s forecasts (CRPS = 18.852) are no better than the univariate model’s (18.700).
There is no statistically significant evidence that SST at 95°W is a useful monthly leading indicator of Theewaterskloof Dam levels.
Forecast rankings depend on the test window: the Naive model beat the ARIMA model during the 2019–2021 post-drought recovery. This is why selection used cross-validation rather than a single test set.
Gaps in the buoy record from November 2021 meant that no model could forecast into the 2026/2027 El Niño period.
Model logit-transformed capacity so that prediction intervals stay within 0-100%.

What I would do differently next time:

Use catchment rainfall and water-use data as predictors, since they drive dam inflow and outflow directly.
Use a gap-free ENSO index, such as the Oceanic Niño Index, instead of a single buoy line, so that forecasts could reach 2027.
Fit a regime-switching model that allows the SST–dam relationship to differ between El Niño, La Niña and neutral phases.
Model logit-transformed capacity so that prediction intervals stay within 0–100%.

Introduction
The aim of this project is to use conditional variance models to predict the volatility of JSE All Share Index (ALSI) returns. The risk of JSE returns is not constant with periods of high volatility tending to follow periods of high volatility and periods of low volatility tending to follow periods of low volatility. Modelling returns with a constant-variance model understates the risk when it is high and overstates it when it is low.
ARCH (Engle, 1982) and GARCH (Bollerslev, 1986) models let the current conditional variance depend on recent shocks and, for GARCH models, on yesterday’s variance. GJR-GARCH (Glosten et al., 1993) extends the GARCH model to let negative shocks have a larger effect on volatility than positive ones. This is known as the leverage effect. These models are compared with a constant-variance model and the Exponentially Weighted Moving Average (EWMA) benchmark to determine which model gives the best out-of-sample volatility forecasts.

Data
The series used is the daily FTSE/JSE All Share Index total return index \(P_t\) (ticker J203, dividends reinvested) from the Daily Sampled South African Market Index Data 1994–2017 dataset (Gebbie, 2020). The dataset is publicly available and contains no personal information.
Data access instructions. Download the daily workbook from https://doi.org/10.25375/uct.11302325.v1 and save it as _data/PT-DATA-ALBI-JIBAR-JSEIND-Daily-1994-2017.xlsx next to this file. The ALSI is the column on sheet JSE Various Indices whose first header row is J203:XJSE:IND and whose second header row is TRI; the code below finds this column automatically.


Show code
# Specify data path and series:
data_path  = "_data/PT-DATA-ALBI-JIBAR-JSEIND-Daily-1994-2017.xlsx"
sheet_name = "JSE Various Indices"
ticker     = "J203:XJSE:IND"
field      = "TRI"

# Training and test sets:
train_end   = as.Date("2012-12-31")
ann_factor  = 252 # trading days per year
refit_every = 50  # re-estimate rolling models every 50 trading days

# Read header rows (rows 1-4):
hdr = read_excel(data_path,
                 sheet     = sheet_name,
                 col_names = FALSE,
                 n_max     = 4)

# Read in data (starts row 5):
raw = read_excel(data_path,
                 sheet     = sheet_name,
                 col_names = FALSE,
                 skip      = 4,
                 na        = c("#N/A", "", "NA"),
                 guess_max = 10000)

# Find date and ALSI columns:
date_col = which(sapply(raw, function(x) inherits(x, c("POSIXct", "Date"))))[1]
alsi_col = find_col(hdr, ticker, field)

# Daily log returns (%):
alsi = tibble(
  date = as.Date(raw[[date_col]]),
  tri  = as.numeric(raw[[alsi_col]])) |>
  filter(!is.na(date), !is.na(tri)) |>
  arrange(date) |>
  distinct(date, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  mutate(r = 100 * (log(tri) - lag(log(tri)))) |>
  filter(!is.na(r)) |>
  mutate(sample = if_else(date <= train_end, "Train", "Test"))

n_train = sum(alsi$sample == "Train")
n_test  = sum(alsi$sample == "Test")
r_all   = alsi$r
r_train = alsi$r[alsi$sample == "Train"]
r_test  = alsi$r[alsi$sample == "Test"]

# Save cleaned series:
saveRDS(alsi, "_data/project03_alsi_clean.rds")


The series runs from 30 June 1995 to 3 February 2017. The time index is the trading day, so weekends and public holidays are excluded. The daily log returns (%) are modelled,
\[
r_t = 100\left[\ln P_t - \ln P_{t-1}\right].
\]
Asset prices are non-stationary, with a variance that is not bounded, whereas log returns are approximately stationary. The series consists of 5396 daily returns. The models are estimated on the training set (July 1995 to December 2012, 4373 returns) and evaluated on the test set (January 2013 to February 2017, 1023 returns).

Figure 1 illustrates an increasing trend in the index level from 1995 to 2017. In comparison, Figure 2 shows the daily returns fluctuating around a mean of approximately zero. Periods of large returns tend to be followed by further periods of large returns and periods of small returns tend to be followed by small returns. This is indicative of volatility clustering. This is most visible during the 1997-1998 and 2008-2009 financial crises. The summary statistics in Table 1 show that the returns are negatively skewed (skewness = -0.446) and have heavier tails than a normal distribution (excess kurtosis = 6.005). This suggests that large negative returns occur more often than what would be expected under a normal distribution.

Figure 3: ACF of daily returns, squared returns and absolute returns in the training set. The dashed lines indicate approximate 95% bounds.




Figure 3 illustrates that the returns are weakly autocorrelated, since most of the sample autocorrelations lie within the 95% bounds. In comparison, both the squared and absolute returns have significant autocorrelations that decay slowly as the lag increases. This suggests that the size of the returns can be predicted even if the direction cannot. This is indicative of volatility clustering and motivates the use of conditional variance models, which allow the variance of the returns to change over time.

Model fitting
Conditional variance models consist of both a mean and a variance equation (Department of Statistical Sciences, 2026):
\[
r_t = \mu_t + \varepsilon_t, \qquad \varepsilon_t = \sigma_t z_t, \qquad z_t \overset{iid}{\sim} D(0,1),
\]
where \(\mu_t=\mu+\phi r_{t-1}\), \(\sigma_t^2\) is the conditional variance and \(D\) is the standard normal or a standardised Student-\(t\) distribution with \(\nu\) degrees of freedom.
In the ARCH model, the conditional variance depends on past squared shocks. The GARCH model lets the conditional variance depend on its own past as well as on past squared shocks. The GJR-GARCH model is a threshold model that captures the leverage effect, where negative shocks increase volatility more than positive shocks of the same magnitude.


Table 2: Conditional variance equations of the candidate models.






Model
Conditional variance \(\sigma_t^2\)




ARCH(\(q\))
\(\alpha_0 + \sum_{i=1}^{q}\alpha_i\varepsilon_{t-i}^2\)


GARCH(\(p,q\))
\(\alpha_0 + \sum^q_{i=1} \alpha_i \varepsilon_{t-i}^2 + \sum^p_{j=1} \beta_j \sigma_{t-j}^2\)


GJR-GARCH(\(p,q\))
\(\alpha_0 + \sum^q_{i=1} (\alpha_i + \gamma_iI_{t-i})\varepsilon^2_{t-i} + \sum^p_{j=1}\beta_j \sigma_{t-j}^2\)




In Table 2, \(I_{t-i}\) is an indicator variable equal to \(1\) if \(\varepsilon_{t-i} < 0\) and \(0\) otherwise. The parameters are restricted so that \(\alpha_0 > 0\) and \(\alpha_i, \beta_j, \gamma_i \ge 0\), which ensures that the conditional variance is always positive. The GARCH and GJR-GARCH models are fitted with \(p = q = 1\).
The persistence, \(\rho\), measures how long a volatility shock lasts. For GARCH(1,1) persistence is defined as \(\rho = \alpha + \beta\). For GJR-GARCH(1,1) with a symmetric distribution \(D\) persistence is \(\rho = \alpha + \beta + \gamma/2\), since negative shocks occur approximately half of the time. If \(\rho < 1\), the variance process is stationary and volatility reverts to a long-run level. This long-run level is the unconditional variance, \(\alpha_0/(1-\rho)\). The half-life of a volatility shock, \(\log(0.5)/\log(\rho)\), is the number of trading days it takes for the effect of a shock to halve.
These models are compared with two benchmarks. The first is a constant-variance model, \(\sigma_t^2 = s^2\), where \(s^2\) is the variance of the training sample. The second is EWMA, \(\sigma_t^2 = 0.94\,\sigma_{t-1}^2 + 0.06\,\varepsilon_{t-1}^2\) (J.P. Morgan/Reuters, 1996). EWMA is a GARCH(1,1) model with \(\alpha_0 = 0\) and \(\alpha + \beta = 1\), where the parameters are fixed as opposed to estimated. Thus, EWMA has no long-run variance to revert to. All ARCH and GARCH models are estimated by maximum likelihood using the rugarch package (Ghalanos, 2024).

Mean model and ARCH effects
Before the volatility of a series can be modelled, the conditional mean of the returns must be modelled. The optimal ARMA model is fitted to the returns to capture any predictable structure in the mean. The residuals of this model represent the shocks, \(\varepsilon_t\), which are then used to model the conditional variance. Any autocorrelation that the mean model does not capture would distort the variance model fitted to these residuals. Thus, the mean model must be specified correctly before an ARCH or GARCH model can be fitted.


Show code
# Parameter grid:
arima_grid = expand_grid(p = 0:2, q = 0:2)

# Function to fit ARIMA model and store information criteria:
arima_fxn = function(dat, p, q) {
  fit = arima(dat, order = c(p, 0, q), method = "ML")
  tibble(`ARIMA(p,d,q)` = paste0("(", p, ",0,", q, ")"),
         loglik         = as.numeric(logLik(fit)),
         AIC            = AIC(fit),
         BIC            = BIC(fit))
}

arima_res = arima_grid |>
  pmap(\(p, q) arima_fxn(r_train, p, q)) |>
  list_rbind() |>
  arrange(BIC)

arima_order = c(1, 0)

Table 3 displays the log-likelihood, AIC and BIC values for all candidate ARIMA models. BIC selects ARIMA(1,0,0) as the optimal model, whereas AIC selects the more complex ARIMA(2,0,2). The log-likelihood always favours the more complicated model, since the addition of more parameters can only improve the fit. However, this can lead to overfitting. BIC penalises additional parameters more heavily than AIC. This is important given the large training sample (over 4000 returns). Thus, ARIMA(1,0,0) is selected as the mean model. The ARIMA likelihood assumes a constant variance, which the tests below reject, so these information criteria are only approximate. The adequacy of the AR(1) mean is therefore checked again on the standardised residuals of the fitted GARCH models (Table 8).
An ARIMA model assumes that the variance of the residuals is constant. This assumption is tested using the Ljung–Box test on the squared residuals as well as Engle’s (1982) ARCH LM test. A small \(p\)-value rejects the null hypothesis of no ARCH effects. This suggests the presence of volatility clustering and justifies the use of an ARCH or GARCH model.


Show code

  `LB squared residuals` = sapply(lags, function(L) Box.test(fit_mean^2, lag = L, type = "Ljung-Box")$statistic),
  `LB p-value`           = sapply(lags, function(L) Box.test(fit_mean^2, lag = L, type = "Ljung-Box")$p.value)

In Table 4, both the Ljung–Box test and Engle’s ARCH LM test reject the null hypothesis of no ARCH effects at all tested lags (\(p\) < 0.001). This indicates that the squared shocks are autocorrelated, which is evidence of volatility clustering. Thus, the assumption of constant variance does not hold, which justifies the use of a conditional variance model.

GARCH(1,1) from first principles


Show code
# Function to calculate negative log-likelihood of Gaussian GARCH(1,1) with constant mean:
garch11_nll_fxn = function(par, r) {
  mu    = par[1]
  omega = par[2] 
  alpha = par[3]
  beta  = par[4]

  # Return large value if parameter constraints broken:
  if (omega <= 0 || alpha < 0 || beta < 0 || alpha + beta >= 1) {
    return(1e10)
  }

  # Calculate shocks:
  e = r - mu

  # Initialise with sample variance:
  n     = length(r)
  s2    = numeric(n)
  s2[1] = mean((r - mean(r))^2)

  # Recursion for conditional variance:
  for (t in 2:n) {
    s2[t] = omega + alpha * e[t-1]^2 + beta * s2[t-1]
  }

  # Negative log-likelihood:
  0.5 * sum(log(2 * pi) + log(s2) + e^2 / s2)
}

# Starting values:
start_val = c(mean(r_train), 0.05 * var(r_train), 0.08, 0.90)

# Maximise log-likelihood:
own_fit = optim(par     = start_val,
                fn      = garch11_nll_fxn,
                r       = r_train,
                method  = "L-BFGS-B",
                lower   = c(-Inf, 1e-8, 0, 0),
                upper   = c(Inf, Inf, 1, 1),
                hessian = TRUE)

own_est = own_fit$par
own_se  = sqrt(diag(solve(own_fit$hessian))) 

# Fit same model with rugarch:

Table 8 displays the diagnostics of the standardised residuals, \(z_t\), of each model. The Ljung–Box \(p\)-values for \(z_t\) are above 0.05 for all models (\(p\) > 0.05). Thus, the null hypothesis of no autocorrelation is not rejected, which suggests that the AR(1) mean equation is adequate.
Before the models were fitted, Engle’s ARCH LM statistic at lag 10 was large (LM = 710.1, \(p\) < 0.001; Table 4). After fitting, the ARCH LM \(p\)-values of the three GARCH models increase (\(p\) = 0.010 to 0.043), although they remain significant at the 5% level. However, with over 4000 observations, even very small autocorrelations become statistically significant. Figure 5 shows that the autocorrelations remaining in the squared standardised residuals are small in comparison to those of the squared returns in Figure 3. This indicates that most of the volatility clustering has been removed.
ARCH(11) performs the best on these diagnostics since its 11 lags absorb the short-term dependence. However, as seen in Table 5, it cannot capture the persistence of volatility. Of the GARCH models, GJR-GARCH-\(t\) has the least remaining dependence in the squared standardised residuals (Ljung–Box \(p\) = 0.017).
The excess kurtosis decreases from the training-sample returns (excess kurtosis = 6.067; Table 1) to the standardised residuals of GJR-GARCH-\(t\) (excess kurtosis = 1.361). This suggests that most of the heavy tails in the returns can be attributed to volatility clustering. The remaining excess kurtosis is close to that of a Student-\(t\) distribution with \(\hat\nu \approx 10\) degrees of freedom (\(6/(\nu - 4) \approx 1.0\)), which supports the use of Student-\(t\) innovations. This is confirmed by the QQ plot in Figure 5, where the points lie on the diagonal except for a few extreme negative standardised residuals.


Out-of-sample evaluation
The conditional variance models are evaluated on the test set using rolling one-day-ahead forecasts. Each model is re-estimated every 50 trading days using an expanding window, so that all of the data available up to each forecast origin is used. This produces a one-day-ahead variance forecast for each of the 1023 days in the test set. The constant-variance model uses the variance of the training sample, while EWMA is initialised using the variance of the first 63 returns in the training set.


Show code

However, QLIKE depends on the ratio of the squared return to the forecast variance, as opposed to their difference. This means that it is less affected by extreme days than MSE. Thus, the models are ranked using QLIKE.

The constant-variance model is a flat line, so it underpredicts volatility when returns spike and overpredicts it in calm periods. In comparison, both EWMA and GJR-GARCH-\(t\) rise sharply after large returns and then decay slowly, which reflects the high persistence estimated earlier. During calm periods, EWMA drops lower than GJR-GARCH-\(t\) since it has no long-run variance to revert to. GJR-GARCH-\(t\) also rises more than EWMA after large falls in the index, due to the leverage effect.


Tests of forecast accuracy
The differences in QLIKE between the models in Table 9 are small, so the Diebold–Mariano test (Diebold & Mariano, 1995) is used to determine whether they are statistically significant. This test is not covered in the course notes, so the dm.test() function from the forecast package (Hyndman & Khandakar, 2008) is used. For each test day, the loss differential is the QLIKE loss of GJR-GARCH-\(t\) minus the QLIKE loss of a competing model. The null hypothesis is that the two models have equal expected loss, so that the mean loss differential is zero. A negative test statistic means that GJR-GARCH-\(t\) has the lower average loss.


Show code
# Note: Patton's (2011) normalised QLIKE is non-negative (needed for dm.test with power = 1)
# and differs from loss table QLIKE by a constant, so loss differentials are unchanged
# QLIKE loss = proxy/h - log(proxy/h) - 1:
qlike_wide = oos |>
  mutate(L = proxy / h - log(proxy / h) - 1) |>
  select(date, Model, L) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = Model, values_from = L)

rivals = setdiff(names(model_cols), "GJR-GARCH-t")

dm_tbl = map(rivals, function(m) {
  dm = dm.test(e1          = qlike_wide[["GJR-GARCH-t"]],
               e2          = qlike_wide[[m]],
               alternative = "two.sided",
               h           = 1,
               power       = 1)
  tibble(Comparison             = paste("GJR-GARCH-t vs", m),
         `Mean loss difference` = mean(qlike_wide[["GJR-GARCH-t"]] - qlike_wide[[m]]),
         `DM statistic`         = unname(dm$statistic),
         `p-value`              = dm$p.value)
}) |>
  list_rbind()

dm_tbl |>
  mutate(`p-value` = format.pval(`p-value`, digits = 3, eps = 0.001)) |>
  kable(digits = 3)

Table 10 shows that at the 5% level, GJR-GARCH-\(t\) has a significantly lower QLIKE loss than Constant, EWMA, ARCH, GARCH-N and GARCH-\(t\). Since the squared return is a very noisy proxy for the true variance, small differences in average loss are difficult to detect over a test set of 1023 days.


Value-at-Risk backtests
The QLIKE loss evaluates the forecast variance, but not the shape of the forecast distribution. The choice between normal and Student-\(t\) innovations matters most in the tails, so the forecasts are also evaluated using the one-day-ahead Value-at-Risk (VaR). The \(100\alpha\%\) VaR is the \(\alpha\) quantile of the forecast return distribution, so it is the lower limit of a \(100(1 - 2\alpha)\%\) prediction interval for the next day’s return. A violation occurs when the realised return falls below the VaR. If the forecasts are correct, violations should occur on a proportion \(\alpha\) of days (tested with Kupiec’s (1995) unconditional coverage test) and should not cluster together (tested with Christoffersen’s (1998) conditional coverage test). These tests are not covered in the course notes, so the VaRTest() function from rugarch is used. The VaR of the GARCH-family models comes from the rolling forecasts, and the VaR of the constant-variance and EWMA benchmarks uses normal quantiles.


Show code
var_levels = c(0.01, 0.05)

# GARCH-family VaR from the rolling forecasts:
var_garch = imap(roll_list, function(roll, model) {
  v = as.data.frame(roll, which = "VaR")
  map(var_levels, function(a) {
    tibble(Model  = model,
           alpha  = a,
           actual = v$realized,
           VaR    = v[[grep(paste0("\\(", a * 100, "%\\)"), names(v))]])
  }) |>
    list_rbind()
}) |>
  list_rbind()

# Benchmark VaR using normal quantiles:
var_bench = oos |>
  filter(Model %in% c("Constant", "EWMA")) |>
  cross_join(tibble(alpha = var_levels)) |>
  transmute(Model  = as.character(Model),
            alpha,
            actual = r,
            VaR    = mu_tr + qnorm(alpha) * sigma)

# Kupiec and Christoffersen tests:
var_tbl = bind_rows(var_bench, var_garch) |>
  group_by(Model, alpha) |>
  group_modify(function(d, key) {
    vt = VaRTest(alpha = key$alpha, actual = d$actual, VaR = d$VaR)
    tibble(Expected           = vt$expected.exceed,
           Violations         = vt$actual.exceed,
           `Kupiec p`         = vt$uc.LRp,
           `Christoffersen p` = vt$cc.LRp)
  }) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(Model = factor(Model, levels = names(model_cols)),
         Level = paste0(alpha * 100, "%")) |>
  arrange(alpha, Model) |>
  select(Level, Model, Expected, Violations, `Kupiec p`, `Christoffersen p`)

Table 11 shows that at the 1% level, Constant, GARCH-\(t\) and GJR-GARCH-\(t\) pass both tests, while EWMA, ARCH and GARCH-N are rejected by at least one test. At the 1% level, 1023 test days give approximately 10 expected violations. Models with normal innovations (EWMA, ARCH and GARCH-N) understate the probability of extreme losses, which shows as more violations than expected, whereas the Student-\(t\) models allow for heavier tails. At the 5% level, the choice of distribution matters less, since the 5% quantiles of the normal and Student-\(t\) distributions are similar. However, the test set contains few extreme days, so these tests have limited power.

Forecasting
The preferred model, GJR-GARCH(1,1)-\(t\), is re-estimated on the full sample (1995–2017) and used to forecast volatility over the next 63 trading days.


Show code
# Refit the best model on the full sample:
final_fit = ugarchfit(spec = spec_list[[best_name]], data = r_xts, solver = "hybrid")

# Forecast 63 trading days ahead:
h_max = 63
fc    = ugarchforecast(final_fit, n.ahead = h_max)

# Forecast dates (weekdays only, ignoring public holidays):
all_days     = seq(max(alsi$date) + 1, by = "day", length.out = 2 * h_max)
future_dates = all_days[wday(all_days, week_start = 1) <= 5][1:h_max]

# Standardised t quantiles for the 95% interval:
nu_final = coef(final_fit)["shape"]
q_lo     = qdist("std", p = 0.025, mu = 0, sigma = 1, shape = nu_final)
q_hi     = qdist("std", p = 0.975, mu = 0, sigma = 1, shape = nu_final)

fc_df = tibble(date  = future_dates,
               h     = 1:h_max,
               mu    = as.numeric(fitted(fc)),
               sigma = as.numeric(sigma(fc))) |>
  mutate(lo95 = mu + q_lo * sigma,
         hi95 = mu + q_hi * sigma)

Figure 7 illustrates the 63-day volatility forecast from the model fitted to the full sample. During 2016, volatility peaked at the end of June (approximately 31% p.a.), which could be attributed to the Brexit vote. Volatility then decayed to below its long-run level and was low at the end of the sample (approximately 13% p.a.), below the unconditional volatility indicated by the dashed line. Thus, the forecast rises gradually towards the long-run level, reaching 16.8% p.a. after 63 trading days (Table 13). The forecast has not yet reached the long-run level by this point, which reflects the high persistence of the model.
The forecast mean return is just above zero, which highlights that the returns themselves cannot be predicted. The 95% prediction intervals widen over the forecast horizon since the forecast volatility increases towards its long-run level.

Table 13 reports the annualised volatility forecasts at selected horizons. The forecast volatility increases steadily over the forecast period, from the first trading day (13.0% p.a.) to one month ahead (14.8% p.a. after 22 trading days) and three months ahead (16.8% p.a. after 63 trading days). However, even after three months the forecast remains below the long-run level of volatility (unconditional volatility = 19% p.a.). This reflects the high persistence of the model, as volatility shocks take a long time to die out.

Discussion

Model recommendations
The optimal model for the volatility of daily ALSI returns is the GJR-GARCH(1,1) model with Student-\(t\) innovations and an AR(1) mean equation. This model has the lowest BIC on the training set (BIC = 2.983) as well as the lowest loss on the test set (QLIKE = 0.805). Its parameter estimates are also stable between the training sample and the full sample (Table 12). The model captures the three main features of the data. Firstly, volatility is highly persistent. Secondly, negative shocks increase volatility more than positive shocks of the same size, which is known as the leverage effect. Lastly, the returns have heavy tails, even after volatility clustering has been accounted for. In comparison to EWMA, GJR-GARCH-\(t\) reverts to a long-run level of volatility. Thus, it does not underestimate risk after long periods of low volatility.


Limitations
There were several limitations to this analysis. Engle’s ARCH LM test indicates that some dependence remains in the squared standardised residuals of all three GARCH models (\(p\) = 0.010 to 0.043). This suggests that the GJR-GARCH-\(t\) model does not capture all of the volatility dynamics in the returns, although part of this significance can be attributed to the large sample size.
The squared return is a very noisy proxy for the true variance, so small differences in QLIKE are difficult to detect. The Diebold–Mariano tests (Table 10) show which differences are statistically significant, and the ranking of the GARCH models is less certain than their improvement over the constant-variance model.
The test period (2013–2017) is calmer than the training period and contains no crisis comparable to 1997–1998 or 2008–2009. Thus, the forecasts, and especially the VaR backtests, have not been evaluated under extreme conditions. The constant-variance benchmark is also not re-estimated during the test period, unlike the GARCH models, which partly explains its large loss.
The model assumes that the parameters remain constant from 1995 to 2017, a period that includes the 1997–1998 and 2008–2009 financial crises. The rolling models are also only re-estimated every 50 trading days. This means that the model may adapt slowly to structural changes in volatility. Lastly, the data end in February 2017, so the forecast is a historical exercise rather than a current prediction.


Improvements
The returns are negatively skewed (skewness = -0.446), which a symmetric Student-\(t\) distribution cannot capture. It may be useful to fit the models with a skewed Student-\(t\) distribution instead.
Realised volatility, calculated from intraday returns, would provide a less noisy proxy for the true variance than squared daily returns, and would allow the forecasts to be evaluated more reliably. Lastly, extending the data beyond February 2017 would allow the model to be used to forecast current volatility.

title: Predicting the volatility of daily Johannesburg Stock Exchange All Share Index returns
text:
Predicting the volatility of daily Johannesburg Stock Exchange All Share Index returns
Section and topic: Section 1 - Conditional variance models (ARCH and GARCH).
Type of project: Implementation and model comparison on real-world data. The GARCH(1,1) likelihood is coded from first principles.
Aim: To model and forecast the volatility of daily JSE All Share Index (ALSI) returns, and to determine which model, ARCH, GARCH or GJR-GARCH, gives the best out-of-sample volatility forecasts compared to the constant-variance and EWMA benchmarks.
Data used:

Daily FTSE/JSE All Share total return index (J203, dividends reinvested), 30 June 1995 to 3 February 2017. Source: Gebbie, T. (2020), Daily Sampled South African Market Index Data 1994–2017, University of Cape Town, https://doi.org/10.25375/uct.11302325.v1.

Daily log returns (%) were modelled. July 1995 to December 2012 is used as the training set and January 2013 to February 2017 as the test set. Download instructions are in the detailed analysis.
Methods used: The mean equation is selected by comparing candidate ARIMA models using BIC. The residuals of this model are tested for ARCH effects using the Ljung-Box test on the squared residuals and Engle’s ARCH LM test. The order of a pure ARCH model is chosen using BIC and compared to a GARCH(\(1,1\)) model with the same mean and normal innovations. The candidate models, ARCH(\(q\)), GARCH(\(1,1\)) with normal and Student-\(t\) innovations and GJR-GARCH(\(1,1\)) with Student-\(t\) innovations, are estimated by maximum likelihood. The GARCH(\(1,1\)) likelihood is coded from first principles and maximised using optim. The fitted models are assessed using diagnostics on the standardised residuals. The rolling one-day ahead volatility forecasts are compared to the constant-variance and EWMA benchmarks using MSE and QLIKE, Diebold–Mariano tests of equal predictive accuracy and Value-at-Risk backtests. The optimal model is used to forecast volatility over the following 63 trading days.
Key findings:

The returns are only weakly autocorrelated, so an AR(1) mean model is sufficient. However, there is strong evidence of ARCH effects (\(p\) < 0.001). Thus, volatility is predictable even though returns are not.
A pure ARCH model requires 11 lags and still has a higher BIC than a GARCH(1,1) model. Volatility shocks in the ARCH model have a half-life < 5 trading days as opposed to the GARCH models with half-lives ranging from 55 to 98 trading days.
GJR-GARCH(1,1) with Student-\(t\) errors is the best model both in sample (BIC = 2.983) and out of sample (QLIKE = 0.805), outperforming EWMA (QLIKE = 0.849) and the constant-variance model (QLIKE = 1.063). Negative shocks increase the following day’s variance approximately 2.8 times more than positive shocks of the same size. Volatility is highly persistent (persistence = 0.987) and the errors have heavier tails than the normal distribution (\(\hat{\nu} = 9.9\)).
Diebold–Mariano tests show that at the 5% level, GJR-GARCH-\(t\) has a significantly lower QLIKE loss than Constant, EWMA, ARCH, GARCH-N and GARCH-\(t\).
Value-at-Risk backtests show that at the 1% level, Constant, GARCH-\(t\) and GJR-GARCH-\(t\) pass both tests, while EWMA, ARCH and GARCH-N are rejected by at least one test.
My implementation of the GARCH(1,1) likelihood, from first principles, reproduced the rugarch estimates to 3 decimal places.
At the end of the sample, volatility (13.0% p.a.) is below its long-run level (19.0% p.a.). Thus, the forecast rises slowly towards the long-run level and reaches 16.8% p.a. after 63 trading days.

What I would do differently next time:

The returns are negatively skewed, which a symmetric Student-\(t\) distribution cannot capture. I would compare the models with skewed Student-\(t\) innovations.
I would extend the dataset beyond February 2017. This would allow for current volatility forecasts and would test the stability of the estimated parameters.

Introduction
A hidden Markov model (HMM) is a state-space model with a discrete state. An unobserved state \(C_t \in \{1, \dots, m\}\) follows a Markov chain with transition probability matrix \(\Gamma\), \(\gamma_{ij} = P(C_t = j \mid C_{t-1} = i)\), and the observation \(X_t\) is drawn from a distribution that depends on the current state, \(p_i(x) = P(X_t = x \mid C_t = i)\) (Zucchini et al., 2016; Department of Statistical Sciences, 2026). Marginally each observation comes from a mixture of the state-dependent distributions, but because the state is persistent, the observations are correlated.
This project has two parts.

Part A implements all the core algorithms (the scaled forward algorithm for the likelihood, the backward algorithm, local decoding, the Viterbi algorithm, state forecasts and forecast distributions) from first principles as one small toolkit, and checks it against depmixS4 (Visser & Speekenbrink, 2010) on the earthquake data from the HMM tutorial. The other tutorial questions are in the Hidden Markov Models section of Section 2.
Part B uses the same toolkit to look for regimes in daily JSE All Share Index returns, the data used in Project 3. In Project 3, volatility was modelled as a continuous process with GJR-GARCH. In this project I ask whether the returns can be described by a small number of discrete market regimes, when these regimes occurred, and whether a Gaussian HMM forecasts the distribution of returns as well as GJR-GARCH.

Data

Earthquakes: annual counts of major earthquakes (magnitude 7 and above) worldwide, 1900–2006, the data set used in the notes and the tutorial (Zucchini et al., 2016). The 107 counts are entered in the code below and are the same values as earthquakes.csv from the tutorial.
JSE All Share Index: the daily FTSE/JSE All Share total return index (J203) from 30 June 1995 to 3 February 2017 (Gebbie, 2020), as in Project 3. Daily log returns (%) are modelled. July 1995 to December 2012 is the training set and January 2013 to February 2017 the test set.

Both data sets are publicly available and contain no personal information, so no consent, anonymisation or POPIA steps were needed.
Data access instructions. Download the daily workbook from https://doi.org/10.25375/uct.11302325.v1 and save it as _data/PT-DATA-ALBI-JIBAR-JSEIND-Daily-1994-2017.xlsx next to this file (the same file as in Project 3). The earthquake counts are entered in the code.

section: Hidden Markov Models from first principles

text:
Discussion

Model recommendations
For the earthquake counts, a three-state Poisson HMM is preferred by both AIC and BIC. It identifies periods of low, medium and high activity that each last several years, and its forecast distributions take the current state of the process into account.
For the JSE returns, Gaussian HMMs with three or four regimes capture the main stylised facts of daily returns: volatility clustering, heavy tails and lower mean returns in more volatile regimes (?@tbl-regimes, Table 7). The decoded crisis regime identifies the 1998 and 2008–2009 crises (Table 6), and the volatility implied by the HMM is closely related to the GJR-GARCH volatility (Figure 4). However, for forecasting the distribution of the next day’s return, GJR-GARCH-\(t\) remains the better model (Table 8). I would therefore use the HMM to describe the market, for example to date regimes, measure how long they last and estimate the probability that the market is currently in a crisis regime, and GJR-GARCH to forecast risk, as recommended in Project 3.


Interactive explorer
The JSE regime explorer is a Shiny app based on the same models (code in scripts/shiny-app/). It displays the regimes for one to four states using global decoding, local decoding or filtered probabilities, allows the user to zoom in on crisis periods, and compares the HMM volatility and log scores with those of GJR-GARCH. Switching between the smoothed and filtered probabilities shows clearly that the filtered regimes, which use only past returns, change later than the smoothed ones.


Limitations

The number of states was chosen by BIC, which was still decreasing at four states, and models with more states were not fitted. The “right” number of regimes is therefore not well defined; additional states mainly divide the volatility range more finely.
The state-dependent distributions are normal and their means do not depend on the previous return. The model therefore ignores the small AR(1) effect found in Project 3 (Table 7) and can only produce heavy tails by switching between regimes.
The parameters were estimated once, on 1995–2012, and assumed to be constant, and the transition probabilities do not depend on covariates such as the exchange rate or global volatility.
The likelihood was maximised numerically. Five random starting values per model (Table 3) make it more likely that the global maximum was found, but cannot guarantee it. The depmixS4 check covered only the two-state model, and it showed how easily an optimiser can stop at the wrong solution when the starting values are poor.
The standard errors in Table 5 are based on the Hessian and the delta method, which give symmetric intervals and assume that the log-likelihood is approximately quadratic near the maximum. They also ignore the uncertainty in choosing the number of regimes.
The decoded regimes are estimates. Near regime switches, the local decoding probabilities can be far from 0 or 1, so the regime assigned to an individual day should not be over-interpreted.



Improvements

Markov-switching GARCH. Combining the two approaches, with GARCH dynamics within each regime and Markov switching between regimes (Haas et al., 2004), would keep both the interpretability of regimes and the responsiveness of GARCH.
More flexible state-dependent distributions. Student-\(t\) distributions within each regime, and an AR(1) term in each state, which gives a Markov-switching autoregression (Hamilton, 1989).
Time-varying transition probabilities. Allowing \(\Gamma\) to depend on covariates, such as the SAVI volatility index or the exchange rate, could make regime changes partly predictable.
More thorough evaluation. Rolling re-estimation, Value-at-Risk backtests as in Project 3, and parametric bootstrap confidence intervals for the transition probabilities and expected durations.
Link to Project 2. The same regime-switching approach could be applied to the El Niño Southern Oscillation, which moves between El Niño, La Niña and neutral phases. I suggested this as an improvement in Project 2, and HMMs handle the missing SST months naturally, since the forward algorithm simply skips the update when an observation is missing.

title: Hidden Markov models: from first principles to market regimes on the JSE
text:
Hidden Markov models: from first principles to market regimes on the JSE
Section and topic: Section 2 - Hidden Markov models (likelihood, forward and backward probabilities, local and global decoding, forecasting).
Type of project: Implementation (all core HMM algorithms coded from first principles and checked against depmixS4), extended to model comparison on real-world data, with an interactive Shiny app.
Aim: To implement the HMM algorithms from first principles, validate them on the tutorial’s earthquake data. Use the HMM algorithms to determine whether daily JSE All Share Index returns can be described by a small number of market regimes, when these regimes occurred, and whether a Gaussian HMM forecasts the distribution of returns as well as the GJR-GARCH model from Project 3.
Data used:

Annual counts of major earthquakes (magnitude 7 and above), 1900–2006. Source: Zucchini, MacDonald and Langrock (2016), as in the course notes and tutorial.
Daily FTSE/JSE All Share total return index (J203), 30 June 1995 to 3 February 2017. Source: Gebbie, T. (2020), Daily Sampled South African Market Index Data 1994–2017, University of Cape Town, https://doi.org/10.25375/uct.11302325.v1.

Daily log returns (%) were modelled, with July 1995 to December 2012 as the training set and January 2013 to February 2017 as the test set (as in Project 3). Download instructions are in the detailed analysis and the code and data appendix.
Methods used: I implemented the main HMM algorithms from first principles: the scaled forward and backward algorithms, local decoding, the Viterbi algorithm, the stationary distribution and forecast distributions. Parameters were estimated by numerically maximising the likelihood with nlm() and optim() on unconstrained working parameters. The implementation was validated against depmixS4 using Poisson HMMs for the earthquake counts; the remaining tutorial questions are in the Hidden Markov Models section of Section 2.
For the JSE returns, Gaussian HMMs with one to four states were fitted from several sets of starting values and compared using AIC and BIC. The selected model was assessed with normal pseudo-residuals, decoded with the Viterbi algorithm and local decoding, and given approximate standard errors using the Hessian and the delta method. It was then compared with GJR-GARCH(1,1)-\(t\) using filtered volatility and one-step-ahead log scores on the test set, with a Newey-West test of equal predictive ability. A Shiny app presents the fitted regimes interactively.
Key findings:

My likelihood code reproduced the depmixS4 log-likelihoods for the earthquake data exactly (−341.88 and −328.53), but only once the initial distribution was estimated freely, as depmixS4 does. A three-state Poisson HMM (about 13, 20 and 30 earthquakes per year) is selected by both AIC and BIC.
For JSE returns, BIC selects four regimes, although three regimes already remove the heavy tails and the volatility clustering from the pseudo-residuals. The regimes range from a calm market (annualised volatility of about 8%) to a crisis regime (about 45%) with a negative mean return, which lasts about 20 trading days on average and is entered gradually through the intermediate regimes.
The crisis regime picks out the 1998 emerging market crisis andmthe 2008–2009 global financial crisis. The HMM’s real-time (filtered) volatility is strongly correlated with the GJR-GARCH volatility.
With its default starting values, depmixS4 stopped at a one-state solution for the JSE data, so I refitted it with starting values for a calm and a turbulent state. This showed how easily an optimiser can stop at the wrong point.
Out of sample, GJR-GARCH-\(t\) forecasts the next day’s return distribution significantly better than every HMM (log score −1.317 compared with −1.326 for the best HMM). HMMs are useful for describing market regimes, while GARCH remains better for forecasting risk.

What I would do differently next time:

Use a parametric bootstrap instead of the delta method for confidence intervals, especially for the expected durations of the regimes.
Use Student-\(t\) state distributions with an AR(1) mean in each regime, or a Markov-switching GARCH model, to combine the interpretability of regimes with the responsiveness of GARCH.
Apply the same regime-switching approach to El Niño, La Niña and neutral phases in the Project 2 sea surface temperature data.

Link to the detailed analysis: Detailed analysis and code
Interactive app: JSE regime explorer (opens on shinyapps.io; it can take a few seconds to wake up). Code: scripts/shiny-app/ (see the code and data appendix).

title: Lagged & Loaded
text:
When I signed up for Time Series Analysis, I had never worked with time series data. I understood, conceptually, that today’s observation can depend on yesterday’s but I didn’t know how to model this. Sulaiman’s section answered my questions, one model at a time. The first clarifying moment was distinguishing between autoregressive (AR) and moving average (MA) terms. An AR process carries the influence of its own past forward, meaning that the effects of a shock can persist. Whereas, an MA process depends on a finite number of past shocks, that only influence observations for a fixed time period. Almost every series I worked with had some sort of seasonal pattern that became visually apparent when decomposing the series into it’s seasonality, trend and residuals, so naturally this lead us to SARIMA models.
In Portfolio Theory, the assignments were based on Johannesburg Stock Exchange data, and many of the methods we implemented assumed that the variance was constant. This was not the case, and the conditional variance models section, in Time Series, offered an explanation as to why. Volatility clustering describes how periods of high volatility tend to follow periods of high volatility and periods of calm tend to follow periods of calm. ARCH and GARCH models were a new way to account for this in the data.
I thought that I’d left trigonometry behind in high school, but sine and cosine terms made an unexpected return in spectral analysis. Representing a time series as a combination of waves provided me with a new perspective on patterns that I’d been viewing through the time domain only. A seasonal pattern could now be described by the sum of Fourier terms.
With Section 1 done and dusted, Birgit’s section started connecting these different ideas. State-space models represent a time series through two equations: an observation equation which describes what is observed and a state equation which describes the evolution of an underlying, unobserved state. What initially appeared to be a completely different modelling framework started connecting methods I’d previously regarded as separate. Exponential smoothing had initially seemed like an intuitive way of calculating weighted averages but expressing it in state-space form cemented the statistical formulation, which allowed me to calculate prediction intervals.
The Kalman filter tied my whole semester together. I’m taking Portfolio Theory, Time Series Analysis and Bayesian Computational Methods. I had expected the concepts covered in these respective courses to remain fairly distinguishable but the Kalman filter changed that. Its recursive updating procedure was familiar from Bayesian statistics. The prediction step provides the prior distribution, the new observation contributes to the likelihood and the resulting posterior becomes the prior at the next iteration. In Bayes, we’d constructed MCMC algorithms and now these were applicable in Time Series. Implementing this filter in Stan made this connection even more tangible and it was rewarding to see concepts, from courses I thought were unrelated, come together in a single modelling framework.
I revisited the Portfolio Theory data in the Hidden Markov Models (HMM) section, but with a different perspective on market behaviour. GARCH models provided a framework for describing how conditional volatility evolves, but they do not explicitly identify distinct market regimes or describe how long the market might remain in a particular state. HMMs approach this differently by treating the market as switching between unobserved regimes representing different levels of market volatility. In Project 4, the regime-switching model did not outperform GARCH in volatility forecasting, but it provided a different type of insight into the market. While GARCH produced stronger volatility forecasts, the HMM offered an interpretable account of when market conditions changed and how persistent the different regimes were.
Not only did I learn a new way of modelling sequential data, I also learnt new ways in which to analyse the outcomes: the Diebold–Mariano test for assessing whether differences in predictive accuracy are statistically meaningful, and the QLIKE loss function for evaluating volatility forecasts. Finally, this course tied together concepts that initially seemed disconnected and provided me with a more rounded view on sequential data. At the start of the semester I knew that past observations may influence the future, but now not only do I know how to model, analyse and forecast that relationship, I also know that I will probably never escape sine and cosine functions.
