title: Lagged & Loaded
text:
Methodological Challenges
Real data, I discovered, has not read the textbook.
In Project 2, sea surface temperature and Theewaterskloof Dam levels appeared strongly related. This looked promising until I realised that much of the apparent relationship was due to the two seasonal series being out of phase. Prewhitening before computing the cross-correlation substantially changed the interpretation and showed me how easily autocorrelation and shared seasonality can manufacture an apparently meaningful relationship. Including SST in a dynamic regression also did not improve forecasts over the univariate model. Another challenge arose because the TAO/TRITON buoys contained missing observations, meaning that the set of buoys contributing to the average SST changed over time. This had to be accounted for before interpreting the series, since changes in which buoys were reporting could otherwise create artificial changes in the calculated SST.
Electricity demand provided a clear lesson in how inconvenient real-world time series can be. Demand fell drastically during the 2020 COVID-19 lockdown and recovered slowly afterwards. Fitting a model to the entire series would have treated fundamentally different periods as though they were generated by the same underlying process, potentially leading to inaccurate forecasts. A Bai–Perron structural break test helped identify the disruption, but there was uncertainty around the appropriate end date. I therefore started the modelling period in March 2021, tying the statistical evidence to South Africa’s move to alert level 1. I also attempted to include an annual adjustment, which improved performance on the test set but worsened it on the validation set. Keeping it would have meant allowing knowledge of the out-of-sample test data to influence model selection, so the adjustment was not retained.
The JSE returns in Project 3 highlighted the limitations of standard modelling assumptions. The returns themselves were only weakly autocorrelated, but their squared residuals showed strong ARCH effects. The distributional assumption also mattered more than I had anticipated. Gaussian models performed worse in the presence of heavy tails, whereas Student-(t) innovations were better able to accommodate extreme returns. The asymmetry captured by GJR-GARCH further complicated the analysis, since negative shocks increased the following day’s variance substantially more than positive shocks of the same magnitude. This reinforced the lesson that, although modelling assumptions may be mathematically convenient, they still need to be defensible in real-world data.
In the Hidden Markov Models project, depmixS4, using its default starting values, converged to what was effectively a one-state solution for the JSE data. After refitting the model using alternative starting values, I obtained substantially better solutions. This highlighted the importance of using multiple random starts in optimisation problems, particularly when the likelihood may contain several local optima. A model converging successfully does not necessarily mean that it has converged to the best available solution.
Uncertainty created a different challenge across several projects. In Project 1, the model-based prediction intervals were wider than their nominal coverage required because a smoothing parameter close to one caused uncertainty to accumulate almost like a random walk. Unusually large holiday residuals also inflated the estimated variance. In Project 2, however, residual autocorrelation suggested that the dam model’s prediction intervals were too narrow, while its long-horizon forecasts eventually produced intervals extending beyond the physically possible bounds for dam capacity. In Project 4, standard errors obtained using the Hessian and delta method were only approximate. Together, these examples emphasised that uncertainty is not simply an extra quantity reported alongside a forecast. How uncertainty is estimated, and which sources of uncertainty are omitted, can materially change the conclusions drawn from a model.

title: Lagged & Loaded
text:
Ethical and Reproducibility Considerations
None of the datasets I used contained personal information. Eskom electricity demand, City of Cape Town dam levels, NOAA buoy temperatures, JSE index prices and earthquake counts are all aggregate or publicly available datasets, so issues such as consent, anonymisation and POPIA compliance were not central to the analysis. The more relevant ethical considerations concerned how the results were interpreted and communicated. Dam levels and electricity demand are linked to decisions around water restrictions and load shedding, both of which have real consequences. Presenting a point forecast without its uncertainty, or overstating a weak relationship between El Niño and dam levels, could therefore create a misleading impression of certainty. For this reason, I reported prediction intervals and coverage alongside point forecasts and was careful to distinguish association from causation. Similarly, a VaR model that performs well over one evaluation period should not automatically be treated as reliable under all market conditions, particularly during periods of financial stress. I also documented data-cleaning decisions, including duplicated dam observations and changing buoy coverage, so that the analysis remained transparent.
The portfolio was developed as a Quarto project under version control with Git. Each analysis uses a fixed random seed where required, saves its results, and allows the summary pages to read numerical outputs directly from those saved objects using inline R. This became increasingly important as the projects evolved. In earlier drafts, I occasionally found that the written interpretation no longer matched the tables after changing a model or specification. Linking the reported values directly to the analysis reduced the risk of this happening. Shared code, such as the HMM functions, was also kept in a common script rather than duplicated across projects. The Shiny application was deployed through shinyapps.io, while the appendix records data sources, access dates and the required rendering order. Freezing computationally expensive analyses also made the project substantially easier to manage.
I used Claude (Anthropic) to assist with selected aspects of the portfolio. It was mainly used to debug code, translate my pseudocode into R, explain statistical concepts I did not yet fully understand, clarify how particular functions or packages should be implemented, and verify my interpretation of model output. I also used it periodically to check my projects against the portfolio guidelines and ensure that I remained on track. In addition, it assisted with plotting, table formatting, LaTeX equations, Quarto presentation, development of the Shiny application and the creation of interactive HTML revision material.
The most important distinction for me was between using AI to accelerate the work and using it to replace the statistical reasoning behind the work. AI allowed me to move more quickly through coding, formatting and debugging, but the resulting output still had to be checked carefully against the underlying theory and the behaviour of the data. In several cases, an answer that initially appeared convincing turned out to be incorrect once I examined the implementation or model output more closely. I therefore treated AI-generated code and explanations as suggestions rather than final answers, and I independently ran, checked and interpreted the model implementations and outputs.
AI can make analysis faster, but it does not remove the responsibility to understand it. Used carefully, it was valuable for improving efficiency, clarifying concepts and reducing the time spent on technical formatting. It was a tool that supported the development of the portfolio rather than a substitute for doing the portfolio itself.

title: Lagged & Loaded
text:
Future Areas for Development
Projects 3 and 4 analysed the same JSE returns from two different perspectives: GARCH treated volatility as continuously evolving, while the HMM represented market behaviour through discrete regimes. A natural extension would be a Markov-switching GARCH model that combines both ideas. Project 2 also left room for development. I would like to replace the incomplete buoy-based SST measure with a gap-free ENSO index and include more directly relevant predictors such as rainfall and water use. Since dam capacity is physically bounded between 0% and 100%, I would also explore models that respect these limits. Finally, I would like to improve how uncertainty is represented. Bootstrap or Bayesian intervals could incorporate parameter uncertainty rather than treating fitted parameters as fixed. I would also like to spend more time on spectral analysis, which I enjoyed but applied less extensively.
In July, I was mainly learning how the methods worked. By October, I was questioning assumptions, comparing alternatives and asking whether the output actually made sense. That shift, from fitting models to critically evaluating them, is what I would most like to carry forward.

title: Foundations
text:
Explain what a time series is and how it differs from cross-sectional data, and say why temporal dependence calls for its own methods.

A time series is an ordered sequence of observations on one process. The same observation is recorded at successive time points. Cross-sectional data record many units at a single time point. Thus, their order does not carry information. In a time series, observations are sequentially correlated, so their order carries information. Standard methods assume independent errors whereas a time series needs this dependence to be modelled explicitly.

Treat an observed series as one realisation of a stochastic process.

An observed series is treated as one realisation of a stochastic process. Each \(y_t\) is a random variable (before being observed), after being observed it becomes a realised value. A stochastic process defines a series of these random variables. Thus, the observed data is one sample path out of all the possible paths the same mechanism could have produced. Although different realisations differ visually, they have the same statistical character. How far different realisations appear from each other is dependent on the underlying statistical process. In a white noise process, different realisations will lie around a fixed level. In a random walk, the different realisations will drift apart, since shocks accumulate.

Explain what forecasting is, judge when a process is predictable, and keep forecasts, goals and plans separate.

Forecasting is when we use available information to estimate an unobserved quantity. A forecast consists of both a point estimate and a prediction interval since the future value is a random variable (and has some uncertainty associated with it). The predictability of a series is dependent on how well its driver are understood, if sufficient relevant data exists, if the series is stable and if publishing the forecasts will change the outcome. A series can only be predictable if the horizon and sampling interval is stated. Forecasting describes what is likely to happen in the future based on past observations, goal setting describes what we want to happen in the future and planning describes the actions implemented to achieve our goal based on our forecasts.

Match a forecast horizon to the decision it supports, and read a forecast as a random variable rather than a single number.

The decision determines the forecast horizon (short-term, medium-term, long-term). The horizon then narrows down the choice of model. Uncertainty increases as the forecast horizon increases.

Identify trend, seasonality, cycle and irregular variation in a plot, and describe the shapes each of them takes in practice.

Trend describes the long-run direction of movement of a series. Seasonality is the repeated pattern, that has a fixed length whereas the cycle refers to longer oscillations in the data often driver by the underlying process. Irregular variation is what remains after removing the trend, seasonality and cycle. Ideally this would just be the innovations but in practice this often still contains short-term dependence. Trend can be linear, exponential, polynomial. Seasonality can be additive, multiplicative or have a single spike.

Produce the four benchmark forecasts, and evaluate any competing model against them on data it has not seen.

The Mean forecasts averages all past observations and carries that value into the future. The Naive carries the last observational value into the future. The Seasonal naive model is where every future cycle repeats the last observed cycle. The Drift model carries the slope of the line between the first and last observation into the future.

Use the lag and lead operators, and the algebra built on them, to write models compactly.

The lag operator \(L\) shifts a series back by a period, \(L^k y_t = t_{t-k}\) and the lead operator \(F = L^{-1}\) shifts the series forward, \(F y_t = y_{t+1}\). Both of the operators are linear and we can use this to write models compactly. AR(2) \(y_t = \phi_1 y_{t-1} + \phi_2 y_{t-2} + \varepsilon_t\) can be written as \((1 - \phi_1 L - \phi_2 L^2)y_t = \varepsilon_t\).

Define weak stationarity, say which of its conditions a given series violates, and choose a transformation that restores it.

A process is weakly stationary if its mean is constant, its variance is constant and finite and the autocorrelation depends only on \(h\) on on \(t\). The Airpassengers dataset is an example of a non-stationary process. To restore stationarity you can transform the data (log/Box-Cox transformation) and difference the series.

Define white noise, MA, AR, ARMA, ARIMA and SARIMA processes, derive their basic properties, and identify them from an ACF and a PACF.

White noise \(\varepsilon_t \sim WN(0,\sigma^2)\) has \(E(\varepsilon_t)=0\), \(\text{Var}(\varepsilon_t)=\sigma^2\) and \(\gamma(h)=0\) for \(h\neq0\), so its ACF and PACF show no significant spikes.
MA(\(q\)), \(y_t=\mu+\sum_{j=0}^{q}\theta_j\varepsilon_{t-j}\) with \(\theta_0=1\) is always stationary and \(E(y_t)=\mu\). The \(\varepsilon\) terms are uncorrelated, so \(\gamma(0)=\sigma^2\sum_{j=0}^{q}\theta_j^2\). When the lag is \(h \le q\), \(y_t\) and \(y_{t-h}\) have some common shocks (\(\varepsilon_{t-h},\dots,\varepsilon_{t-q}\)). Only the shared shocks contribute to the covariance, so \(\gamma(h)=\sigma^2\sum_{j=0}^{q-h}\theta_j\theta_{j+h}\) and \(\rho(h)=\gamma(h)/\gamma(0)\). When the lag is \(h>q\), there are no shocks in common, so \(\gamma(h)=0\). Thus, the ACF of an MA(\(q\)) cuts off after lag \(q\).
AR(1), \(y_t=c+\phi y_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t\) is stationary when \(|\phi|<1\). Since the mean is constant, \(\mu=c+\phi\mu\), so \(E(y_t)=c/(1-\phi)\). \(\varepsilon_t\) is uncorrelated with \(y_{t-1}\), so \(\gamma(0)=\phi^2\gamma(0)+\sigma^2=\sigma^2(1-\phi^2)\), which is only finite when \(|\phi|<1\). Multiplying the mean-adjusted equation by \(y_{t-h}-\mu\) and taking expectations gives \(\gamma(h)=\phi\gamma(h-1)\), so \(\rho(h)=\phi^h\). Thus, the ACF of an AR(\(p\)) tails off. Once \(y_{t-1},\dots,y_{t-p}\) are included, further lags add no new information, so the PACF cuts off after lag \(p\).
ARMA(1,1), \(y_t=c+\phi y_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t+\theta\varepsilon_{t-1}\) is stationary when \(|\phi|<1\) and \(E(y_t)=c/(1-\phi)\). The MA term only affects the covariance at lag 1. When the lag is \(h\ge2\), \(\gamma(h)=\phi\gamma(h-1)\), thus the ACF decays like an AR(1) after lag 1. The process can be written as both an MA(\(\infty\)) and an AR(\(\infty\)) (when \(|\theta|<1\)), so neither the ACF nor the PACF cuts off. Thus, both the ACF and PACF of an ARMA(\(p,q\)) tail off.
ARIMA(0,1,0), \(y_t=y_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t\) is the simplest ARIMA (a random walk). Substituting back gives \(y_t=y_0+\sum_{i=1}^t\varepsilon_i\). The \(\varepsilon\) terms are uncorrelated, thus \(\text{Var}(y_t)=t\sigma^2\), which grows with \(t\), so the process is non-stationary. \(\text{Cor}(y_t,y_{t-h})=\sqrt{(t-h)/t}\approx1\), thus the ACF decays very slowly. Differencing gives \((1-L)y_t=\varepsilon_t\), which is white noise. Thus, an ARIMA(\(p,d,q\)) is differenced \(d\) times and the ARMA(\(p,q\)) is then identified from the differenced series.
SARIMA\((p,d,q)(P,D,Q)_s\) applies the same results at the seasonal lags \(s, 2s, \dots\). For example, the seasonal MA(1), \(y_t=\varepsilon_t+\Theta\varepsilon_{t-12}\), only shares a shock with \(y_{t-12}\), thus \(\gamma(12)=\Theta\sigma^2\) and \(\gamma(h)=0\) at every other lag \(h\neq0\). Thus, the ACF of a seasonal MA has spikes at multiples of \(s\) that cut off after lag \(Qs\), and the PACF of a seasonal AR has spikes at multiples of \(s\) that cut off after lag \(Ps\). A slow decay at lags \(s, 2s, \dots\) means a seasonal difference is needed.

Fit, diagnose and forecast these models in R, following the workflow of Box and Jenkins, and test residuals against the white noise standard.

The Box–Jenkins workflow has four steps: identification, estimation, diagnostic checking and forecasting. I applied this to the AirPassengers series in Section 1. I also followed the full workflow on real data in Project 2, where I fitted and compared AR, MA, ARMA and SARIMA models for Theewaterskloof Dam capacity and sea surface temperature.

Explain volatility clustering and fit ARCH and GARCH models to it.

Volatility clustering describes how large movements tend to follow large movements and small movements tend to follow small movements. I tested for ARCH effects and fitted ARCH, GARCH and GJR-GARCH models to daily JSE All Share Index returns in Project 3.


Time series is a single measurement taken at multiple points across time. Technically we are modelling the same thing over and over again (this makes sense as to why there is sequential correlation).






Note



Time series model dependence through sequential observations.








Assumption



Equally spaced measurements.








Assumption



Autocorrelation across time.





Example: Continuous series

Figure 1 plots the number of monthly airline passengers over a 12 year period. This figure clearly illustrates the concepts of seasonality and trend.
Example: Discrete series





Figure 2: Time series plot of the number of seals from 1957 to 1999.




Figure 2 plots the changing number of observed seals over a period of 43 years.
What to do when you have missing observations in a time series?
In discrete time series to deal with missing observations you can express the model in state-space form (ARIMA or Structural Time Series). For a missing observation \(y_t\), skip the update step in the Kalman filter and only run the prediction step. The likelihood is evaluated only over the observed time points.






Kalman filtering



Kalman filtering (linear quadratic estimation) is an algorithm that uses a series of measurements over time to estimate unknown variables, by estimating a joint probability distribution over the variables for each time-step.


In continuous time series, missing observations look like irregularly spaced sampling intervals. You can model the underlying system using Stochastic Differential Equations (CARMA) or you can aggregate the irregular time steps into regular, discrete intervals.



Aggregating up can either smooth out high-frequency structure (stock returns, etc) or can reveal low-frequency structure (Sales, etc).



Noise in the data introduces different realisations. If your model fits one dataset perfectly then it is overfitting.

A time series is an ordered sequence of observations on one process. The same observation is recorded at successive time points. Cross-sectional data record many units at a single time point. Thus, their order does not carry information. In a time series, observations are sequentially correlated, so their order carries information. Standard methods assume independent errors whereas a time series needs this dependence to be modelled explicitly.

Treat an observed series as one realisation of a stochastic process.

In a white noise process, different realisations will lie around a fixed level. In a random walk, the different realisations will drift apart, since shocks accumulate.

text:
Question 4


Code
# Read in data:
knives = ts(c(19,15,39,102,90,29,90,46,30,66,80,89,82,17,26,29),
            start = c(1991,1), 
            frequency = 12)



a
A \(k\)-month moving average forecasts the next month using the average of the last \(k\) months:
\[
\hat{y}_{T+1 \mid T} = \frac{1}{k}\sum_{j=0}^{k-1} y_{T-j}.
\]


Code
k_val = c(3,5,7,9,11)

# Forecast: 
ma_fc = numeric(length(k_val)) 

# For loop to calculate forecasts:
for (i in seq_along(k_val)){
  ma_fc[i] = mean(tail(knives, k_val[i]))
}


knitr::kable(
  data.frame(k = k_val, 
             `Forecast for May 1992` = ma_fc, 
             check.names = FALSE),
      digits = 2)





k

The forecasts range from 24 (3-month MA) to about 56 (7-month MA). The 3-month MA only uses February to April 1992, which were all very low months, so it gives a much lower forecast than the longer averages.


b) Which \(k\) minimises the errors?
To choose \(k\), each moving average is used to make one-step-ahead forecasts within the data (as if we were standing at each month and forecasting the next). The errors are compared over the same months (December 1991 to April 1992), since the 11-month MA can only start forecasting in December 1991. Comparing over the same period is fairer than letting each \(k\) use all the months it can.


Code
# Load data:
y = as.numeric(knives)
n = length(y) # no. observations

# Initialise error matrix:
names = paste0('MA(',k_val,')')

err = matrix(NA,
             nrow=n,
             ncol=length(k_val),
             dimnames=list(NULL,names))

for (j in seq_along(k_val)) {
  k = k_val[j]
  for (t in (k+1):n) {
    # One-step-ahead MA forecast:
    fc = mean(y[(t-k):(t-1)])
    
    # Store forecast error:
    err[t,j] = y[t]-fc
  }
}

a)





Figure 15: Number of strikes in the USA (1951–1980) and the first differences, with their ACFs and PACFs.




Figure 15 shows that the number of strikes wanders without a fixed mean. The series decreases until 1961 then increases until about 1974 and then decreases again. The ACF of the strikes decays slowly (0.73 at lag 1, 0.66 at lag 2, 0.56 at lag 3). This is indicative of a non-stationary series. Thus, first differencing is needed (\(d = 1\)). The first differences fluctuate around zero with no apparent trend. Thus, the differenced series appears stationary. The ACF of the differenced series has one negative spike at lag 1 (\(-0.34\), close to the significance bound) and cuts off after lag 1, while the PACF tapers off. This pattern is indicative of an MA(1). Thus, an ARIMA(0,1,1) model seems appropriate.


b)
\[
(1-L)y_t = (1+\theta_1 L)\varepsilon_t.
\]
This expands to \(y_t = y_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t + \theta_1\varepsilon_{t-1}\).

The fitted model is \((1-B)Y_t = (1 - 0.3094B)e_t\), with \(\hat\theta_1 = -0.3094\) (s.e. = 0.1515) and \(\hat\sigma^2 = 330{,}817\). In Figure 16 the residuals fluctuate around zero with no pattern and none of the autocorrelations are significant. The Ljung–Box test fails to reject the null hypothesis (\(p = 0.780\)). Thus, the residuals appear like white noise and the ARIMA(0,1,1) model is satisfactory.


d)
From the model, \(Y_{T+1} = Y_T + e_{T+1} + \theta_1 e_T\). Future errors have expected value zero, and \(e_T\) is estimated by the last residual, so
\[
\hat{Y}_{T+1 \mid T} = Y_T + \hat{\theta}_1 \hat{e}_T, \qquad \hat{Y}_{T+1 \mid T} = \hat{Y}_{T+2 \mid T} = \hat{Y}_{T+3 \mid T},
\]
since for \(h \geq 2\) both \(e_{T+h}\) and \(e_{T+h-1}\) are future errors. The forecasts are therefore flat. The forecast variance is \(\sigma^2[1 + (h-1)(1+\theta_1)^2]\), which grows linearly with \(h\).

In Figure 18 the T-bill rate wanders with no fixed mean and its ACF decays slowly. This suggests that the series is non-stationary. The changes in the T-bill rate fluctuate around zero and its ACF dies out quickly but the size of the changes is not constant. There are periods of large changes and periods of small changes, which is indicative of volatility clustering. The variance of the changes also depends on the level of the rate, since the changes are largest when the T-bill rate is high (around 1980) and smaller when the rate is low. Table 4 displays the results from the ADF and KPSS tests. For the T-bill rate, the ADF test does not reject a unit root (\(p = 0.608\)) and the KPSS test rejects stationarity (\(p < 0.01\)), so the series is non-stationary. For the changes in T-bill rate, the ADF test rejects a unit root (\(p < 0.01\)) and the KPSS test does not reject stationarity (\(p > 0.10\)), so the changes are stationary. Thus, the first differences are modelled.

title: Foundations
text:
Problem 3

a
The “ACF of residuals” panel in Figure 19 plots the autocorrelations of the raw residuals \(\hat a_t = y_t - \hat\mu_t\) from the mean equation. Almost all autocorrelations lie within the significance bounds, with only small spikes at lags 7 and 16. Thus, the AR(1) term captures most of the dependence in the mean.


b
The “ACF of squared residuals” panel plots the autocorrelations of the squared raw residuals, which measure dependence in the variance. There are large significant spikes at lags 1, 4 and 8. Thus, the squared residuals are autocorrelated. This suggests that a constant variance model is not suitable, since there are ARCH effects present in the series.


c
The “ACF of squared std. residuals” panel plots the autocorrelations of \((\hat a_t/\hat\sigma_t)^2\). These should be uncorrelated if the variance equation is sufficient. Almost all autocorrelations lie within the bounds, with only lag 4 on the boundary. Thus, the ARCH(1) term captures most of the volatility clustering present in the series. This agrees with the Ljung–Box tests on \(R^2\) (\(p > 0.27\)). The spike at lag 4 suggests there may be some yearly pattern in the volatility that the ARCH(1) term does not capture.


d
garch.model.Tbill@sigma.t contains the fitted conditional standard deviations \(\hat\sigma_t\) from the variance equation, one for each quarter. Dividing the residuals by \(\hat\sigma_t\) gives the standardised residuals.


e
The “Standardised residuals” panel shows the standardised residuals are more evenly spread than the raw residuals, since the large changes around 1980 have been scaled down. However, the variance is still not constant. The standardised residuals are small in the 1950s and larger after about 1970, which suggests the variance also depends on the level of the T-bill rate and this is not captured by the ARCH(1) model. Thus, a heavier-tailed distribution (the \(t\) distribution) may be more appropriate.

title: Foundations
text:
Setup and toolkit


Code
library(tidyverse)
library(patchwork)

col_obs = "deeppink"   # observed series
col_ref = "purple"     # true/reference line
col_bar = "grey50"     # periodogram ordinates

# Note: element k + 1 of fft(y) is frequency k/n
# Function to calculate raw periodogram at Fourier frequencies j/n:
pgram = function(y, demean = TRUE) {
  n = length(y)
  if (demean) y = y - mean(y)
  I = Mod(fft(y))^2 / n
  j = 1:floor(n / 2)
  tibble(freq = j / n, period = n / j, I = I[j + 1])
}

# Function to calculate theoretical ARMA spectral density (unit innovation variance):
arma_spec = function(f, ar = numeric(0), ma = numeric(0), sigma2 = 1) {
  vapply(f, function(ff) {
    num = if (length(ma))
      Mod(1 + sum(ma * exp(-2i * pi * ff * seq_along(ma))))^2 else 1
    den = if (length(ar))
      Mod(1 - sum(ar * exp(-2i * pi * ff * seq_along(ar))))^2 else 1
    sigma2 * num / den
  }, numeric(1))
}

# g = max ordinate / sum of ordinates
# P(G > g) = sum_{k=1}^{floor(1/g)} (-1)^{k-1} choose(q, k) (1 - k g)^{q-1}
# Function for Fisher's g test (H0: white noise):
fisher_g_test = function(y) {
  y = y - mean(y)
  n = length(y)
  I = Mod(fft(y))^2 / n
  m = floor((n - 1) / 2)          # ordinates exponential under H0
  I = I[2:(m + 1)]
  q = length(I)
  g = max(I) / sum(I)
  K = floor(1 / g)
  k = 1:K
  terms = (-1)^(k - 1) * exp(lchoose(q, k) + (q - 1) * log1p(-k * g))
  p = min(max(sum(terms), 0), 1)
  jmax = which.max(I)
  list(g = g, p.value = p, freq = jmax / n, period = n / jmax)
}

title: Foundations
text:
The question spectral analysis asks
The time domain asks how the past influences the present. The frequency domain asks which oscillations are present in the series and how much of the variance each of them explains. Both describe the same process but some features are much easier to see in the frequency domain.






Q: A monthly series has a strong annual pattern. What period and frequency represent this cycle?



A: The period is \(s = 12\) months, so the frequency is \(\omega = \frac{1}{12} \approx 0.083\) cycles per month.

title: Foundations
section: Period, frequency and the ts() collision
text:
Period, frequency and the ts() collision
A sinusoid with period \(m\) has frequency \(f = \frac{1}{m}\) cycles per observation and angular frequency \(\omega = 2\pi f = 2\pi/m\) radians per observation.






frequency in ts() is a period



In ts(y, frequency = 12) the frequency argument is the number of observations per cycle, which is the period \(m\), not the frequency \(f\). Passing frequency = \frac{1}{12} would tell R that the series is annual.

title: Foundations
text:
The Nyquist frequency and aliasing
You need at least two observations per cycle (one near the peak and one near the trough). Thus, the fastest oscillation a sampled series can show has a period of 2 observations. This is the Nyquist frequency, \(f_N = \frac{1}{2}\) cycle per observation. Faster oscillations do not disappear. They are folded back into \([0, \frac{1}{2}]\) and appear at a lower frequency, which is known as aliasing.





Figure 22: Two sinusoids with periods of 1.5 and 3 observations. Sampled at the integer time points (dots) they give identical values.




A period of 1.5 is a frequency of \(\frac{2}{3}\), which is above the Nyquist frequency. It is folded to \(|\frac{2}{3} - 1| = \frac{1}{3}\), the frequency of the period-3 wave, which is why the two waves agree at every sampled point in Figure 22.






Q: A process oscillates at a true frequency of \(\frac{2}{3}\) cycles per observation. Can a series sampled once per observation resolve it, and can any later analysis recover it?



A: No. The true frequency is above the Nyquist frequency \(f_N = \frac{1}{2}\), so there are fewer than two observations per cycle. At the observed times, the true oscillation gives exactly the same values as a slower oscillation at the alias frequency \(|f - k|\). Since the sampled values are identical, no later analysis can recover the true frequency. The periodogram will show a peak at the alias instead. The only fix is to sample more often.

title: Foundations
section: A series as a sum of waves
text:
A series as a sum of waves
A sinusoid with amplitude \(A\), frequency \(f\) and phase \(\varphi\) can be written as
\[
A\cos(2\pi f t + \varphi) = a\cos(2\pi f t) + b\sin(2\pi f t), \qquad A = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}.
\]
The right-hand side is linear in \(a\) and \(b\), so for a known frequency it is just a regression with two columns. At the Fourier frequencies \(f_j = \frac{j}{n}\) the sine and cosine columns are orthogonal. Thus, the total sum of squares splits exactly across the frequencies, and the periodogram is an analysis of variance by frequency. The regression is fitted below at the frequency of a known cycle and compared with the periodogram ordinate.

title: Foundations
text:
The periodogram
The periodogram \(I(f)\) measures how much of the variation in a series comes from an oscillation at frequency \(f\). Its population version is the spectral density \(S(f)\), which spreads the variance of a stationary process over the frequencies. For example, a tall ordinate at \(f = \frac{1}{12}\) in monthly data means that a 12-month cycle explains a large share of the variance.
In R, spec.pgram() is used to estimate the periodogram. By default it removes a linear trend, tapers the ends of the series, pads the series and rescales by frequency(x). Thus, its values only match pgram() when these options are switched off.






Q: Monthly data show a large ordinate at \(f = 0.0833\). What do you report?



A: The period, with units: \(\frac{1}{0.0833} \approx 12\), which is an annual cycle.

A: The largest ordinate is at \(f = 10/240 = 0.0417\), a period of 24 observations. This is exactly how the series was built. Since \(240/24 = 10\), the cycle lies exactly on a Fourier frequency, so all its power is in one ordinate. The other ordinates are tiny in comparison (Figure 24). The time plot showed an oscillation, but the periodogram tells us its length immediately.

title: Foundations
text:
Reading a periodogram: five steps

Step 1: convert the peak to a period
Find the largest ordinate, invert its frequency and attach the units of the data.


Step 2: check for harmonics
A seasonal pattern that is not a pure sinusoid needs harmonics at \(2/m, 3/m, \dots\) to build its shape. The sharper the pattern, the more harmonics it needs.






Q: A monthly series has large peaks at 1/12, 2/12 and 3/12. Are these three cycles of 12, 6 and 4 months?



A: No, they are the fundamental (12 months) and the harmonics of one annual pattern that is not shaped like a sine wave. I would report a single twelve-month cycle and note that the 6- and 4-month peaks are its harmonics.




Step 3: do not trust a single tall ordinate
The raw periodogram is unbiased but not consistent. This means that each ordinate estimates \(S(f)\) correctly on average but its standard deviation is roughly as large as its mean and does not shrink as \(n\) grows.






Q: A raw periodogram has one very tall peak. Does that prove a real cycle?



A: No. There are many ordinates and each one is very noisy, so some will always look large by chance. To separate real cycles from noise you need to smooth the spectrum and test the largest peak.




Step 4: smooth, and keep what survives
Neighbouring ordinates estimate almost the same value of a smooth spectrum. Thus, averaging them reduces the noise. In spec.pgram() the spans argument sets how many neighbours are averaged.





Figure 25: Periodogram of one simulated AR(2) series with no smoothing and with three increasing spans, against the true spectral density (purple), on a log scale.










Q: What goes wrong if the smoothing span is (1) too small, or (2) too large?



A: If the span is too small the spectrum will remain noisy but if it is too large true peaks are averaged out.




Step 5: test the largest peak
Fisher’s test compares the largest ordinate with the sum of all of them, \(g = \max_j I(f_j)/\sum_j I(f_j)\) and its null distribution accounts for having picked the maximum.


Code

fisher_g_test(rnorm(240))

Q: What is the null hypothesis, and what does rejecting it mean?



A: Null hypothesis is that the series is white noise. Rejecting the null hypothesis is because there is insignificant evidence that the series is white noise.

Preparing a series
The three routine steps are all spec.pgram() defaults. Remove the mean (and usually the trend), taper the ends and cosmetically pad the series.

text:
Spectral signatures of familiar models





Figure 26: Theoretical spectral densities (unit innovation variance) of five processes.

Process

AR(1), \(\phi < 0\)
Power concentrated at high frequencies (“blue”)

A peak at an interior frequency

A cycle that is not seasonal
The AR(2) \(y_t = 1.5y_{t-1} - 0.75y_{t-2} + \varepsilon_t\) has complex roots and a spectral peak at about \(f \approx 0.08\), a period of about 12.4 observations:


Code

peak_frequency    peak_period 
          0.08          12.50 








Q: Would a periodogram peak near twelve months prove deterministic annual seasonality?



A: No. An AR(2) with complex roots can also give a peak near 12 months, but its cycles vary in length and are not tied to the calendar. The difference is the width of the peak. A stochastic cycle gives a broad peak, whereas deterministic seasonality gives a narrow spike at \(1/m\) and its harmonics.

title: Foundations
section: What differencing does to a spectrum
text:
What differencing does to a spectrum
Filtering a series multiplies its spectrum by a fixed curve. For the first difference \((1-L)\) the curve is \(|1 - e^{-2\pi i f}|^2 = 4\sin^2(\pi f)\), and for the seasonal difference \((1 - L^{12})\) it is \(4\sin^2(12\pi f)\).





Figure 27: Multipliers applied to the spectrum by the first difference (left) and the seasonal difference at lag 12 (right).




The first difference multiplies the power at \(f = 0\) by zero (it removes the level and strongly damps a trend) but it multiplies the power at \(f = 1/2\) by four. The seasonal difference has zeros at \(f = 0, 1/12, 2/12, \dots, 6/12\), so it removes the level and every seasonal harmonic (Figure 27).






Q: Why is unnecessary differencing harmful rather than merely unhelpful?



A: Differencing removes low-frequency variation and amplifies high-frequency variation. If there is no trend, it removes a component that was not there and amplifies the fastest, least informative variation. Differencing white noise doubles the variance and creates a lag 1 autocorrelation of \(-0.5\), which is not invertible.

section: The frequency domain versus the ACF
text:
The frequency domain versus the ACF




Table 10: How each domain handles common tasks, and which is better suited.








Task

Narrow peak = regular cycle; broad peak = irregular cycle

Each cycle appears as its own peak

The time and frequency domains contain the same information, since the spectral density is the Fourier transform of the autocovariance function. However, Table 10 shows that each domain makes different questions easy to answer. The frequency domain describes the series but does not forecast it, which is why ARIMA models are used for forecasting.






Q: A series appears to contain cycles of roughly 7, 30 and 365 observations. Which representation makes these simultaneous periodicities easier to see?



A: The frequency domain. The three cycles appear as three separate peaks at \(1/7\), \(1/30\) and \(1/365\). The overlapping patterns in an ACF would be difficult to distinguish.

In Figure 30 the peak near \(1/30\) is still there after heavier smoothing. It becomes wider and slightly lower, but it is still well above the rest of the spectrum, which is roughly flat. This is why two spans are compared: a real cycle remains when the smoothing is increased, whereas a peak caused by noise tends to disappear.


Task 3: formal test.


Code

$g
[1] 0.6690766

$p.value
[1] 5.812113e-84

$freq
[1] 0.03333333

Fisher’s test rejects white noise (\(g = 0.669\), \(p < 0.001\)), and the largest ordinate is at a period of 30. Thus, the largest ordinate is too large to be a chance maximum under white noise. The smoothed spectrum adds information about where the cycle is and how broad it is.


Final interpretation.
The spectrum has one dominant peak at a frequency of about 0.033 cycles per observation, which is a cycle of about 30 observations. The peak remains after smoothing, so it is not just a single noisy ordinate, and Fisher’s test gives strong evidence against white noise (\(p < 0.001\)). The rest of the spectrum is roughly flat, so the noise around the cycle looks like white noise. Thus, the series does not need to be prewhitened before testing.

title: Exponential Smoothing
text:
All data in this section are public data sets that come with R packages (marathon, oil, books and uschange from fpp2, and Nile and co2 from base R) or are simulated. None of them contain personal information, so no consent, anonymisation or POPIA steps were needed.


Exponential smoothing forecasts are weighted averages of past observations, with weights that decrease exponentially the further back we go. Each method in Table 1 adds a component, and each component has its own smoothing parameter.


Table 1: Exponential smoothing methods. \(m\) is the seasonal period and \(k = \lfloor (h-1)/m \rfloor\).








Method
Components
Forecast \(\hat{y}_{T+h \mid T}\)
Use when




Simple (SES)
level \(\ell_t\) (\(\alpha\))
\(\ell_T\)
no trend, no seasonality


Holt’s linear
level, trend \(b_t\) (\(\alpha, \beta\))
\(\ell_T + hb_T\)
a linear trend


Damped trend
level, damped trend (\(\alpha, \beta, \phi\))
\(\ell_T + (\phi + \dots + \phi^h)b_T\)
a trend that is expected to flatten out


Holt-Winters additive
level, trend, season \(s_t\) (\(\alpha, \beta, \gamma\))
\(\ell_T + hb_T + s_{T+h-m(k+1)}\)
seasonal swings of constant size


Holt-Winters multiplicative
level, trend, season (\(\alpha, \beta, \gamma\))
\((\ell_T + hb_T)s_{T+h-m(k+1)}\)
seasonal swings proportional to the level




Written in error-correction form, each method becomes a state-space model with a single source of error (the ETS models). This gives a likelihood (so parameters can be estimated by maximum likelihood and models compared by AICc) and prediction intervals. ets() chooses between the error, trend and seasonal types automatically. In Project 1 I implemented additive Holt-Winters with a damped trend from first principles on Eskom electricity demand.



Simple exponential smoothing (SES) forecasts the next observation with a weighted average of past observations, where the weights decrease exponentially:
\[
\hat{y}_{t+1 \mid t} = \alpha y_t + \alpha(1-\alpha) y_{t-1} + \alpha(1-\alpha)^2 y_{t-2} + \cdots, \quad 0 < \alpha < 1.
\]
The same forecast can be written as two updating equations:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Forecast:} \quad \hat{y}_{t+h \mid t} &= \ell_t \\
\text{Smoothing:} \quad \ell_t &= \alpha y_t + (1-\alpha)\ell_{t-1}
\end{aligned}
\]






Note



The level \(\ell_t\) is a local mean. Forecasts from SES are flat: there is no new information after time \(T\), so every forecast is \(\ell_T\).


To start the recursion we need \(\ell_0\), and in most cases we also need to estimate \(\alpha\). Both are found by minimising the sum of squared one-step-ahead errors:
\[
\text{SSE} = \sum_{t=1}^{T}(y_t - \hat{y}_{t \mid t-1})^2.
\]




The marathon data are the winning times (in minutes) of the Boston marathon from 1897 to 2016.


Code
# Read in data:
data(marathon)
# View(marathon)

cat("Start:", start(marathon), " End:", end(marathon), " Frequency:", frequency(marathon), "\n")


Start: 1897 1  End: 2016 1  Frequency: 1 






Code
y = marathon

# Function to implement simple exponential smoothing:
# y:      time series 
# alpha:  smoothing parameter 
# level0: initial level 
ses_fxn = function(y, alpha, level0) {
  n = length(y) 
  y_hat = numeric(n) # store estimates
  level = numeric(n) # store levels
  l = level0
  
  for (t in 1:n) {
    y_hat[t] = l 
    l        = alpha*y[t] + (1-alpha)*l
    level[t] = l
  }
  
  res = y - y_hat
  sse = sum(res^2)
  list(
    yhat      = y_hat,
    level     = level,
    residuals = res,
    sse       = sse,
    forecast  = l
  )
}

# Function to return the one-step-ahead forecast: 
ses_forecast_fxn = function(y, alpha, level0) {
  ses_fxn(y ,alpha, level0)$forecast
}

# Function to optimise:
my_sse = function(par, y) {
  ses_fxn(y, alpha = par[1], level0 = par[2])$sse
}

# Optimise:
opt = optim(par = c(0.5,y[1]), 
            fn = my_sse, 
            y = y, 
            method = 'L-BFGS-B',
            lower = c(0.0001,-Inf), 
            upper = c(0.9999, Inf))

alpha_hat = opt$par[1]
l0_hat    = opt$par[2]

my_fit = ses_fxn(y,alpha=alpha_hat,level0=l0_hat)
# my_fit$forecast

# Compare with ses():
fit = ses(y,h=1)
# fit$model$par
# fit$mean

rbind(
  mine = c(alpha = alpha_hat, l0 = l0_hat,
           sse = opt$value, forecast = my_fit$forecast),
  ses  = c(fit$model$par["alpha"], fit$model$par["l"],
           sum(residuals(fit)^2), fit$mean[1])
)


         alpha       l0      sse forecast
mine 0.3456464 167.1724 3594.147 130.3560
ses  0.3457325 167.1741 3594.147 130.3563

check = ses_fxn(y, alpha  = fit$model$par["alpha"],
                   level0 = fit$model$par["l"])
round(unname(check$forecast) - fit$mean[1], 10)


[1] 0


Using the ses() parameter estimates in my own function yields the same forecast. My estimates are very close to the ses() estimates (\(\hat{\alpha} = 0.3456\) vs 0.3457). The small difference is due to how each optimisation works. ses() maximises a likelihood rather than minimising the SSE directly.

z      = qnorm(0.975)
s      = sqrt(check$sse/(n-2))

  mine = c(forecast = unname(check$forecast),
           lower = unname(check$forecast) - z*s,

mine 130.3563 119.5394 141.1733

Both give the same point forecast and 95% interval: \(\hat{y}_{T+1|T} \pm 1.96\,\hat{\sigma}\), with \(\hat{\sigma} = \sqrt{SSE/(n-2)}\).








Figure 1: Boston marathon winning times (grey) with the SES fitted values (one-step-ahead forecasts, pink).




Figure 1 shows that the fitted values follow the observations but lag one step behind them. SES has no trend term, so during the long downward trend (until about 1980) the fitted values almost always predicted a longer winning time than what is actually observed.





Code

    mine      ses 
5.518956 5.518956 


A typical one-step-ahead forecast is off by about \(\hat{\sigma} \approx 5.52\) minutes. ses() divides the SSE by \(T-2\) to correct for the two estimated parameters.






Code

# View(oil)

# Fit SES and forecast four years ahead:
oil_fit = ses(oil, h = 4)
oil_fit$model$par


   alpha        l 
  0.9999 110.8832 







Figure 2: Annual oil production in Saudi Arabia with SES fitted values and four-year forecasts (80% and 95% prediction intervals).




An \(\hat{\alpha} \approx 1\) value means the forecast relies mostly on the last observation. The four forecasts are all equal to 542.3. In Figure 2 the prediction intervals widen with the horizon.




Code
# Standard deviation of the residuals:
sd_oil = sd(residuals(oil_fit))

# Manual 95% prediction interval for first forecast:
PI_oil_upper = oil_fit$mean[1] + 1.96*sd_oil
PI_oil_lower = oil_fit$mean[1] - 1.96*sd_oil

# 95% prediction interval by R:
PI_oil_R = c(oil_fit$lower[1, "95%"], oil_fit$upper[1, "95%"])

kable(data.frame(
  Method = c("$\\hat{y} \\pm 1.96\\,s$", "ses()"),
  Lower  = c(PI_oil_lower, PI_oil_R[1]),
  Upper  = c(PI_oil_upper, PI_oil_R[2]),
  SD = c(paste0("$s$ = ", round(sd_oil, 2)),
         paste0("$\\hat{\\sigma}$ = ", round(sqrt(oil_fit$model$sigma2), 2)))
), digits = 2, row.names = FALSE,

\(s\) = 47.71

The two intervals are similar but not identical. This is because they use different estimates of the standard deviation. sd() divides by \(T-1\) (1 degree of freedom for the estimated mean) and subtracts the mean of the residuals. R uses \(\hat{\sigma}^2 = \sum e_t^2/(T-2)\), which does not subtract the mean and divides by \(T-2\) (2 degrees of freedom for the estimated \(\alpha\) and \(\ell_0\)).
For \(h > 1\) we cannot just use \(s\), since the forecast variance grows with the horizon. For SES (the ETS(A,N,N) model) the \(h\)-step forecast variance is \(\sigma^2[1 + \alpha^2(h-1)]\).


Code
h = 1:4
alpha_oil = oil_fit$model$par["alpha"]

# Forecast variance for h = 1, ..., 4:
var_h = oil_fit$model$sigma2 * (1 + alpha_oil^2 * (h - 1))
upper_manual = oil_fit$mean + qnorm(0.975) * sqrt(var_h)

kable(data.frame(h = h,
                 Upper_manual = as.numeric(upper_manual),

In error-correction form, SES and Holt’s method are state-space models with a single source of error:
\[
\begin{aligned}
y_t &= \ell_{t-1} + b_{t-1} + e_t, \qquad e_t \sim N(0, \sigma^2) \\
\ell_t &= \ell_{t-1} + b_{t-1} + \alpha e_t \\
b_t &= b_{t-1} + \alpha\beta^* e_t
\end{aligned}
\]
For SES, \(b_t = 0\) and \(\beta^* = 0\).


Code
# Function to simulate from SES or Holt's method:
# n:   no. observations 
# par: parameters 
sim_fxn = function(n, par) {
  l     = par$l0
  b     = par$b0
  y     = numeric(n)
  level = numeric(n)
  
  for (t in 1:n) {
    e        = rnorm(1, 0, par$sigma)
    y[t]     = l + b + e                        # observation equation
    l        = l + b + par$alpha * e            # level
    b        = b + par$alpha * par$beta * e     # trend
    level[t] = l
  }
  list(y = ts(y), level = level)
}

Question: How do different prediction intervals differ and what are their sources of uncertainty?
I used the simulated SES series from Question 5, fitting each method to the first 80 observations and forecasting 10 steps ahead.


Under the ETS(A,N,N) model, \(y_t = \ell_{t-1} + e_t\) with \(e_t \sim N(0, \sigma^2)\) independent. Given \(\alpha\), \(\ell_0\) and \(y_{1:t-1}\), the level \(\ell_{t-1}\) is known, so \(y_t \mid y_{1:t-1} \sim N(\ell_{t-1}, \sigma^2)\). Writing the joint density as a product of these conditional densities gives the likelihood
\[
L(\alpha, \ell_0, \sigma; \boldsymbol{y}) = \prod_{t=1}^{T} \frac{1}{\sigma}\,\phi\!\left(\frac{e_t}{\sigma}\right), \qquad e_t = y_t - \ell_{t-1},
\]
where \(\phi\) is the standard normal density and \(e_t\) depends on \((\alpha, \ell_0)\) through the SES recursion. The priors are \(\alpha \sim \text{Uniform}(0, 1)\) and flat priors on \(\ell_0\) and \(\log\sigma\).
A random walk Metropolis-Hastings algorithm is used to sample from the posterior. The random walk steps are drawn from a multivariate normal distribution, which has support over the entire real line, whereas \(\alpha \in (0, 1)\) and \(\sigma > 0\). Therefore, the parameters are mapped to the real line using
\[
\phi_1 = \text{logit}(\alpha), \qquad \phi_2 = \ell_0, \qquad \phi_3 = \log\sigma,
\]
and the random walk is performed over \(\boldsymbol{\phi} = (\phi_1, \phi_2, \phi_3)\), with proposals \(\boldsymbol{\phi}^* = \boldsymbol{\phi} + \boldsymbol{e}\). Since we sample \(\boldsymbol{\phi}\) rather than \(\boldsymbol{\theta} = (\alpha, \ell_0, \sigma)\), the Jacobian of the transformation must be included in the log posterior. The flat prior on \(\log\sigma\) is already defined on the transformed scale, so only \(\alpha\) needs a Jacobian:
\[
\log p(\boldsymbol{\phi}) = \log L(\alpha, \ell_0, \sigma; \boldsymbol{y}) + \log\{\alpha(1-\alpha)\} + \text{const}.
\]
Since the proposal is symmetric, \(\boldsymbol{\phi}^*\) is accepted with probability \(\min\{1, \exp[\log p(\boldsymbol{\phi}^*) - \log p(\boldsymbol{\phi})]\}\). The steps are initially drawn from \(\boldsymbol{e} \sim N(\boldsymbol{0}, 0.5^2\,\mathbf{I}_3)\). The first 3 000 iterations are a burn-in, and the covariance matrix \(\Sigma\) of the transformed parameters is estimated from the last 1 500 of these. The retained draws then use \(\boldsymbol{e} \sim N\left(\boldsymbol{0}, \frac{2.38^2}{3}\Sigma\right)\) (Roberts et al., 1997). The chain starts at the ses() estimates.
Each retained draw \((\alpha^{(j)}, \ell_0^{(j)}, \sigma^{(j)})\) is then used to compute \(\ell_T^{(j)}\) and simulate one future path from the state-space model. This gives draws from the posterior predictive distribution of \(y_{T+1}, \ldots, y_{T+h}\).


Code
# 1. SES log-likelihood: 
SES_Log_Likelihood = function(y, alpha, l0, sigma) {
  e   = ses_fxn(y, alpha, l0)$residuals
  out = sum(dnorm(e, 0, sigma, log = TRUE))
  if (!is.finite(out)) -Inf else out
}

# 2. Parameter transforms: 
to_real = function(theta) {
  c(qlogis(theta[1]), theta[2], log(theta[3]))
}

from_real = function(phi) {
  c(plogis(phi[1]), phi[2], exp(phi[3]))
}

# 3. Log posterior on the transformed scale (priors + Jacobian):
log_target = function(phi, y) {
  theta = from_real(phi)
  ll    = SES_Log_Likelihood(y, theta[1], theta[2], theta[3])
  if (!is.finite(ll)) return(-Inf)

  # Note: flat priors on l0 and log(sigma) only add a constant
  # Uniform(0, 1) prior on alpha x logit Jacobian:
  lp_alpha = plogis(phi[1], log.p = TRUE) + plogis(-phi[1], log.p = TRUE)

  ll + lp_alpha
}

# 4. Metropolis-Hastings loop:
mh_run = function(phi, jitters, y) {
  n         = nrow(jitters)
  cur       = log_target(phi, y)
  phi_draws = matrix(NA, n, 3)
  accepted  = logical(n)

  for (i in seq_len(n)) {
    prop      = phi + jitters[i, ]
    prop_val  = log_target(prop, y)
    log_alpha = if (is.finite(prop_val)) min(0, prop_val - cur) else -Inf

    if (log(runif(1)) < log_alpha) {
      phi         = prop
      cur         = prop_val
      accepted[i] = TRUE
    }
    phi_draws[i, ] = phi
  }
  list(phi_draws = phi_draws, last = phi, accept_rate = mean(accepted))
}

# 5. Two-phase sampler: 
# Phase 1: burn-in with isotropic jitter, Sigma = covariance of later burn-in draws
# Phase 2: retained iterations with proposals ~ N(0, scale * Sigma)
MH_SES = function(y, init, iterations = 20000, burn = 3000, burn_sd = 0.5,
                  cov_frac = 0.5, scale = 2.38^2/3) {
  phi0 = to_real(init)

  # Phase 1:
  burn_jit = rmvnorm(burn, mean = rep(0, 3), sigma = burn_sd^2 * diag(3))
  b        = mh_run(phi0, burn_jit, y)
  keep     = seq.int(floor(burn * (1 - cov_frac)) + 1, burn)
  Sigma    = cov(b$phi_draws[keep, , drop = FALSE])

  # Phase 2:
  main_jit = rmvnorm(iterations, mean = rep(0, 3), sigma = scale * Sigma)
  m        = mh_run(b$last, main_jit, y)

  draws = t(apply(m$phi_draws, 1, from_real))
  colnames(draws) = c("alpha", "l0", "sigma")
  
  list(
    draws = draws, 
    burn_accept = b$accept_rate, 
    accept_rate = m$accept_rate)
}


As a check on my sample, I also fitted the same model in Stan (Carpenter et al., 2017) to sample from the posterior. Stan uses the No-U-Turn Sampler (NUTS), an adaptive form of Hamiltonian Monte Carlo that uses the gradient of the log posterior to propose new points. The parameters block restricts \(\alpha\) to \((0, 1)\) and \(\sigma\) to \((0, \infty)\), and Stan maps them to the real line and includes the Jacobian automatically. The model block runs the SES recursion, with \(y_t \sim N(\ell_{t-1}, \sigma^2)\) at each step. The generated quantities block computes \(\ell_T\) for each posterior draw and simulates one future path from the state-space model, which gives draws from the posterior predictive distribution of \(y_{T+1}, \ldots, y_{T+h}\).


Code
# SES model written in Stan:
modelString = "
  data {
    int<lower=1> N;                   // number of observations
    vector[N] y;                      // time series
    int<lower=1> N_new;               // forecast horizon
  }

  parameters {
    real<lower=0, upper=1> alpha;     // smoothing parameter
    real l0;                          // initial level
    real<lower=0> sigma;              // error standard deviation
  }

  model {
    real level = l0;

    // Priors (flat priors on l0 and sigma):
    alpha ~ uniform(0, 1);
    target += -log(sigma);            // flat prior on log(sigma)

    // Likelihood: one-step-ahead errors are iid N(0, sigma^2)
    for (t in 1:N) {
      y[t] ~ normal(level, sigma);
      level = level + alpha * (y[t] - level);
    }
  }

  generated quantities {
    real level_T;
    vector[N_new] y_new;

    // Final level for this draw:
    {
      real level = l0;
      for (t in 1:N) level = level + alpha * (y[t] - level);
      level_T = level;
    }

    // One future path from the state-space model:
    {
      real lev = level_T;
      for (h in 1:N_new) {
        real e = normal_rng(0, sigma);
        y_new[h] = lev + e;
        lev = lev + alpha * e;
      }
    }
  }
"

My Metropolis-Hastings sampler and Stan give almost identical posterior means and 95% credible intervals for all three parameters, which confirms that my sampler is correct. All three true values lie inside the credible intervals. The posterior for \(\alpha\) is wide (roughly 0.34 to 0.65), so even with 80 observations there is considerable uncertainty about the smoothing parameter. This is the uncertainty that the plug-in intervals ignore. The initial level \(\ell_0\) has the widest interval relative to its value, because only the first few observations carry information about it (as in Question 5).
Error variance estimates. Each method estimates \(\sigma^2\) slightly differently:


Code

  Estimate = c("$\\text{SSE}/(n-2)$ (`ses()`, normal intervals)",
               "$\\text{SSE}/n$ (implied by bootstrapping the residuals)",
               "$\\widehat{\\text{Var}}(e_t)$ (`var()`: divides by $n-1$, centres at $\\bar{e}$)",

               "$E(\\sigma^2 \\mid \\boldsymbol{y})$ (Stan)",
               "True $\\sigma^2$"),

             mean(sigma_d^2), mean(post_stan$sigma^2), p_ses$sigma^2)
), digits = 4, row.names = FALSE, escape = FALSE,
col.names = c("Estimate", "$\\hat{\\sigma}^2$"))

What I found:

The normal interval by hand reproduces ses() exactly, so ses() uses \(\hat{\sigma}^2 = \text{SSE}/(n-2)\) and \(\text{Var}(y_{T+h}) = \sigma^2[1+\alpha^2(h-1)]\).
The two bootstrap intervals differ at \(h = 1\) (widths 1.67 and 2.17) but are close to the normal interval at \(h = 10\). At \(h = 1\) a bootstrap interval is just the 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles of the 80 residuals, so it depends on the few most extreme residuals and is very noisy. At longer horizons several resampled errors are added together, so this effect averages out. Bootstrapping only assumes independent errors, so it is safer when residuals are skewed or heavy-tailed, but it needs more data than the normal approach.
Both Bayesian intervals are wider than the normal interval at every horizon, and the difference grows with \(h\) (from about 0.03 at \(h=1\) to about 0.17 at \(h=10\)), because every future path uses a different draw of \((\alpha, \ell_0, \sigma)\). They are the only methods that include parameter uncertainty. My Metropolis-Hastings sampler and Stan give almost identical widths, which confirms that my sampler is correct.
Compared with the interval using the true parameters, the ses() interval is too narrow at \(h=1\) but too wide at \(h=10\). In this realisation \(\hat{\sigma}\) is slightly too small and \(\hat{\alpha}\) slightly too large, which shows that the plug-in interval depends on how good the parameter estimates happen to be.
None of the approaches includes uncertainty about the choice of model or whether the process will keep behaving the same way. This is why prediction intervals in practice are usually too narrow.




A credible interval describes uncertainty about an unknown quantity, here the current level \(\ell_T\). A prediction interval describes uncertainty about a future observation \(y_{T+h}\), so it also includes the future error \(e_{T+h}\).

The interval for the level is much narrower than the prediction interval, because most of the uncertainty about a single future observation comes from the noise \(e_{T+1}\), not from estimating the level.



A 95% prediction interval should contain the future value 95% of the time. I simulated 300 series (\(n = 30\)), fitted ses() and checked how often the 95% interval contained the true \(y_{T+1}\) and \(y_{T+10}\).


Code
set.seed(4)
cover = t(replicate(300, {
  sim    = sim_fxn(n = 40, par = p_ses)$y
  tr     = window(sim, end = 30)
  fc     = ses(tr, h = 10, level = 95)
  future = as.numeric(window(sim, start = 31))
  c(h1   = future[1] >= fc$lower[1] & future[1] <= fc$upper[1],
    h10  = future[10] >= fc$lower[10] & future[10] <= fc$upper[10])
}))
colMeans(cover)


  h1  h10 
0.96 0.95 


The coverage is 96% at \(h=1\) and 95% at \(h=10\). With 300 replicates the Monte Carlo standard error is about 1.3%, so both are consistent with the nominal 95%. Even though the plug-in intervals ignore the uncertainty in \(\hat{\alpha}\) and \(\hat{\sigma}\), this has little effect on coverage here. One reason is that dividing the SSE by \(n-2\) rather than \(n\) already widens the intervals slightly. Another is that the errors really are normal and the model is correct, which is the best case for these intervals. With real data, where the model is only an approximation, the coverage would usually be lower.

title: Exponential Smoothing
text:
All data in this section are public data sets that come with R packages (marathon, oil, books and uschange from fpp2, and Nile and co2 from base R) or are simulated. None of them contain personal information, so no consent, anonymisation or POPIA steps were needed.


Exponential smoothing forecasts are weighted averages of past observations, with weights that decrease exponentially the further back we go. Each method in Table 1 adds a component, and each component has its own smoothing parameter.


Table 1: Exponential smoothing methods. \(m\) is the seasonal period and \(k = \lfloor (h-1)/m \rfloor\).








Method
Components
Forecast \(\hat{y}_{T+h \mid T}\)
Use when




Simple (SES)
level \(\ell_t\) (\(\alpha\))
\(\ell_T\)
no trend, no seasonality


Holt’s linear
level, trend \(b_t\) (\(\alpha, \beta\))
\(\ell_T + hb_T\)
a linear trend


Damped trend
level, damped trend (\(\alpha, \beta, \phi\))
\(\ell_T + (\phi + \dots + \phi^h)b_T\)
a trend that is expected to flatten out


Holt-Winters additive
level, trend, season \(s_t\) (\(\alpha, \beta, \gamma\))
\(\ell_T + hb_T + s_{T+h-m(k+1)}\)
seasonal swings of constant size


Holt-Winters multiplicative
level, trend, season (\(\alpha, \beta, \gamma\))
\((\ell_T + hb_T)s_{T+h-m(k+1)}\)
seasonal swings proportional to the level




Written in error-correction form, each method becomes a state-space model with a single source of error (the ETS models). This gives a likelihood (so parameters can be estimated by maximum likelihood and models compared by AICc) and prediction intervals. ets() chooses between the error, trend and seasonal types automatically. In Project 1 I implemented additive Holt-Winters with a damped trend from first principles on Eskom electricity demand.



Simple exponential smoothing (SES) forecasts the next observation with a weighted average of past observations, where the weights decrease exponentially:
\[
\hat{y}_{t+1 \mid t} = \alpha y_t + \alpha(1-\alpha) y_{t-1} + \alpha(1-\alpha)^2 y_{t-2} + \cdots, \quad 0 < \alpha < 1.
\]
The same forecast can be written as two updating equations:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Forecast:} \quad \hat{y}_{t+h \mid t} &= \ell_t \\
\text{Smoothing:} \quad \ell_t &= \alpha y_t + (1-\alpha)\ell_{t-1}
\end{aligned}
\]






Note



The level \(\ell_t\) is a local mean. Forecasts from SES are flat: there is no new information after time \(T\), so every forecast is \(\ell_T\).


To start the recursion we need \(\ell_0\), and in most cases we also need to estimate \(\alpha\). Both are found by minimising the sum of squared one-step-ahead errors:
\[
\text{SSE} = \sum_{t=1}^{T}(y_t - \hat{y}_{t \mid t-1})^2.
\]

title: Exponential Smoothing
text:
The marathon data are the winning times (in minutes) of the Boston marathon from 1897 to 2016.


Code
# Read in data:
data(marathon)
# View(marathon)

cat("Start:", start(marathon), " End:", end(marathon), " Frequency:", frequency(marathon), "\n")


Start: 1897 1  End: 2016 1  Frequency: 1 






Code
y = marathon

# Function to implement simple exponential smoothing:
# y:      time series 
# alpha:  smoothing parameter 
# level0: initial level 
ses_fxn = function(y, alpha, level0) {
  n = length(y) 
  y_hat = numeric(n) # store estimates
  level = numeric(n) # store levels
  l = level0
  
  for (t in 1:n) {
    y_hat[t] = l 
    l        = alpha*y[t] + (1-alpha)*l
    level[t] = l
  }
  
  res = y - y_hat
  sse = sum(res^2)
  list(
    yhat      = y_hat,
    level     = level,
    residuals = res,
    sse       = sse,
    forecast  = l
  )
}

# Function to return the one-step-ahead forecast: 
ses_forecast_fxn = function(y, alpha, level0) {
  ses_fxn(y ,alpha, level0)$forecast
}

# Function to optimise:
my_sse = function(par, y) {
  ses_fxn(y, alpha = par[1], level0 = par[2])$sse
}

# Optimise:
opt = optim(par = c(0.5,y[1]), 
            fn = my_sse, 
            y = y, 
            method = 'L-BFGS-B',
            lower = c(0.0001,-Inf), 
            upper = c(0.9999, Inf))

alpha_hat = opt$par[1]
l0_hat    = opt$par[2]

my_fit = ses_fxn(y,alpha=alpha_hat,level0=l0_hat)
# my_fit$forecast

# Compare with ses():
fit = ses(y,h=1)
# fit$model$par
# fit$mean

rbind(
  mine = c(alpha = alpha_hat, l0 = l0_hat,
           sse = opt$value, forecast = my_fit$forecast),
  ses  = c(fit$model$par["alpha"], fit$model$par["l"],
           sum(residuals(fit)^2), fit$mean[1])
)

mine 0.3456464 167.1724 3594.147 130.3560
ses  0.3457325 167.1741 3594.147 130.3563

check = ses_fxn(y, alpha  = fit$model$par["alpha"],
                   level0 = fit$model$par["l"])
round(unname(check$forecast) - fit$mean[1], 10)


[1] 0


Using the ses() parameter estimates in my own function yields the same forecast. My estimates are very close to the ses() estimates (\(\hat{\alpha} = 0.3456\) vs 0.3457). The small difference is due to how each optimisation works. ses() maximises a likelihood rather than minimising the SSE directly.

Figure 1: Boston marathon winning times (grey) with the SES fitted values (one-step-ahead forecasts, pink).




Figure 1 shows that the fitted values follow the observations but lag one step behind them. SES has no trend term, so during the long downward trend (until about 1980) the fitted values almost always predicted a longer winning time than what is actually observed.

The two intervals are similar but not identical. This is because they use different estimates of the standard deviation. sd() divides by \(T-1\) (1 degree of freedom for the estimated mean) and subtracts the mean of the residuals. R uses \(\hat{\sigma}^2 = \sum e_t^2/(T-2)\), which does not subtract the mean and divides by \(T-2\) (2 degrees of freedom for the estimated \(\alpha\) and \(\ell_0\)).
For \(h > 1\) we cannot just use \(s\), since the forecast variance grows with the horizon. For SES (the ETS(A,N,N) model) the \(h\)-step forecast variance is \(\sigma^2[1 + \alpha^2(h-1)]\).

var_h = oil_fit$model$sigma2 * (1 + alpha_oil^2 * (h - 1))

In the state-space form, \(\ell_t = \ell_{t-1} + \alpha e_t\), so each future innovation enters the level with weight \(\alpha\) and persists in all later levels. Writing \(y_{T+h} = \ell_T + \alpha \sum_{j=1}^{h-1} e_{T+j} + e_{T+h}\), with independent errors \(e_t \sim N(0, \sigma^2)\), gives \(\text{Var}(y_{T+h} \mid y_{1:T}) = \sigma^2[1 + \alpha^2(h-1)]\), which increases linearly in \(h\).

Figure 3: Daily sales of paperback and hardcover books over 30 days.




Figure 3 shows that both series are very noisy from day to day and both have an upwards trend over the month. There is no clear seasonal pattern and 30 days of data is insufficient to estimate one reliably. The upwards trend suggests that a flat forecast (SES) will be inadequate.

ses_hc = ses(books[, "Hardcover"], h = 4)

# Holt's linear method:
holt_pb = holt(books[, "Paperback"], h = 4)
holt_hc = holt(books[, "Hardcover"], h = 4)

  accuracy(fc)["Training set", "RMSE"]

  Series = c("Paperback", "Hardcover"),
  SES = c(rmse(ses_pb), rmse(ses_hc)),

\[
\begin{aligned}
\hat{y}_{t+h \mid t} &= \ell_t + h b_t \\
\ell_t &= \alpha y_t + (1-\alpha)(\ell_{t-1} + b_{t-1}) \\
b_t &= \beta^*(\ell_t - \ell_{t-1}) + (1-\beta^*) b_{t-1}
\end{aligned}
\]
Holt’s method has a lower training RMSE than SES for both paperback and hardcover sales (paperback: 31.14 vs 33.64; hardcover: 27.19 vs 31.93). However, Holt’s linear method estimates two more parameters than SES, so it should always fit the training data at least as well. Training RMSE does not tell us how well a model will perform out-of-sample. Although SES is just an updating rule, ses() and holt() fit the corresponding state-space models (ETS(A,N,N) and ETS(A,A,N)) with normal errors, so both have a likelihood. This means the models can be compared using AICc, which penalises the additional parameters and is more informative about which model to choose.

Both series have an upward trend, but the AICc gives different answers for the two. For hardcover sales, Holt’s method has a clearly lower AICc than SES (312.7 vs 316.8), even after the penalty for its two extra parameters. The trend is strong enough that SES’s fitted values lag behind it, so its one-step-ahead errors are larger. For paperback sales, SES has a slightly lower AICc (319.9 vs 320.8). The paperback series is noisier, so the small improvement in fit from accounting for the trend in the data is not worth the two extra parameters. However, since the difference in AICc is less than 1, there is no real evidence that one method is better than the other for paperback sales. Overall, Holt’s method is preferred for the hardcover series and SES for paperback sales but with only 30 days of data it is not reliable for long-term forecasting.

title: Exponential Smoothing
text:
In error-correction form, SES and Holt’s method are state-space models with a single source of error:
\[
\begin{aligned}
y_t &= \ell_{t-1} + b_{t-1} + e_t, \qquad e_t \sim N(0, \sigma^2) \\
\ell_t &= \ell_{t-1} + b_{t-1} + \alpha e_t \\
b_t &= b_{t-1} + \alpha\beta^* e_t
\end{aligned}
\]
For SES, \(b_t = 0\) and \(\beta^* = 0\).


Code
# Function to simulate from SES or Holt's method:
# n:   no. observations 
# par: parameters 
sim_fxn = function(n, par) {
  l     = par$l0
  b     = par$b0
  y     = numeric(n)
  level = numeric(n)
  
  for (t in 1:n) {
    e        = rnorm(1, 0, par$sigma)
    y[t]     = l + b + e                        # observation equation
    l        = l + b + par$alpha * e            # level
    b        = b + par$alpha * par$beta * e     # trend
    level[t] = l
  }
  list(y = ts(y), level = level)
}






Code
set.seed(2026)

# True parameters:
p_ses = list(alpha = 0.4, beta = 0, l0 = 3, b0 = 0, sigma = 0.5)

# Simulate:
sim_ses = sim_fxn(n = 100, par = p_ses)
y_ses = sim_ses$y

# Estimate with optim() and ses():
fit_sim = optim(par = c(0.5, y_ses[1]), 
                fn = my_sse, 
                y = y_ses,
                method = "L-BFGS-B", 
                lower = c(0.0001, -Inf), 
                upper = c(0.9999, Inf))
ses_sim = ses(y_ses)

kable(data.frame(

title: Exponential Smoothing
text:
Question: How do different prediction intervals differ and what are their sources of uncertainty?
I used the simulated SES series from Question 5, fitting each method to the first 80 observations and forecasting 10 steps ahead.


Under the ETS(A,N,N) model, \(y_t = \ell_{t-1} + e_t\) with \(e_t \sim N(0, \sigma^2)\) independent. Given \(\alpha\), \(\ell_0\) and \(y_{1:t-1}\), the level \(\ell_{t-1}\) is known, so \(y_t \mid y_{1:t-1} \sim N(\ell_{t-1}, \sigma^2)\). Writing the joint density as a product of these conditional densities gives the likelihood
\[
L(\alpha, \ell_0, \sigma; \boldsymbol{y}) = \prod_{t=1}^{T} \frac{1}{\sigma}\,\phi\!\left(\frac{e_t}{\sigma}\right), \qquad e_t = y_t - \ell_{t-1},
\]
where \(\phi\) is the standard normal density and \(e_t\) depends on \((\alpha, \ell_0)\) through the SES recursion. The priors are \(\alpha \sim \text{Uniform}(0, 1)\) and flat priors on \(\ell_0\) and \(\log\sigma\).
A random walk Metropolis-Hastings algorithm is used to sample from the posterior. The random walk steps are drawn from a multivariate normal distribution, which has support over the entire real line, whereas \(\alpha \in (0, 1)\) and \(\sigma > 0\). Therefore, the parameters are mapped to the real line using
\[
\phi_1 = \text{logit}(\alpha), \qquad \phi_2 = \ell_0, \qquad \phi_3 = \log\sigma,
\]
and the random walk is performed over \(\boldsymbol{\phi} = (\phi_1, \phi_2, \phi_3)\), with proposals \(\boldsymbol{\phi}^* = \boldsymbol{\phi} + \boldsymbol{e}\). Since we sample \(\boldsymbol{\phi}\) rather than \(\boldsymbol{\theta} = (\alpha, \ell_0, \sigma)\), the Jacobian of the transformation must be included in the log posterior. The flat prior on \(\log\sigma\) is already defined on the transformed scale, so only \(\alpha\) needs a Jacobian:
\[
\log p(\boldsymbol{\phi}) = \log L(\alpha, \ell_0, \sigma; \boldsymbol{y}) + \log\{\alpha(1-\alpha)\} + \text{const}.
\]
Since the proposal is symmetric, \(\boldsymbol{\phi}^*\) is accepted with probability \(\min\{1, \exp[\log p(\boldsymbol{\phi}^*) - \log p(\boldsymbol{\phi})]\}\). The steps are initially drawn from \(\boldsymbol{e} \sim N(\boldsymbol{0}, 0.5^2\,\mathbf{I}_3)\). The first 3 000 iterations are a burn-in, and the covariance matrix \(\Sigma\) of the transformed parameters is estimated from the last 1 500 of these. The retained draws then use \(\boldsymbol{e} \sim N\left(\boldsymbol{0}, \frac{2.38^2}{3}\Sigma\right)\) (Roberts et al., 1997). The chain starts at the ses() estimates.
Each retained draw \((\alpha^{(j)}, \ell_0^{(j)}, \sigma^{(j)})\) is then used to compute \(\ell_T^{(j)}\) and simulate one future path from the state-space model. This gives draws from the posterior predictive distribution of \(y_{T+1}, \ldots, y_{T+h}\).


Code
# 1. SES log-likelihood: 
SES_Log_Likelihood = function(y, alpha, l0, sigma) {
  e   = ses_fxn(y, alpha, l0)$residuals
  out = sum(dnorm(e, 0, sigma, log = TRUE))
  if (!is.finite(out)) -Inf else out
}

# 2. Parameter transforms: 
to_real = function(theta) {
  c(qlogis(theta[1]), theta[2], log(theta[3]))
}

from_real = function(phi) {
  c(plogis(phi[1]), phi[2], exp(phi[3]))
}

# 3. Log posterior on the transformed scale (priors + Jacobian):
log_target = function(phi, y) {
  theta = from_real(phi)
  ll    = SES_Log_Likelihood(y, theta[1], theta[2], theta[3])
  if (!is.finite(ll)) return(-Inf)

  # Note: flat priors on l0 and log(sigma) only add a constant
  # Uniform(0, 1) prior on alpha x logit Jacobian:
  lp_alpha = plogis(phi[1], log.p = TRUE) + plogis(-phi[1], log.p = TRUE)

  ll + lp_alpha
}

# 4. Metropolis-Hastings loop:
mh_run = function(phi, jitters, y) {
  n         = nrow(jitters)
  cur       = log_target(phi, y)
  phi_draws = matrix(NA, n, 3)
  accepted  = logical(n)

  for (i in seq_len(n)) {
    prop      = phi + jitters[i, ]
    prop_val  = log_target(prop, y)
    log_alpha = if (is.finite(prop_val)) min(0, prop_val - cur) else -Inf

    if (log(runif(1)) < log_alpha) {
      phi         = prop
      cur         = prop_val
      accepted[i] = TRUE
    }
    phi_draws[i, ] = phi
  }
  list(phi_draws = phi_draws, last = phi, accept_rate = mean(accepted))
}

# 5. Two-phase sampler: 
# Phase 1: burn-in with isotropic jitter, Sigma = covariance of later burn-in draws
# Phase 2: retained iterations with proposals ~ N(0, scale * Sigma)
MH_SES = function(y, init, iterations = 20000, burn = 3000, burn_sd = 0.5,
                  cov_frac = 0.5, scale = 2.38^2/3) {
  phi0 = to_real(init)

  # Phase 1:
  burn_jit = rmvnorm(burn, mean = rep(0, 3), sigma = burn_sd^2 * diag(3))
  b        = mh_run(phi0, burn_jit, y)
  keep     = seq.int(floor(burn * (1 - cov_frac)) + 1, burn)
  Sigma    = cov(b$phi_draws[keep, , drop = FALSE])

  # Phase 2:
  main_jit = rmvnorm(iterations, mean = rep(0, 3), sigma = scale * Sigma)
  m        = mh_run(b$last, main_jit, y)

  draws = t(apply(m$phi_draws, 1, from_real))
  colnames(draws) = c("alpha", "l0", "sigma")
  
  list(
    draws = draws, 
    burn_accept = b$accept_rate, 
    accept_rate = m$accept_rate)
}


As a check on my sample, I also fitted the same model in Stan (Carpenter et al., 2017) to sample from the posterior. Stan uses the No-U-Turn Sampler (NUTS), an adaptive form of Hamiltonian Monte Carlo that uses the gradient of the log posterior to propose new points. The parameters block restricts \(\alpha\) to \((0, 1)\) and \(\sigma\) to \((0, \infty)\), and Stan maps them to the real line and includes the Jacobian automatically. The model block runs the SES recursion, with \(y_t \sim N(\ell_{t-1}, \sigma^2)\) at each step. The generated quantities block computes \(\ell_T\) for each posterior draw and simulates one future path from the state-space model, which gives draws from the posterior predictive distribution of \(y_{T+1}, \ldots, y_{T+h}\).


Code
# SES model written in Stan:
modelString = "
  data {
    int<lower=1> N;                   // number of observations
    vector[N] y;                      // time series
    int<lower=1> N_new;               // forecast horizon
  }

  parameters {
    real<lower=0, upper=1> alpha;     // smoothing parameter
    real l0;                          // initial level
    real<lower=0> sigma;              // error standard deviation
  }

  model {
    real level = l0;

    // Priors (flat priors on l0 and sigma):
    alpha ~ uniform(0, 1);
    target += -log(sigma);            // flat prior on log(sigma)

    // Likelihood: one-step-ahead errors are iid N(0, sigma^2)
    for (t in 1:N) {
      y[t] ~ normal(level, sigma);
      level = level + alpha * (y[t] - level);
    }
  }

  generated quantities {
    real level_T;
    vector[N_new] y_new;

    // Final level for this draw:
    {
      real level = l0;
      for (t in 1:N) level = level + alpha * (y[t] - level);
      level_T = level;
    }

    // One future path from the state-space model:
    {
      real lev = level_T;
      for (h in 1:N_new) {
        real e = normal_rng(0, sigma);
        y_new[h] = lev + e;
        lev = lev + alpha * e;
      }
    }
  }
"







Code
n_tr    = 80
h_max   = 10
y_train = window(y_ses, end = n_tr)
y_test  = window(y_ses, start = n_tr + 1, end = n_tr + h_max)

# 1. Normal intervals from ses():
fc_norm = ses(y_train, h = h_max, level = 95)

# 2. Manual normal intervals: 
a_hat        = fc_norm$model$par["alpha"]
res          = as.numeric(residuals(fc_norm))
sig2_hat     = sum(res^2)/(n_tr-2)
sd_h         = sqrt(sig2_hat*(1+a_hat^2*(1:h_max-1)))
manual_lower = fc_norm$mean-qnorm(0.975)*sd_h
manual_upper = fc_norm$mean+qnorm(0.975)*sd_h

# 3. Bootstrapped residuals: 
set.seed(2026)
B      = 5000
lev    = rep(fc_norm$mean[1], B)         
y_boot = matrix(NA, B, h_max)

for (k in 1:h_max) {
  e           = sample(res, size = B, replace = TRUE)
  y_boot[, k] = lev + e
  lev         = lev + a_hat * e
}
boot_pi = apply(y_boot, 2, quantile, probs = c(0.025, 0.975))

# 4. forecast():
fc_fboot = forecast(fc_norm$model, h = h_max, level = 95,
                    bootstrap = TRUE, simulate = TRUE, npaths = 5000)

# 5. Bayesian posterior predictive:
set.seed(2026)
init   = c(fc_norm$model$par["alpha"], fc_norm$model$par["l"], sqrt(fc_norm$model$sigma2))
fit_mh = MH_SES(y_train, init = init)

alpha_d = fit_mh$draws[, "alpha"]
l0_d    = fit_mh$draws[, "l0"]
sigma_d = fit_mh$draws[, "sigma"]

# One future path per posterior draw:
n_d = nrow(fit_mh$draws)
y_bayes = matrix(NA, n_d, h_max)
level_T = numeric(n_d)

for (j in 1:n_d) {
  lev_j      = ses_fxn(y_train, alpha_d[j], l0_d[j])$forecast  
  level_T[j] = lev_j
  
  for (k in 1:h_max) {
    e             = rnorm(1, 0, sigma_d[j])
    y_bayes[j, k] = lev_j + e
    lev_j         = lev_j + alpha_d[j] * e
  }
}
bayes_pi = apply(y_bayes, 2, quantile, probs = c(0.025, 0.975))

# 6. Bayesian posterior predictive (Stan):
rstan_options(auto_write = TRUE)

stan_mod  = stan_model(model_code = modelString)
stan_data = list(N = n_tr, y = as.numeric(y_train), N_new = h_max)

stanFit = sampling(stan_mod,
                   data    = stan_data,
                   chains  = 3,
                   iter    = 6000,
                   warmup  = 1000,
                   seed    = 2026,
                   refresh = 0)

post_stan     = rstan::extract(stanFit)
bayes_pi_stan = apply(post_stan$y_new, 2, quantile, probs = c(0.025, 0.975))

# True values (from simulation):
lev_true = sim_ses$level[n_tr]
sd_true  = p_ses$sigma * sqrt(1 + p_ses$alpha^2 * (1:h_max - 1))
